  [seed runner](#seed-runner-in-ci), 3,000 ops in a text form (`put aa v26x`, `del aa`, `delrange a ab`,
  `flush`, `flushfail 3`, `floor aca`), drawn by weight: puts 35, removals 10, range removals 3,
  gets 15, floors 8, scans 5, views 11 (open 2, get 5, scan 2, close 2), flushes 5, failed flushes 1,
  compactions 4, restarts 1; keys of 1-6 letters a-f, a put's key new one time in four, a range
  removal half the time over every key with its start as prefix. With `Check` on, every set's
  history equals the map model's line by line (Pebble's `internal/metamorphic`, a7b8321871e3).
  The 13 sets take about 4 s for 20 seeds on an Apple M4 Pro; seeds 0-10,002 passed once with
  the change that added the test, and seeds 0-199 with the filter sets.

  | Set | Pieces | Flushes | Compaction | Other |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | F | 1 MiB | none: memtable only, a restart replays every write | none | |
  | A | 1 MiB | the generated ones | the generated ones, installed at once | |
  | B | 4 KiB | generated, and after every 40 writes | after every flush until none is due | |
  | C | 256 B | generated, and after every 10 writes | never | |
  | D | 512 B | generated, and after every 25 writes | picked at an op, installed between the pieces of the next flush, or at the next compact op if that comes first | up to 4 ops, writes and reads, between a flush's pieces |
  | E | 1 KiB | every flush fails after one piece first; also after every 30 writes | eager | a restart after every flush that finds no view open |
  | G | 4 KiB | after every 2 writes | only after every 40th flush | |
  | Two merges | 1 KiB | after every 3 writes | after every 8th flush, two merges of disjoint adjacent runs picked at once, installed newest last | |
  | Fixed limit | 1 KiB | after every 5 writes | eager, with a fixed run limit of 4 against the auto-tuned one | |
  | Point removals | 4 KiB | after every 20 writes | eager | each range removal replaced by the point removals of the keys it covers (Pebble's `replace_single_delete`) |
  | Linear merge | 1 KiB | after every 15 writes | eager | scans, flushes and merges compare every layer at every step instead of keeping the heap, so the flush's and merge's drop counts and reads during a flush meet the reference too; up to 4 ops between a flush's pieces |
  | Filters off | 256 B | as C | as C | lookups probe no run filter and search every run (`Config.Probe = FiltersOff`) |
  | Filters maybe | 256 B | as C | as C | lookups probe every run filter and take each answer as "maybe" (`FiltersMaybe`) |

- Each set reaches the extreme it is there for on seed 0: F never flushes, C keeps over 100 runs
  and G 40, E fails flushes and restarts more than A, D installs merges while a memtable is frozen,
  Two merges runs two at once, Fixed limit compacts, and Filters off and Filters maybe search more
  layers than C ([Filter option sets](#filter-option-sets)).
- [property] The chunk index's `TestMetamorphic` (`internal/chunkstore`): seeds 0-19 in `go test`, 1,000
  ops drawn by weight: writes 30, punches 6, whole-chunk punches 1, cuts 2, releases of frozen
  versions 2, cleaner moves 8, reads of blocks live 12 and at a snapshot epoch 10, chunk entries 3,
  `FrozenAt` 3, live counts per record 4, `Check` 2, and the structural ops as above. Writes and
  punches cover 1-4 blocks (one in eight up to 16) of blocks 0-15 of 4 chunks, a chunk's in version
  order; a freeze of the chunk's newest version (version 0 if it has none) goes before its first
  write after each cut; a move copies one block a live or frozen map holds. Every op names its record's LBA, so
  histories are comparable, and a move is logged and replayed after a restart as the cleaner's copy
  record will be. The model is per chunk an entry, a live map and frozen maps, block by block. The
  tree is configured by `TreeConfig`, so its filters hold chunk prefixes as in production. The
  sets are internal/lsm's but Linear merge, with the pieces of C, Filters off and Filters maybe
  512 bytes, since a 256-byte root lists 13 pieces, fewer than a flush of 10 index writes takes;
  Point removals sets the index's own point-removal switch, so range trims read as point removals.
  A seed costs about 0.2 s over the 12 sets on an Apple M4 Pro; at 3,000 ops about 4 s, as runs
  pile up to 300 under C and Two merges. Seed 0 holds an absent freeze, a whole-chunk punch, a
  move that changes a map, a release and a read that finds a frozen version. Seeds 0-10,001
  passed once with the change that added the test, and seeds 0-299 with the filter sets.
- Planted bugs, each one line behind a test switch in `internal/lsm` and run with `Check` off so
  the history diff alone finds them, fail at least one seed of 20 under the set each is checked
  under, and the failing seed differs from set F too:

  | Bug | Checked under | The spike found it under |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | A flush drops every removal, even one hiding a key in an older run | A | every set with flushes |
  | A merge's output is installed as the oldest run | B | G only |
  | A restore loads runs in the order the manifest lists them, not by age | E | every set with restarts |
  | Reads skip the frozen memtable | D | the sets that read while a memtable is frozen: A, B, D, E |
  | A merge drops removals that hide keys in runs older than its inputs | B | G only |

  The merge bugs show under more sets here than in the spike: with Two merges, Fixed limit and the
  universal picker, merges leave older runs out under every set that merges but G. G no longer
  does: its runs of two writes are mostly filter, so the picker sees runs of one size and merges
  them all.

- A set's "after every n writes" counts the writes since the last flush began, writes run between
  that flush's pieces included, so no flush is skipped when those writes cross a multiple of n:
  with n = 2 and one write between a flush op's pieces, the next write flushes
  (`TestRunFlushEveryCountsAbsorbedWrites`).
- A failing seed prints its replay command and its ops reduced to the fewest that still fail, as a
  data-driven case; a case whose cadence comes from its set is rewritten with explicit ops before it
  goes under `testdata/regressions`, before the fix. The planted flush bug's first failure on seed
  0 reduces from 80 ops to under 10 (5: `put f v27xx`, `flush`, `del f`, `flush`, `scan f 4`).
- Regression cases (`internal/lsm/testdata/regressions`), each also run against the model: from the
  spike, `put aa v26x`, `flush`, `del aa`, `flush`, `floor aca` gives none, and fails with the
  planted flush bug; `put e v30xxx`, `flush`, `del e`, `flushfail 3`, `flush`, `restart`, `floor e`
  gives none. The chunk index's (`internal/chunkstore/testdata/regressions`): a chunk first written
  after a cut reads absent at the snapshot before and after a restart that replays its absent
  freeze, and a move after the restart changes only the live map and moves the record's live count.
- A malformed ops line (an unknown op, a wrong argument count, a range whose start is not below
  its end, a non-numeric count, a failed flush of 0 pieces, a chunk-index block outside blocks 0-15
  that is not a whole-chunk punch) is an error naming its line.

## Run filters

Lookups:

- A get of a key in no run searches only the memtables and the runs whose filter lets it through
  and whose first and last keys bracket it; each run keeps its last key.
- Filters are probed newest first: a key in the newest run probes no older run's filter, and a
  covering fragment in a newer run stops the get before any older filter is probed.
- A floor inside a chunk written whole searches only the run holding it, plus false positives.
- A floor bounded to a prefix equals a plain floor plus the prefix check, and a prefix scan equals a
  plain scan cut at the prefix's last key, under the range-removal property with prefix filters
  (prefixes alone, and whole keys with prefixes).
- A filter never holds fragments: with one run holding fragment [c, f) and its filter ruling out
  d, a get of d, which an older run holds, is absent (RocksDB returned such keys twice,
  `HISTORY.md:1451`, `:2783` at v11.8.1).

Filter build and layout:

- A flush sizes its filter partition from the frozen memtable's entry count (twice it for whole keys
  with prefixes) and fills it as the run streams out; a merge step sizes its partition from the keys
  it wrote, plus one for its fence's prefix, once its blocks are built. For 1,000,000 keys at 10 bits per key, Pebble's writer rounds 10,000,000 bits up to
  19,532 lines of 64 bytes, then to the odd 19,533: 1,250,112 bytes plus a 5-byte trailer. The
  flush's peak is the frozen tree, one piece, the run and the filter, and its allocations do not grow
  with the entry count.
- A prefix filter holds each distinct prefix once, so a chunk's extents add one key; a filter of
  whole keys and prefixes holds each key and each prefix that is not a whole key.
- It follows the run's entries and range removals in pieces of its own, marked in the trailer, as
  partitions: each the filter's length, the filter, headed by what it holds (whole keys, prefixes
  or both) and its key count, then a fence flag, length and key. A flush or a merge in one step
  writes one unfenced partition; a merge in steps one per step, each fenced by its step's bound but
  the last. The run golden bytes cover an entry piece, a fragment piece and the filter piece, one
  unfenced partition, as root, and a fenced partition's bytes are golden too. Decoding partitions
  refuses an unfenced partition before the last, fences out of order, a bad flag and any truncation
  but at a partition's end (fuzzed, and with the run loaders). A run with no filter,
  a truncated one, or entries or fragments after it is Malformed on load, and so is a run whose
  filter holds other keys than the tree's `Config.Filter` (fuzzed with the run loader). A restore
  loads each run's filter from its pieces without hashing a key, and lookups search as before the
  restart.
- The port carries Pebble's BSD notice and its tests (`sstable/tablefilters/bloom` at
  a7b8321871e3): the filter of "hello" and "world" encodes to RocksDB's golden bits, the hash
  matches RocksDB's vectors, and every added key may match. Over 1,000,000 absent random 16-byte
  keys, a 10 bits-per-key filter's false positives stay within 1.0 to 1.4% (1.17% measured, 1.16%
  in the read path spike).
- Every run has a filter, the oldest one included.
- Each run's filter has a checksum beside its blocks': a flipped filter bit fails the next merge of
  the run and a flush that rewrites it with `ErrCheck`. With `Config.Check`, a flush checks that its
  filter holds every key of each entry block it built; a planted filter that leaves a key out
  panics there.
- A prefix is closed: every key that starts with a prefix has that prefix, and a key too short for
  one has none. The property tests' 3-byte prefix gives none to shorter keys, and probes of 1 and 2
  bytes run as plain floors and scans; a prefix of at most 3 bytes, which breaks the rule, fails
  them.

What each index's filter holds (`Config.Filter` and `Config.Prefix`):

| Index | Filter holds | Lookup that probes it | Probes with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chunk index | each chunk's prefix `(pool, h, chunk_id)`, 28 bytes, one key per chunk, and each record count's whole key | floor bounded to a chunk's prefix, prefix scan, get | the prefix, once per lookup |
| MetaStore | whole keys and each key's inode prefix `fs/{volume}/{inode}` | get; prefix scan of one inode (`readdir`) | the key; the prefix |
| An index with whole keys only | whole keys | get | the key |

Targets (the [LSM read path spike](../spikes/lsm-study-reads/) over 24 runs, about 2 million
entries; counts are the bar, times on the shared VM):

| Lookup | Runs searched | Time (spike) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MetaStore get of an absent name | at most 0.5 on average (0.22 measured; 0.03 in the package's test) | 1.9 µs against 13.3 µs unfiltered |
| Chunk-index read of a chunk written whole | about 1.18 (1.01 in the package's test) | 5.1 µs against 31.5 µs |
| Chunk-index read of an unwritten chunk | about 0.19 (0.01 in the package's test) | 1.35 µs against 30.5 µs |
| Chunk-index read under random 4 KiB overwrites | about 7.2 (every large run holds every hot chunk) | 19.8 µs against 33.2 µs |
| Filter memory | 0.76% of the chunk index's run bytes, 2.6 to 2.9% of the MetaStore's | |

- Every probe, get and prefix floor allocates nothing.

## Filter option sets

- Both indexes' metamorphic tests (`TestMetamorphic` in `internal/lsm` and `internal/chunkstore`)
  pass under two more option sets with C's cadence: Filters off, whose lookups probe no run filter,
  and Filters maybe, whose every probe answers "maybe" (`lsm.Config.Probe`). The chunk index's
  runs under every set hold its chunk-prefix filters.
- On seed 0, in both indexes, both sets search the same number of layers, more than C; Filters
  off probes no filter, and Filters maybe probes as many as C (`Tree.FilterProbes`), so a Filters
  maybe that skips its probes fails (`TestMetamorphicOpsCoverTheIndex`,
  `TestMetamorphicSetsReachTheirExtremes`).

## Chunk reader

- A read of blocks 3, 4 and 700 of one chunk takes one reader: it probes the filters once with the
  chunk's prefix and serves 4 by stepping forward from 3, as Pebble's `TrySeekUsingNext` does, and
  allocates nothing.
- A read of ascending blocks searches each layer once, then steps; a block exactly 16 entries past
  a layer's candidate steps, and one 17 past, or below it, searches that layer again.
- A reader read after the index changes panics under `Check`.
- [property] The reader reads every block as the per-block lookup does, live and at snapshot
  epochs, with range or point removals, with filters on and off: the range-removal property's
  readers, the metamorphic tests' lookups (each read ascending, then its first block again) and the
  fuzzed index. In `internal/lsm`, one iterator's prefix floors over every probe, ascending with a
  prefix seek between, then descending, equal the map model under the range-removal property.

## Heap merge

- A scan merges the memtables and runs with a min-heap, as Pebble's `mergingIter` does. Review: a
  scan step over 24 runs costs less than twice the step over 6 (`BenchmarkIterNextRuns` on the
  Apple M4 Pro: 41 against 61 ns, where the linear merge took 54 against 151), and a seek and a step
  allocate nothing.
- Ties: when several sources hold one key, the newest layer's entry is returned once and the
  others are stepped past; a removal in the newest layer hides the key.
- A scan of n steps that crosses k fragments of one layer does at most k + 1 fragment searches in
  that layer, checked with a search counter.
- [property] Scans forward from every probe, plain and bounded to a prefix, equal the map model
  over the range-removal property's seeds (0-59) under its seven configurations; the metamorphic
  tests run scans under every option set.
- A seek and the 20 steps after it allocate nothing over 24 runs with range removals.
- [property] The heap merge and the linear merge, kept for tests, return identical scans from the
  start and up to 8 steps from every probe, and bounded from every other one, every 300 ops of the
  range-removal property's seeds (0-59) under its seven configurations. The metamorphic tests
  extend this to flushes, merges and reads during a flush with their Linear merge option set.
- A scan over one source (memtable only) and over zero runs works, and a scan that exhausts
  every source reports the end once.

## Absent freeze

- The "Chunk index" seed 22 property stays as it is: its epochs count freezes of chunks already written, with no
  volume cut, so reading a never-frozen chunk as live is right there. E3 below is the regression
  with volume cuts.

Scenarios (records fed to the index):

- A record with freeze(chunk 9, v0, epoch 1) and a 1-block write v1 leaves chunk 9's entry at v1,
  epoch 1, and a read at epoch 1 finds nothing. A second record at epoch 1, a write v2 with no
  freeze, follows. After cut 2, a record freezes v2 at epoch 2: a read at epoch 1 still finds
  nothing, and one at epoch 2 finds v2. Each record applied again changes nothing.
- A record with freeze(chunk 9, v0, epoch 1) and a punch v1 records the chunk absent at epoch 1,
  as a write would: a read at epoch 1 finds nothing, a live read zeros.

The chunk epochs spike's cases are regression tests. The index at 676095b refused a freeze of
version 0 outright; the column below is what it read when the writer left that freeze out:

| Case | Steps | Index at 676095b | With the absent freeze |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E1 | cut 1; write v1 (block 0, with freeze v0 at epoch 1); write v2 (block 1); read snapshot 1 | snapshot 1 reads v1 | snapshot 1 reads nothing |
| E2 | cut 1; write v1 (freeze v0, epoch 1); cut 2; write v2 (freeze v1, epoch 2) | snapshot 1 reads v1 | snapshot 1 reads nothing; snapshot 2 reads v1 |
| E3 [property] | seeds 0-49 (PCG(seed, 10)), 400 steps: a cut one time in 10, otherwise a 1- to 4-block write or, one time in six, a punch, over 4 chunks of 16 blocks | 35 of 50 seeds read a snapshot wrong | 0 of 50; a rebuild from the records and the records applied twice equal the index |

- The absent version is an empty frozen map under `(…, 0)` holding its freeze epoch. `LookupAt`
  at an epoch it covers reads a miss, not zeros and not the live map.
- It is listed among the chunk's frozen versions, before any other.
- Cleaner moves skip it: a move of block 3 of chunk 9 changes the live map and real frozen
  versions only, and the absent version stays empty.
- A freeze of version 0 replayed for a chunk that now exists and holds the absent marker changes
  nothing (replay after a restart applies the same record again).
- Releasing a frozen version belongs to the snapshot deletion sweep ([Deletion](design.md#snapshots-and-clones)),
  which has no index operation yet. When it lands: releasing the absent version removes no keys,
  the live map reads as before, and a record with that freeze of version 0, replayed after the
  release, changes nothing and is never refused.
- A chunk with a tombstone has a version, so the first write after a cut freezes the tombstone's
  version, not version 0: a read at that snapshot returns zeros, not a miss.

## Single-node ChunkStore

The byte-range oracle applies every acknowledged write's and punch's bytes in version order;
after every step, every block, live and at every snapshot epoch, must equal it. A chunk is 1,024
blocks. "Pending" is a write whose record is not yet durable. Tests feed requests and disk
completions to `chunkstore.Store` and read the records it writes back from the disk actions.

Byte ranges to whole blocks:

| Operation (chunk C, empty unless stated) | Logged | Read back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Write(off 0, 4,096 B of 0x11) | one whole block, no base read | block 0 = 0x11 |
| Write(off 100, 1 B 0x22) | block 0 merged with zeros | zeros except byte 100 |
| Write(off 4,000, 200 B) | blocks 0 and 1, both merged | bytes 4,000-4,199 set, rest zeros |
| Write(off 3 × 4,096 + 10, 3 × 4,096 B) | 4 blocks: 2 merged edges, 2 whole | exact range |
| Punch(off 0, 8,192) | one punch entry, blocks 0-1 | zeros |
| Punch(off 100, 8,192) over written blocks 0-2 | one version: block 1 a punch entry, blocks 0 and 2 merged with zeros as write entries, 2 base reads | 100..8,291 zeros, the rest unchanged |
| Punch(off 0, 4 MiB) | whole-chunk punch, tombstone | zeros; the chunk entry stays with the new version |
| Punch of a chunk that does not exist | nothing; version 0 | zeros |
| Read(off 100, 10 B) of a written block | | those 10 bytes |
| Read of a chunk never written | | zeros, and no chunk entry |
| Write after a tombstone | the version continues past the tombstone's | the written bytes, other blocks zeros |

API edges (`TestAPIEdges`):

- A write or punch running past 4 MiB, and a zero-length write, punch or read, is refused with
  `ErrRange` and no disk action; the store frees a refused write's buffer.
- A punch returns its new version; a punch of a chunk with no version returns 0.
- `expectVer` = 0 on an absent chunk creates it; on an existing chunk it fails with `ErrVersion`.
- `Seal` returns `ErrSeal`.

Merging against the newest ordered version (the [sub-block writes spike](../spikes/sub-block-writes/)):

- W1 = Write(off 0, 10 B 'a') pending, then W2 = Write(off 5, 10 B 'b'): W2's base is W1's
  pending block, with no base read, so the block reads `aaaaabbbbbbbbbb` then zeros.
- [property] M1 and M9 as a regression bar: seeds 0-499, 400 steps, two clients with 8 writes
  pipelined each, 1 byte to 3 blocks at random offsets in 4 blocks: 0 seeds wrong. Merging
  against the committed version instead (M2, a plant) loses bytes on each of seeds 0-19.
- A base read from disk checks the block's CRC32C. A base that fails it, or whose read fails
  with Io, is never merged: the write fails with `ErrBadChecksum` or the disk's error, logs
  nothing, and the chunk's next write goes on; a read of that block fails the same way.
- A base read in flight holds the chunk's later operations: W1 partial (base on disk), then W2
  whole-block to the same block, then W3 to another chunk. W3's round goes out at once; no record
  of C is written before W1's base read completes, W2 is ordered after W1, and the block ends as
  W2.

Versions (32-bit interval over a 32-bit counter):

| State | Next write's version |
| --- | --- |
| Chunk with no version, local interval 1 | (1, 1) = 0x0000000100000001 |
| Chunk at (1, 7) committed; at (1, 6) with (1, 7) pending | (1, 8) |
| Chunk at (1, 0xFFFFFFFF) | the local interval is raised: (2, 1) |
| Another chunk at (1, 5), and a chunk with no version, after that raise | (2, 1) |

- Version 0 is the absent chunk and is never assigned.
- No two durable writes of a chunk get one version, across restarts too: the interval starts at
  1 at each open and never drops below the interval of the version it increments, so a restart
  reuses only a version no durable record holds.
- `expectVer`: compared with the newest ordered version, so with W1 pending at v, expectVer = v
  succeeds and expectVer = the committed version fails with `ErrVersion`.
- `atVer`: a read at a frozen version returns that version's bytes; a read at version 0 of a
  chunk frozen absent reads zeros; a read at a version no snapshot pins is `ErrNoVersion`.
- A read without `atVer` while W is pending issues its block reads at once and returns the
  previous version's blocks.

Commit and mapping:

- A write is mapped when its record is durable, and a chunk's writes are mapped in version order
  (the chunk epochs spike's R2 failed 200 of 200 seeds out of order), each answered when mapped.
  A lane takes items in submit order, so a 1-block W2 behind a whole-chunk W1 is durable no
  earlier than W1's last item; W2 is mapped and answered after W1, and merges against W1's
  pending block.
- Snapshot epochs on the writer side: each write and punch carries its volume's snapshot epoch.
  The first write after a cut to a chunk at version v puts freeze(v, epoch) before its blocks;
  with a pending W1 at epoch 1, W2 at epoch 2 freezes W1's version; a second write at epoch 2
  carries no freeze; a chunk with no version gets a freeze of version 0 (Absent freeze); a punch
  of a chunk with no version logs nothing; in a volume whose snapshot epoch is 0 nothing freezes.
- A write larger than one record goes as several items of one version. Group commit refuses an
  item whose record exceeds the round less one block, so with 1 MiB rounds an item holds 254 data
  blocks and a whole 4 MiB chunk goes as 5 items (254, 254, 254, 254 and 8); on the 1 GiB test
  disk (64-block rounds) an item holds 62 data blocks and a chunk takes 17 items (16 × 62 + 32),
  acknowledged once all are durable, the freeze, if any, before the first.
- While such a write is partly durable, the replay point stays at the record before its first
  item's (design.md: a replay point never passes a pending write's record).
- A crash with some of its items durable recovers them mapped under its version: the
  unacknowledged write is partly visible, and the chunk's next write takes the next version.
- A write that fails with `NoSpace` part-way stays applied as recovery would replay it, and its
  error carries its version, against which an `expectVer` write succeeds; one whose only durable
  item is its freeze gives the chunk its previous version back.
- A write merging into a block of a failed write still pending behind one in flight takes its base
  from the versions left, never the failed write's freed buffers; the live index equals a rebuild.

Events from the log:

- `Failed(NoSpace)` fails the writes it names to their callers in submit order: with only the
  reserve free, every write before the first failure succeeds and every one after it fails, and
  no buffer is left out of the pool.
- `InDoubt` items are never acknowledged: a write in flight when a flush fails reports
  `ErrInDoubt`, one queued behind it the disk's error, and the store refuses writes with
  `ErrUnavailable` until it is opened again.
- `CheckpointFailed` (no segment left): the index keeps its frozen memtable and its runs, and reads
  go on; the next checkpoint writes it again from its first piece (the "LSM tree" scenario).
- A checkpoint that finds the pool full waits for a piece buffer and finishes once one frees; the
  store keeps serving.
- A flush that fails a run check (`lsm.ErrCheck`, a plant): the store refuses operations, lets its
  rounds finish, recovers its log once more as an open does, reloading the named manifest's runs
  and replaying after them, and the rebuilt index equals the oracle's, live and at every snapshot.
  A merge that fails its check (a plant) takes the same path. A check that fails again after the
  rebuild, before any checkpoint completes (a plant failing every flush's check), stops the store
  with `lsm.ErrCheck` after one rebuild (`TestARunCheckFailingAfterARebuildStopsTheStore`).
- The store hands the log one run piece at a time, each once the one before is durable: no step
  of a workload with multi-piece runs has two pieces in flight.
- Under steady pipelined load (5,000 writes) the store's list of items handed to the log stays
  short.
- `Flush(cs)` completes at once with no disk action when nothing is pending, and otherwise once
  every write and punch to cs submitted before it is answered.

Invariants and faults (simulator): acknowledged writes readable; reads equal the byte-range
oracle live and at every snapshot; punched ranges read zeros; no two durable writes of a chunk
share a version; a live map never holds two entries for one block (`Index.Check`); a rebuilt
index equals the recovered one. Faults: crash at every action of a workload with unaligned
writes, a cut, a whole-chunk write and a checkpoint, with no unflushed block landing, a seeded
half and all of them, each recovery checked against the crash oracle's model, each chunk's entry
and every block either holds, then rebuilt; unaligned writes pipelined to one block; a merge base failing its checksum; a
failed base read; a failed flush.

Performance: `Write` of a whole block, `Write` of one byte with its base in a pending write, and
`Read` of one block report 0 allocations per operation. A merge against a pending write copies
into the write's own buffer; one against the disk reads the block and its record header block.
The cache of recently merged blocks is under [Replica primary](#replica-primary).

## Index recovery tests on the Store

The chunk index's recovery tests run through `chunkstore.Store` requests, so recovery, checkpoints
and restores are the Store's own. Their workload, on a 1 GiB simulated disk with 16-block records,
a checkpoint due every 96 blocks of records and merges running as the daemon runs them, sends
rounds of 1-4 requests over 14 chunks and settles after each: a write of 1 byte to 6 blocks within
a chunk's first 64 blocks, unaligned one time in two, a punch of such a range two times in ten, or
a punch of the whole chunk one in ten; one request in 40 first cuts, so the next write of each
chunk freezes it, absent for a chunk with no version, and two of the chunks are first written
after the first cut. Every recovery is checked against the crash oracle ([Chunk index under the
crash oracle](#chunk-index-under-the-crash-oracle)). Each merge here finishes in one step, so no
recovery lands between two steps of a merge, with its inputs bounded; `TestTwoMergesRunAtOnce`
([Cleaner](#cleaner)) restarts there, and a recovery that drops a bounded input run fails it.

- [property] Seeds 0-3, 200 in `scripts/seeds.sh`, three generations of 150 rounds
  (`TestRecoveryAndRebuildEqualLiveIndex`): after each, recovery from the manifest's runs plus
  replay, and then a rebuild from every record header, as a failed run check starts, both equal
  the live index, and each give the pools' live blocks the store kept. On its own four seeds every recovery loads runs and replays records past its
  manifest, and every seed writes multi-piece runs, carries runs, merges and cuts; a widened run
  checks only the equalities.
- A lost checkpoint carrying merge output (seeds 0-3, `TestCrashBetweenRunAndManifest`): after
  three manifests, the first checkpoint that writes a merge step's pieces to a merge worker's lane
  is crashed once its manifest record is durable and before any segment header names it. Recovery
  loads an earlier manifest, without the step's output, plus replay, and the next checkpoint's
  restart recovers from a later one to the live index.
- A write's freeze kept and its blocks lost: at cut 1, a write of twice a record's blocks to chunk
  c, behind a write of one block less than a record to another chunk, logs c's freeze in a record
  ahead of its blocks, and a crash at one of the next 12 actions, nothing unflushed landing, keeps
  the freeze and loses the blocks.
  - c never written (`TestAbsentOnlyChunkRecovers`): c is left frozen absent, at version 0 and
    epoch 1, and recovers by replay, and after two checkpoints from a run, as the crash oracle's
    model.
  - c holding 0x11 at v1 (`TestRefreezeAfterLostWrite`): c is left at v1 frozen at epoch 1. After
    the next write, 0x44 at cut 2, which freezes v1 again, and a restart, the snapshot at cut 2
    reads 0x11, and c's entry and v1's freeze carry epoch 2. An index that kept v1's first freeze
    epoch read 0x44 there, and `TestRecoveriesMatchTheCrashOracle` caught it on seed 3.
- Planted bugs: replay that drops block-range punches fails these tests and the crash oracle's
  property, as it fails `TestCrashAtEveryActionWithCleaning`.

## Segment reserve

The reserve, ⌈(2 × `max_replay_bytes` + merge workers × `compaction_step_bytes`) ÷ segment⌉ +
victims per pass (4, as in the cleaner spikes), at least 8, with both byte settings at 64 MiB
(`ReserveSegments`):

| Disk | Segment | Merge workers | Reserve |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 GiB and up | 64 MiB | 1 | 3 + 4 = 7 by the formula; 8, the floor |
| 256 GiB and up | 64 MiB | 2 | 4 + 4 = 8 |
| 255 GiB | 32 MiB | 1 | 6 + 4 = 10 |
| 1 GiB | 256 KiB | 1 | 768 + 4 = 772 of 4,096 |

- A reserve of every usable segment or more (3 on a 16-block disk) is BadConfig: Format refuses it
  and leaves nothing allocated, and open of a formatted disk fails recovery with BadConfig before it
  reads a segment header. The small disks of the tests set the reserve directly.
- Full disk waits: a 16-block disk (3 usable 4-block segments) with a reserve of 1 and a cleaner
  that has a victim. Two 2-block writes fill segments 1 and 2 (LBAs 4 and 8); a third is held:
  `Stalled`, no disk action, its buffer kept. A checkpoint's 10-byte piece still
  opens the reserve segment (segment header and the 2-block record, LBAs 12-14); its manifest finds
  no segment free and waits. Once segments 1 and 2 are freed (a test hook standing in for the
  cleaner), the held write goes into segment 1 and the manifest into segment 2, the checkpoint
  completes, and nothing failed.
- A checkpoint finishes in the reserve: a 32-block disk (7 usable segments) with a reserve of 2.
  Five 2-block writes fill segments 1 to 5 and a sixth write is held; the checkpoint's piece and
  manifest go into segments 6 and 7 of the metadata stream and it completes, while the held write
  stays held. A cold punch is held too, since the cold lane would have to open a segment of the
  reserve. When the owner reports no victim (`FailStalled`), both fail with NoSpace, one Failed
  event per stream (hot, then cold), and their buffers are freed.
- A merge piece opens a segment of the reserve as the checkpoint's items do: on that disk with
  five 2-block writes in segments 1 to 5 and a sixth write held, a merge piece goes into segment 6
  and the write stays held, `Stalled` but not `CheckpointStalled`, until the no-victim report fails
  it.
- A stall ends when a segment frees: on that disk with a reserve of 2, a hot write stalls with
  segments 6 and 7 free; a cold punch then takes the only round slot. Once segment 1 is freed the
  write is no longer `Stalled`, a no-victim report fails nothing, and the write goes into segment 1.
  `Stalled` is worked out when asked, never left over from the last round placed.
- A checkpoint waits until no victim: on the full-disk-waits disk, a checkpoint's first 2-block
  piece fills the reserve segment and its second finds no segment free; both it and the held write
  wait, with no disk action. `FailStalled` then reports Failed(NoSpace) for the held write (hot),
  CheckpointFailed(NoSpace) and Failed(NoSpace) for the waiting piece (metadata lane 0); End then says
  NoCheckpoint.
- Settings: a `max_replay_bytes` past 2^62 is BadConfig, since the hold compares against twice
  it, and `ReserveSegments` saturates rather than wraps.

Who may use the reserve:

| Item while only the reserve is free | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Chunk write, punch, freeze, Raft entries | held in submit order |
| Checkpoint run pieces and manifest | written into the reserve |
| Merge output (`MergePiece`) | written into the reserve |
| Cleaner copy records | written into the reserve (with the Cleaner) |

- Review, for checkpoints: a disk filled to its reserve still finishes a checkpoint, and an
  ordinary item never opens a reserve segment (each fails under a planted bug); it cannot append to
  one, since only the metadata stream opens them. The
  merge step and the cleaner pass join the check with their items; the simulator invariant that the
  bytes held beyond what the manifests name never exceed the reserve arrives with the invariant
  checker.
- Crash with the disk full except the reserve, during a checkpoint in the reserve: recovery
  succeeds and the held items were never acknowledged (`TestCrashAtEveryActionInTheReserve`, under
  [Crash at every action](#crash-at-every-action)).

## Merge steps

The "LSM tree" section's compaction scenarios hold for a merge that fits one step; these are the
merges that take several.

- Four runs merged in steps of two pieces, the first step installed while a flush writes: after it,
  a get at or below the bound reads the output and above it the inputs; a range removal across the
  bound is clipped to start past it; a view opened before the step still reads the four runs; the
  merge's copies of the input blocks wholly at or below the bound are gone. That flush's manifest
  names the inputs whole; the next, a manifest alone, names the bounded inputs and the partial
  output and reports dead the input pieces wholly at or below the bound. A crash after it recovers
  both and resumes from the bound; each later checkpoint writes one step, the one after the last
  names the merged run alone, and every key reads as before the merge throughout.
- A step merges up to `compaction_step_bytes` (64 MiB) of output; the owner appends the step's
  blocks to the output run and sets each input's bound to the last key the step consumed; the next
  checkpoint writes the step's pieces to the merge worker's lane through `MergePiece`, a new root
  for the output listing all its pieces, and a manifest holding the bounds with each input's dead
  pieces. The manifest waits for those pieces and names the root; a snapshot carries the bounds,
  an edit replaces them, and a bound on a run the index does not hold is Malformed.
- With no checkpoint due, the owner begins one for the step alone (`BeginStepCheckpoint`): it
  leaves the memtable unflushed and the replay LSN unchanged, and the log's replay bytes after it
  are as many as before it, where an ordinary checkpoint lowers them to its own records. A reopen
  once a header names the step manifest counts the same replay and held bytes, from the replay
  floor rather than the step's base.
- Bounded runs: an input holds only its keys above its bound, so output and inputs never share a
  key. With inputs A (newer) and B over keys a..z, B lacking g, and a step ending at f, a get of c
  or f reads the output alone, a get of q reads A, a get of r reads A then B, a scan from a returns
  each key once, and a floor of g returns f from the output.
- A lookup of a key at or below an input's bound never searches that input, even when its filter
  says maybe.
- An input piece wholly at or below the bound is reported dead once the manifest naming that bound
  is durable, and a restore never reads it; the piece the bound falls in stays whole and live. Its
  blocks below the bound leave memory unless a view holds them, so a merge's memory peak is one
  step. The usage table's live blocks for dead run pieces come with the Cleaner.
- Output fills its merge worker's lane of the metadata stream: with two indexes merging in steps on
  one worker and checkpoint flushes going on, no output piece shares a segment with a flush piece
  or a manifest. When a merge ends, the worker's next merge continues the same open segment,
  whatever index it merges.
- The scheduler hands each merge the lowest free worker and the merge keeps it until a manifest
  names its last step: with one worker, index B's merge waits for that manifest, then takes worker
  1; with two, it takes worker 2. A merge's next step is picked only once the manifest naming its
  previous one is durable, before any new merge.
- Concurrent merges: a merge of the newest runs picked while a stepped merge holds the oldest runs
  runs in its own steps on another worker, one manifest names both merges' bounds, a restart
  resumes both, and every key reads the same throughout.
- Restart between steps resumes the merge from the bound in the manifest: crash after step 2's
  manifest of a 5-step merge, recover, and the merge's next step starts past step 2's bound; every
  key reads the same before the merge, between steps, after the crash and after the merge.
- Crash after a step's pieces are durable but before its manifest: recovery uses the previous
  manifest's bound, and the step is merged again into the same blocks.
- A checkpoint that fails while writing a step reports the step's pieces it wrote dead and keeps
  the inputs' bounds, and the next writes the step again; one that fails after the step's root is
  durable reports nothing dead, and the next names the step without writing it again.
- A run check that fails in a later step, a bit flipped in an input above the bound, fails that
  step's install with `ErrCheck`, and the merge is never picked again; the index is rebuilt (Run
  checks).
- A step finishes on a disk filled to its reserve: with only the reserve free and a write held, a
  checkpoint writes a merge step into a reserve segment of the worker's lane and its manifest is
  durable.
- Filter partitions: a merge in steps writes a partition of its keys per step, fenced by the step's
  bound, and a get, a prefix floor and a prefix seek each probe the one partition covering their key
  or prefix, allocating nothing (`BenchmarkPartitionedLookups`, over 20 or more partitions). Under
  filters of whole keys, prefixes and both, with fixed two-byte prefixes and prefixes up to a slash
  of one or two letters, straddling steps, and removals the merge drops ending steps, gets, floors,
  prefix floors and prefix scans read like the map between steps, after and after a restore; with
  the fence's prefix left out of its partition, a lookup by prefix misses keys of a later partition
  under prefix filters (a prefix filter's get among them) and nothing changes under whole keys.
- A merge in steps is picked only when its output's root can list every piece with each step's
  short pieces and fenced partition: four runs of five 270-byte entries (6,120 bytes) are refused
  in 512-byte pieces and steps, where the output would need about 40 pieces for 27 references, and
  1 MiB pieces in 64 MiB steps still allow about 55 GiB.
- With steps whose partitions span several pieces, a merge holds at most a step of entries and
  fragments and its own partition beyond the manifests, the last step included.
- Metamorphic option sets for the tree: `steps` (384-byte pieces, two-piece steps), `steps-restart`
  (one-piece steps, a failed first flush and a restart after every flush) and `steps-deferred`
  (steps installed between a flush's pieces, two merges at once); each must read as the model, and
  seed 0 must install steps under each, resume a merge after a restart under `steps-restart` and
  install a step during a flush under `steps-deferred`.
- Review (the [LSM space spike](../spikes/lsm-study-space/), C2 and C4): at most one step plus a
  checkpoint's flush held beyond the manifests, 2 segments of 64 MiB on a 256 GiB disk with a
  MetaStore index of 2 or 6.25% (whole: 65 and 109; with size amplification 88 and 258), 5 and 2
  segments of 4 MiB with 16 and 4 MiB steps on the 16 GiB stand-in; manifest bytes per flushed
  byte at most 0.0080 with full tables (0.0018 whole). Steps sharing the open segment left 30 to
  57 segments stranded against 8 to 10 in a segment of their own (C5).
- A merge holds at most one step, with its filter partition, beyond what the manifests name,
  checked after every checkpoint of the lane tests; the simulator checks it after every step
  together with the reserve invariant once the invariant checker exists.

## Write admission

Free segments outside the reserve against `clean_free` (16), read by the disk's owner on every
call, time from `ctx.Now`:

| Free segments outside the reserve | Cleaner workers | Chunk write blocks | Ordinary items |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16 and more | 1, idle (no pass starts) | not charged | admitted |
| 15 | 1 | not charged | admitted |
| 14 | 2 | not charged | admitted |
| 9 | 2 | not charged | admitted |
| 8 | 2 | token bucket at 1.0 × the cleaner's net freeing rate | admitted as tokens allow |
| 4 | 2 | at 0.75 × | as tokens allow |
| 1 | 2 | at 0.5625 × | as tokens allow |
| 0 | 2 | at 0.5 × | wait, in submit order |

- The thresholds follow `clean_free`: the second worker joins two below it and the bucket charges
  from half of it; a store whose cleaner runs only for waiting items (`clean_free` below 0)
  never charges.
- The rate is what the cleaner measurably frees, net of every block its copies, checkpoints and
  merges take (`BackgroundBlocks`, headers and the tails their lanes leave included), over the last
  one-second window: a cleaner that freed 2 segments of 64 MiB while those took 1.5 segments'
  worth in the window [0, 1 s) refills the bucket from t = 1 s at 32 MiB/s at 8 free segments and
  at 24 MiB/s at 4. The bucket holds at most a window's worth, 32 MiB at 8.
- An ordinary write and a cold blob add no background blocks; a copy of 2 blocks that opens the
  cleaner's segment adds its segment header, record header and 2 blocks, and a merge piece that
  opens a merge lane's segment its headers and data blocks; a checkpoint adds blocks; copies that
  roll into a new segment add the tail they leave behind in the old one.
- A write is admitted while the bucket holds a token and charged all its blocks: 18 MiB taken from
  14 leaves it 4 MiB in debt, and it next holds a token an eighth of a second later at 32 MiB/s.
- Each window after the first sets the rate to the mean of the last rate and what it measured: a
  window that freed nothing after one at 32 MiB/s leaves 16 MiB/s and the bucket at most 16 MiB.
  A first window that freed no more than it spent leaves no rate, and a held write waits for the
  window's end.
- A window that freed no more than it spent measures 0 and carries the difference into the next:
  450 blocks spent in one window, then a 1,000-block segment freed and 450 more spent in the
  next, measures 100 blocks a second, not 550, for a rate of 50 after the first window's 0. A
  window in which the cleaner stopped, with `clean_free` segments free, carries nothing: after it
  halves the rate to 25, a freed 1,000-block segment sets it to 512.5.
- Before the first window ends there is no rate and nothing is charged, also after an index
  rebuild restarts the log.
- The bucket charges while the cleaner has a pass running or will start one: when its only pass
  ends, a held write stays held; once it has found no victim at the current durable LSN, a held
  write goes out at the next call.
- Raft entries, punches and freezes are never charged: a punch of another chunk goes out while
  chunk writes are held. A punch behind a held write of the same chunk waits with it, as the
  chunk's order requires, and a freeze goes out with the write or punch that carries it, so a
  held write holds its freeze.
- A chunk write the bucket refuses is held unsubmitted by the store, keeping its buffer and its
  place ahead of its chunk's later operations; refused writes go out in the order refused, and a
  write of another chunk waits behind them. The store reports it is not admitting while any is
  held and arms `AdmitTimer` for when the bucket next holds a token or the window ends. How the
  connection stops being read is the Event loop item's (phase 5).
- A held write that leaves without being admitted, cancelled as its PG's interval ends or refused
  `ErrVersion` once an earlier version of its chunk failed, takes its chunk off the held queue
  even while the chunk has a punch pending: the store reports admitting again, and with admission
  off another chunk's write is not held behind it
  (`TestAHeldWriteThatLeavesUnadmittedFreesTheQueue`).
- The simulated runs share their writers and cleaner: 8 closed-loop writers of 16 KiB, each
  sending its next write once its last is answered and the store is admitting, the
  longest-waiting first; a cleaner worker taking 20 ms a victim; disk actions one at a time at the
  simulated disk's latencies; a reserve of 8; the disk filled in order, then overwritten at random
  and measured over the last three quarters of the overwrites. Without admission is a planted bug
  that admits every write.
- The reviews near full share one check (`checkHeld`): each run fails unless free segments outside
  the reserve fall to 8 or fewer, the slow-down band, so the writers outran the cleaner; free
  segments outside the reserve are none at most 1% of the time, no write fails with NoSpace, and
  the wait from a writer's last answer to its next is at most 200 ms at the 99th percentile and one
  window, 1 s, at the most.
- Review under uniform overwrites at 90% full
  (`TestWriteAdmissionHoldsUniformOverwritesAt90PercentFull`, skipped unless `ROCKSOLID_LONG_SIM`
  is set): the disk's fill counting the index's runs, as `TestCleanerWriteAmplification` counts it,
  on its 2,048 segments of 8 MiB in records of 192 KiB, filled in 32-block writes, then overwritten
  uniformly in 16 KiB writes for two disk capacities. Measured, seed 1: 3,494 s of simulated time,
  99.0% of it in the slow-down band, as few as 1 free, none free 0%; writes waited 40.8 ms at the
  99th percentile and 91.5 ms at the most. The run takes 10 minutes on one core of the Mac mini and
  peaks at 2.3 GB resident.
- Review with data at 90 and 95% full and a hot 30% (`TestWriteAdmissionHoldsAt90And95PercentFull`,
  seeded, in `scripts/seeds.sh` over 4 seeds; a plain `go test` runs it only with
  `ROCKSOLID_LONG_SIM` set): data at 90 and 95% of a 16 GiB disk of 1,024 segments of 16 MiB, filled
  in 64-block writes whose 264 KiB records pack a segment whole, then overwritten in 16 KiB writes
  within the first 30% of the data, as block volumes overwrite a hot share, for a tenth of a disk
  capacity. The cold 70% packs whole segments the cleaner never takes, so the hot data works in
  the space it leaves, about 73% full at 90% and 85% at 95%, and the run measures the transient
  from a freshly packed disk. Measured over 8 seeds:

  | Data | In the slow-down band | Fewest free | None free | Wait, 99th percentile | Slowest wait | Measured |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 90% | 60 to 62% of the time | 4 | 0% | 9.2 ms | 17 ms | 31 s |
  | 95% | 99.2 to 100% | 2 | 0% | 92 ms | 447 ms | 198 to 211 s |

  Without admission (seed 0, with `ROCKSOLID_LONG_SIM` set, which the test checks finds none free
  a tenth of the time or more): none free 27% of the time at 90% and 97.9% at 95%, the slowest wait
  349 ms and 4.2 s. A seed takes about 62 s on one core of the Mac mini and peaks at 1.3 GB
  resident. With each window's rate taken alone instead of smoothed, 58 of the 209 windows seed 5
  at 95% cleaned through measured nothing, up to 3 in a row, and writes waited 99 ms at the 99th
  percentile and 2.5 s at the most, over the 1 s bound.
- Review on a small disk (`TestWriteAdmissionKeepsSegmentsFreeAheadOfASlowCleaner`): 512
  segments of 64 blocks, 64 KiB records, at 50 and 65% full, the most the cleaner's net-gain guard
  sustains on segments this small, overwritten uniformly for one disk capacity. Without admission
  the disk has no free segment outside the reserve at least half the time and some writer waits
  two victims' cleaning, 40 ms, or longer; with it, none for at most 1% of the time, no write fails
  with NoSpace, and the slowest wait is shorter than without. Measured: none 0% with admission
  against 94 and 99.6% without, the slowest wait 38 and 57 ms against 57 and 76.
- At 85% full under uniform overwrites (`TestWriteAdmissionAt85PercentFull`, 320 segments of
  1,024 blocks, 64 KiB records, skipped unless `ROCKSOLID_LONG_SIM` is set, about 2.5 minutes,
  0.26 GB resident at peak): admission keeps a free segment for a larger share of the time than
  without it and than a planted rate net of copied blocks alone. Measured: no free segment 0% of
  the time with admission, 98.6% net of copied blocks alone, 99.4% without; the slowest wait
  2.3, 4.4 and 5.2 s. See the cleaning-debt question in design.md.
- An index over its run limit never slows or stops writes (no run-count stall).
- The same wait applies at twice `max_replay_bytes` (see Checkpoint backpressure); both
  conditions holding at once hold items until both clear.

## Durable LSN in record headers

Codec ("Record codec" holds the layout, golden and damage rows):

- The prelude carries the newest LSN durable when the round was built, 8 bytes at byte 48, 56
  bytes in all. The first record of a log carries 0. A durable LSN not below the record's own LSN is
  Malformed, and encoding refuses it.
- The exhaustive single-bit-flip, torn-subset and torn-sector properties cover the new field.

Tail rule. Let g be the first LSN replay does not find. The log ends at g only if no record header
found past g names a durable LSN at or past g, every header found past g lies within
g + `commit_depth` − 1, and no segment header names a manifest at or past g:

| Depth at write / open | Records | Damage or loss | Durable LSNs in later headers | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 / 1 | 1-5 | record 5 torn | none past g | LSNs 1-4 |
| 1 / 1 | 1-5 | record 4 damaged | record 5 names 4 | Corrupt(4) |
| 1 / 1 | 1-5 | record 3 damaged | records 4 and 5 name 3 and 4 | Corrupt(3) |
| 2 / 2 | 1-5, round 5 begun after round 4 was durable | record 4 damaged | record 5 names 4 | Corrupt(4) (the window alone would recover 1-3) |
| 2 / 2 | 1-5, rounds 4 and 5 in flight together | record 4 missing, record 5 whole | record 5 names 3 | LSNs 1-3; record 5's header zeroed |
| 2 / 2 | 1-5, rounds 4 and 5 in flight | record 5 missing, record 4 whole | none past g | LSNs 1-4 |
| 1 / 2 | 1-5 | record 4 damaged | record 5 names 4 | Corrupt(4) |
| 3 / 3 | 1-5, rounds 3, 4, 5 in flight | record 3 torn, 4 and 5 whole | both name 2 | LSNs 1-2; headers 4 and 5 zeroed |
| 2 / 2 | 1-5, rounds 4 and 5 in flight | record 4 damaged, record 5's prelude torn | unreadable | LSNs 1-3 (a torn header names nothing; the window decides) |

These are Pebble's `readAheadForCorruption` cases (`record/record.go:466-588`, the test at 577,
a7b8321871e3): a later valid chunk whose synced offset passes the bad one proves corruption.

- After recovery the next record's durable LSN is the recovered LSN: recovering 1-3 above, the
  next round gets LSN 4 and names 3.
- Existing "Recovery" scenarios that stay as they are: the torn tail of 3 + 1 records, damage in a
  middle record, damage in the last record, "Commit depth 2, a round missing" (the second record
  names 1), the duplicate LSN, and the durable manifest never dropped.
- [property] "Random crashes keep acknowledged records": its commit depth widens from 1-2 to 1-3,
  and it adds: every record header's durable LSN is below its LSN and at most the log's durable
  LSN when its round was built, and a gap that a whole later header names durable is always
  Corrupt.

## Manifest edits and snapshots

- The first checkpoint of a log writes a snapshot: every index's runs and replay LSN and the whole
  usage table. Later checkpoints write an edit: runs added and removed, replay LSNs, merge bounds,
  and the usage rows that changed, a freed segment as a row in state free.
- Snapshot rule (Pebble's `record/rotation.go:40-68`): a checkpoint writes a snapshot instead of
  an edit when the edits since the last snapshot, this one included, would exceed the smaller of
  that snapshot and the next:

| Last snapshot | Edits since, before this one | This edit | Next snapshot | Writes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 KiB | 40 KiB | 20 KiB | 110 KiB | edit (60 ≤ 100) |
| 100 KiB | 90 KiB | 20 KiB | 110 KiB | snapshot (110 > 100) |
| 100 KiB | 40 KiB | 15 KiB | 50 KiB | snapshot (55 > 50) |
| 100 KiB | 0 | 100 KiB | 120 KiB | edit (100 ≤ 100) |

- The rule's state survives a restart: after a snapshot of 100 KiB and two edits of 40 KiB, a
  crash and a recovery, the next checkpoint of a 30 KiB edit writes a snapshot (110 > 100), the
  sizes rebuilt from the last piece's list.
- The manifest's last piece lists the pieces of its snapshot and of every edit since; the segment
  header points at that last piece; recovery reads the snapshot and applies the edits in order.
- Review: open after any crash equals open from a snapshot taken at the same base LSN, and a usage
  table rebuilt from a snapshot plus edits equals the log's own, under the random-crash property.
- Changed bitmap: group commit marks each segment whose row changes. A checkpoint whose edit fails
  after segments 3 and 5 changed keeps the bitmap: the next edit holds 3, 5 and whatever changed
  since. A successful one clears it.
- Edit size: an edit holds at most one row per segment the records since the manifest before it
  changed, independent of the disk's size ([durability study](../spikes/lsm-study-durability/):
  3,071 rows at the median on 16,384 segments, 3,164 on 262,144).
- Space bars (the study's model, counts): on 1 TiB at 90% full with 4 KiB writes, edits plus
  snapshots 0.129% of the log against 0.415% for a full table, recovery reading at most 544 KiB;
  with 262,144 segments of 4 MiB, 0.159% against 6.64%, at most 8.5 MiB (the study's model; the
  tests check the bound below). Recovery reads at most twice a snapshot; the rule weighs every byte
  a checkpoint wrote for the manifest, piece lists included, and snapshots growing between
  rotations may exceed half of what manifests write.
- The cleaner never copies a manifest piece. A segment holding pieces the current manifest lists
  is not a victim; when the cleaner asks for it, the next checkpoint writes a snapshot whatever
  the rule says, and once a segment header naming that snapshot is durable the old pieces are
  dead.
- Quarantined rows are carried by every snapshot and never dropped by an edit.
- `NextSeq`: every snapshot and edit records it, 8 bytes, and both round-trip with it; recovery
  takes the loaded manifest's, the newest a durable segment header names. It is one past the open
  sequence of the newest segment a durable round had opened at the base LSN: with open sequences 1
  to 4 taken by durable rounds and a round in flight that has opened a segment at sequence 5 when
  the checkpoint begins, the manifest records 5, and a crash that keeps that round finds the
  segment at 5, at or past it, and used. Before the first manifest it is 1. Planted bug: taken from
  the log's next sequence number when the checkpoint begins (6 here), recovery frees that segment
  with its durable records, and the
  random-crash property fails (seed 1 in the [log segments study](../studies/log-segments/)).
- Changed existing scenario ("Segment usage table"): "A row for segment 0, rows out of segment
  order or naming one segment twice, a free or unknown state, or a newest LSN past the base LSN is
  Malformed" becomes: in a snapshot, a free row is Malformed; in an edit, a free row is valid; an
  unknown state is Malformed in both. New: an edit that removes a run its base does not hold, or
  names an index twice, is Malformed; an edit with no snapshot before it in the last piece's list
  is Malformed. Both decoders stay fuzzed.
- Changed existing scenario ("Group commit" property): "every finished checkpoint's manifest reads
  back with its base LSN and runs" reads the snapshot plus the edits the last piece lists.
- Crash cases: a crash before an edit's last piece recovers from the manifest before it; a crash
  after a snapshot's last piece but before any segment header names it recovers from the previous
  manifest (the existing "Manifest in pieces" recovery scenario, with edits).

## Checkpoint backpressure

With `max_replay_bytes` 8 blocks, counted in record blocks of ordinary items after the newest
manifest, written or in flight, segment headers and the checkpoint's own records left out:

| Ordinary record blocks after the newest manifest | Ordinary items | Checkpoint items |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | admitted; a checkpoint is due | admitted |
| 15 | admitted | admitted |
| 17 (past twice `max_replay_bytes`) | held in submit order, buffers kept, not `Stalled` | admitted |
| a manifest becomes durable | the held items go out in submit order | |

- Three 3-block and a 2-block write leave 15 blocks; a 1-block write is admitted and leaves 17; a
  hot and a cold write are then held with no disk action. The checkpoint's 100-byte piece goes out
  at once and adds its 2 blocks to the bytes to replay (19), but not to the hold. Once the
  manifest is durable the held hot write, then the held cold write, become durable.
- A checkpoint's pieces and manifest wait in a queue of their own, metadata lane 0, so they never
  wait behind held items and no round carries them with ordinary items (Held items). Merge pieces
  are not ordinary either: with two 3-block writes holding a third, a merge piece goes out at
  once, and the held write after the next checkpoint.
- A checkpoint larger than the bound releases the hold: with `max_replay_bytes` 4 blocks, two
  3-block writes hold a third; a checkpoint of four 2-block pieces and its manifest (14 blocks)
  completes and the held write goes out at once. Reopened, recovery replays from the start, since
  no segment header names the new manifest yet: 24 blocks to replay, of which the hold counts the
  10 of the three writes.
- A checkpoint that fails while items are held keeps them held, and the next checkpoint releases
  them. A failure for want of space, reported when the cleaner has no victim, fails the held items
  with NoSpace too, which bounds the wait: on a 16-block disk with `max_replay_bytes` 4 blocks,
  three 2-block writes fill it and hold a fourth; the checkpoint's piece finds no segment, which is
  `CheckpointStalled`, and the no-victim report fails the piece, the checkpoint and the held write. A write submitted next is
  `Stalled` at once, until a new checkpoint begins.
- Merge pieces (`MergePiece`) stay out of the hold and are never held, as checkpoint items.
- The control-plane host, which runs no cleaner, begins a checkpoint once an ordinary item waits
  for room with only the reserve free, however few records follow the newest manifest: on a disk of
  64 segments of 64 blocks with an 8-segment reserve and `max_replay_bytes` past the disk, it
  answers three disks' worth of counter `Txn`s, each stall checkpointing, compacting and freeing
  segments; before the rule its 462nd `Txn` waited for good (`TestAStallForRoomMakesACheckpointDue`).
  A chunk store leaves a stall to its cleaner: making the log's `CheckpointDue` true on a stall took
  the cleaner's room and failed writes with NoSpace while it had a victim
  (`TestAFullDiskWithNoFreeSegmentEndsInNoSpace`, `TestAStalledSlotWriteFailsTheHotWritesAfterIt`).
- The chunk store stand-in of the recovery tests begins a new checkpoint after a failure once a
  record has become durable since, so held items are released and the random-crash property keeps
  "every accepted ticket ends ...".
- [property] A stalled checkpoint keeps the memtables bounded: seeds 1-10 on a 1 GiB disk, rounds
  of 3 to 16 blocks, commit depth 1-3, `max_replay_bytes` 8 to 40 blocks, 1,000 steps of 1- to
  8-block writes to random streams with completions interleaved, the stand-in withholding its pieces for runs of
  steps. After every event, the ordinary data durable after the newest manifest's base is at most
  twice `max_replay_bytes` plus one round; afterwards every write is durable and none failed.
  Coverage: a write held with nothing in flight. Without the hold it fails at seed 1. The Raft
  entries shards retain join the check with the Raft shard (phase 4).
- Replay after a crash while items were held reads at most twice `max_replay_bytes` plus a round,
  the records the checkpoint wrote and a segment per lane (the term for replicated primaries'
  pending writes arrives with phase 3).


## Held items

- Checkpoint pieces go to the metadata stream, so no round carries them with ordinary items. With
  a hot write in flight, two 1-block cold writes and a 100-byte piece queued behind them go out as
  two records in different segments: the writes' adds 3 blocks to the hold (their data and the
  header), the piece's nothing; a 100-byte cold blob's record adds 2 blocks.
- [property] The hold a record adds, checked against marking each block one by one over 10,000
  random records of writes, punches, freezes and blobs of every kind: none for a record of
  checkpoint items alone, the whole record for one with none, else its header blocks and the
  blocks ordinary payloads touch. Reopened after each case above, with no manifest written,
  recovery restores the hold the log had.
- Close fails what still waits: on the full-disk-waits disk of Segment reserve, Close fails the
  write held for room with Closed and returns its buffer and the log's own. With
  `max_replay_bytes` 4 blocks, two 3-block writes hold a 1-block cold write behind a checkpoint;
  Close is Busy while the checkpoint's piece is in flight, and once it is durable Close reports
  Failed(Closed) for the held write and CheckpointFailed(Closed), leaves no buffer allocated, and a
  submit after it is refused with Closed. A test's own close fails if anything was still waiting.
- An ordinary cold item never waits behind the checkpoint's pieces, which fill a segment of the
  reserve on the metadata stream: on a 1 GiB disk (4,095 usable 64-block segments) at commit depth
  2 with a reserve of 4,093, two 62-block cold writes fill segments 1 and 2, a 100-byte piece
  opens segment 3 from the reserve, and segments 1 and 2 are then freed. A second piece waits for
  the first, which opened segment 3, while a 1-block cold write opens segment 1 beside it in the
  other round slot. Then the second piece goes into segment 3.

## Reserve from settings

- At the default settings (`merge_workers` 1, `compaction_step_bytes` 64 MiB) the log sizes its
  reserve by `ReserveSegments` from the superblock's segments: 772 on a 1 GiB disk of 256 KiB
  segments. A reserve set directly (3) replaces it, and `NoReserve`, which the tests' settings ask
  for by name, gives 0.
- Open sizes the reserve again: on a 64-block disk (15 usable 4-block segments) with
  `max_replay_bytes` 8 blocks and a 1-block step, the reserve is 9 at format and after a reopen.
  Six 1-block writes fill segments 1 to 6 and a checkpoint's manifest opens segment 7 from the
  reserve; after the reopen a cold punch that would fit in segment 7 is `Stalled`.
- Before the reopen, a hot write with only the reserve's 9 segments free is `Stalled`, with no
  disk action.
- BadConfig at Format, leaving nothing allocated: the default reserve of a 64 MiB disk of 16 KiB
  segments (12,292 of 4,096), `NoReserve` together with a reserve, `merge_workers` below 0 or above
  255, and a zero
  `compaction_step_bytes`. Open refuses the first once it has read the superblock, before a segment
  header, and the other three, which no geometry changes, in `Recover` itself, with no action and
  no buffer taken.
- A reserve set directly or `NoReserve` needs no merge settings: with `merge_workers` and
  `compaction_step_bytes` both 0, either one formats, writes and reopens.

## Group commit API guards

- Submit refuses a run piece as "Group commit" lists; the same piece through `CheckpointPiece` is
  accepted and goes out with the checkpoint.
- Close after Format, at each step until the superblock copy's flush completes, is Busy and leaves
  every buffer of the log allocated; once it completes, Close succeeds and returns them.

## Metadata stream

- A third stream tag (2) for sorted runs, compaction output and manifests; the hot stream keeps
  chunk writes and Raft entries, and the cold stream the cleaner's chunk copies, encoded shards and
  other blobs. Submit takes only the hot and cold streams (Malformed for the metadata stream) and
  refuses a run piece with ReservedKind; the checkpoint writes its pieces and manifest to metadata
  lane 0, and `MergePiece` writes merge worker *w*'s output, a run piece, to lane *w*, 1 to
  `merge_workers` (Malformed for 0 or past it, the buffer staying with the caller).
- Segment header round trips, damage rows, golden lines (metadata lane 0 beside the cold header,
  and merge lane 3) and the write-side check of each wrong stream and lane are in "Segments and
  superblock" and "Write-side decode check"; turn order in "Group commit". The format version
  stays 1 before the first release (see design.md "Upgrades").
- `merge_workers` resolves the same way in the log and the merge scheduler: 0 is the default of 1,
  below 0 or above 255 is BadConfig in both.
- Lanes: two merge workers and a checkpoint give three open metadata segments, lanes 0, 1 and 2;
  worker 1's second piece goes into its first one's segment and the second checkpoint's piece into
  lane 0's, so no flush piece lands in a merge lane.
- A worker's segment stays open across its merges, of one index or another (index A's piece at
  block 1, index B's at block 3), and after a restart its next piece follows at block 5 with the
  next LSN; a checkpoint after it opens a segment of lane 0. Merge records are replayed to no
  index (open replays only the hot write, LSN 3) but count for the durable LSN.
- Group commit keeps a queue, a cursor and the append rule per lane, a round writes one record to
  one lane, and rounds take the lanes with work in turn (property: "Every accepted item ends
  durable", with merge pieces on 1-4 lanes). The append rule holds on a merge lane: at commit depth
  2, a worker's second piece waits for the round that opened its segment (LBA 64) to be durable,
  then appends at LBA 67.
- Merge pieces go out past the hold behind a checkpoint and may open a segment of the reserve
  (Checkpoint backpressure, Segment reserve).
- Replay allocates a window for each lane past the hot and slot ones: a pool with room for only
  one of the two that a log with a checkpoint and a merge lane needs fails recovery with
  PoolExhausted and leaves no buffer allocated; with room for both it opens.
- Recovery reads each lane from the last of its segments whose first record is at or before the
  first record to replay, and merges every lane's records by LSN: merge worker 1 opens its segment
  (LSN 2) before the checkpoints' shared metadata segment (LSN 3), takes a piece between the two
  checkpoints and two after the second, whose manifest a hot segment then names. Open replays every
  record past the replay point but the merges' and recovers the newest LSN, whether hot writes
  follow the merge pieces or not. With the per-stream rule planted, replay starts at the shared
  segment and misses the merge records past the replay point: Corrupt at the first of them while a
  hot write follows; when they are the newest durable records, a tail cut before them, after which
  a hot write reuses that LSN and a correct open reports Corrupt there.
- Skipping merge lanes in the same case reads as a gap: Corrupt at the first merge record past the
  replay point.
- A torn merge record at the tail (a 3-block piece whose last data block never landed) is dropped
  and its header erased, and the next piece takes its place and LSN; it is read in full, as other
  records are, never by its header blocks alone.
- A crash in the round that opens a merge's segment: with only the record landed, the segment
  stays free, its record is erased and the next piece opens it again at sequence 3; with the header
  too, the piece is kept and the next one appends at block 3.
- A lane whose worker is gone (2 merge workers, then 1 after a restart): at each of two starts
  recovery reads its segment past the header, keeps its usage row and its record in the durable
  LSN, refuses `MergePiece` on it, and no hot, cold or merge record goes to it.
- Replay reads at most one segment per lane that holds no record past the replay point: the hot and
  merge lanes each fill three segments before it and open a fourth after it, and the trace reads
  past the header one hot and one merge segment before the replay point.
- Recovery scenarios that carry over to the metadata stream are above; the many-segments and
  random-crash properties in "Recovery" run all three streams and 1 to 4 merge lanes.
- Write amplification with runs in this stream belongs to "Cleaner write amplification in
  simulation".

## Cleaner

The built "Chunk index" section already covers the owner's conditional `Move` and the move
property (seed 22).

Copy entry codec:

- A copy entry is a write entry's fields plus the location it copied from, 41 bytes. It
  round-trips, adds its blocks to the data area, joins the torn-write and bit-flip properties,
  and the golden record fixture gains a record of two copy entries. A copy with zero blocks or
  past block 1,024 is BadExtent; a copy entry with a field its kind does not encode set is
  Malformed.
- A copy whose source is location 0 (a punched range) is Malformed to the codec, and group
  commit refuses one whose source lies in segment 0 or past the disk: a copy only ever reads a
  log block. `Submit` refuses a copy entry (ErrReservedKind); only the cleaner's `Copy` writes
  one, to lane 1 of the cold stream, past the hold behind a checkpoint and into the reserve.

Victim choice (score free space × age ÷ copy cost; the spikes use (1 − u) × age ÷ (1 + u), age in
user blocks written since the segment's youngest block was written, capped at one disk capacity;
on the 1 GiB disk one capacity is 262,144 blocks):

| Segment | Live share u | Age | Score | Chosen |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0.50 | 10 | 3.33 | |
| B | 0.90 | 100 | 5.26 | B, of A and B |
| C, frozen snapshot data | 0.95 | 10,000 capacities, capped at 1 | 0.05 × 262,144 ÷ 1.95 = 6,722 | |
| D | 0.50 | 30,000 | 10,000 | D, of C and D; uncapped, C would score 6.7 × 10⁷ and always win |

- A pass takes the 4 best victims that pass the net-gain guard, every segment with nothing live
  first: on the primed 64-segment disk, where merges have left 10 metadata segments with nothing
  live, every victim is one of them. Scored by cost-benefit alone, empty segments ranked by their
  age, which counts only ordinary writes, and the pass took segments with live blocks to copy
  instead; at 90% full in simulation the ones the index wrote while writes waited, at age 0,
  piled up until the free segments, the reserve included, ran out.
- Net-gain guard, header blocks rounded up per record (design: "a victim must free more space than
  copying it costs"). In 16,384-block (64 MiB) segments a copy record of single-block extents
  holds 253 data blocks and 3 header blocks (56 + 253 × 45 = 11,441 bytes; 256 blocks fill the
  1 MiB cap), and one copy holds up to 254 blocks under 1 header block. A record never spans two
  segments, so copies rolling into a new segment split their records between the two and leave
  the old one's tail unused, up to a block short of the largest copy and its header: L live
  blocks cost L + 3(⌈L ÷ 253⌉ + 1) + min(L, 254) + h − 1, with h the header blocks of that
  copy. Estimated in exact bytes, the guard let the cleaner pick 98.9% live victims and livelock
  (cleaner streams spike).
- The guard also charges the header of the segment the copies open, and an estimate of the index
  entries the moves write, 2 × 67 bytes per block of the live count, which holds a block once per
  map referring to it (flushed, then merged again; deeper merges and split extents are not
  charged): a victim is picked only
  when its cost plus that block is below a segment. Copies of 15,936 live blocks cost 16,382 and
  of 15,937 cost 16,383; with the entries, 15,434 live blocks cost 15,877 + 505 = 16,382 and are
  picked, and 15,435 cost 16,383 and are refused. On 16-block segments, without the segment header a
  copy of a nearly full segment filled a new one exactly, and without the split record copies of
  13-block victims filled a segment each (seed 448 of the crash test, and a disk filled with
  live data at a reserve of 10 or 12, whose copies' checkpoints took the whole reserve): either
  way the cleaner churned forever on a disk of live data.
- The charge bounds what the copies take: on 64-block segments of 16-block records, copies of
  14-block items behind a tail just too short for one took 61 blocks of a new segment and
  stranded 13, against 61 charged before the tail was; with it, 300 victims of random copy sizes
  after random fills never take more than charged.
- A victim's copies reach the log together, so they go out in one record where they fit rather
  than the first alone in a round of its own. A copy whose source crosses a segment is Malformed.
- A metadata victim is charged the records its live runs' pieces take now, header blocks included,
  each record once, plus the largest less a block, the tail it can leave unused at a segment's
  end: a 3-block piece in a 4-block record costs 7. Charged the runs' bytes instead, small pieces
  of two blocks each looked like a fraction of one, and after a crash (seed 329) the cleaner
  rewrote the same runs from segment to segment without end.
- Each step of the rewrite is charged too: a record header for its blocks, its filter partition,
  its root's references and bound, and a manifest as large as a snapshot of every segment. On
  16-block segments with steps of a block, a victim charged 13 blocks without them had its runs
  rewritten in 23 blocks of merge-lane records and manifests; with them it is charged 28.
- A chunk victim is taken only if its charge fits the room the cleaner's lane can reach, its open
  segment's tail and every free segment, the reserve included. With a reserve of one segment the
  disk reaches zero free segments; before this check every later write started a pass whose
  copies found no room, copied 10 blocks for nothing and failed. Now a write that finds no room
  fails with NoSpace with nothing copied once new blocks fill the disk.
- A stall on either hot lane fails both hot queues in submit order: with the shared hot lane out of
  room, a freeze and the slot write after it both fail; with the slot lane unable to open a segment
  outside the reserve and the cleaner's only victim quarantined, a whole chunk and the small write
  of the same chunk after it both fail with NoSpace, and the chunk's next write gets a newer
  version.
- A slot write's record goes alone to the hot stream's slot lane, so slot headers share segments
  only with each other: six whole chunks written among overwrites of a small chunk leave their
  headers in one slot-lane segment that holds nothing else, and no other segment holds a slot
  header once the cleaner has run.
- A segment holding the record header of a live whole chunk's slot write is never a victim: the
  index counts the slot's blocks against the header's segment, recounted at open from the slots'
  counts, which keep their record's header. A slot-lane segment the lane has moved on from, whose
  only live blocks are one chunk's, is left alone however short of clean_free, before and after a
  restart. With nine whole chunks' headers among overwrites of a small
  chunk, 3,000 more overwrites never fail, and new data then fails with NoSpace only once no
  segment without a slot header would gain space; scored by their age, the header segments took
  every pass and writes failed while 16 segments with nothing live waited.
- A pass that ends with writes still waiting for room is followed at once by the next, so they
  fail with NoSpace only once no victim is left: four chunks overwritten on the 64-segment disk
  with a reserve of 4 and the cleaner running only for waiting writes never fail. Before, the
  store read "no victim" off a pass that had just finished, and write 2,163 failed with 4 victims
  left.
- A pass that frees nothing starts no other until the durable LSN moves: once the 4 best victims
  each hold a block that fails its checksum, a pass quarantines them all, five reads after it
  start no pass, and a write starts one that frees segments.
- Age cap regression, scripted in Go as the cleaner spike modelled it: a 1 GiB disk of 4,096
  segments at 90% full, 20% of the data frozen by a snapshot, 90/10 hot/cold overwrites, copies in
  age order with moved blocks keeping their write time. Capped, at most a few passes in a row gain
  no segment over 2 million writes; a planted uncapped score takes more passes for the same writes.
  This model's guard keeps the uncapped cleaner out of the spike's livelock (C2: 1,000 passes
  without a free segment), which needed the spike's own record and header layout.
- A segment holding a piece the current manifest lists (Manifest edits and snapshots), or a run
  piece or record that the newest manifest named by a durable segment header needs (a record after
  its replay points), or moves not yet applied, is never a victim; nor is the open segment of any
  lane, nor any segment before a manifest is named. A segment holding a manifest's piece asks for
