  epoch e fails the CRC, and table e − 1 is a gap.
- A gap fetches the whole table: the node holds e and receives the delta for e + 2.
- A node that jumps from e to e + 5 by fetching a whole table loses nothing, and none of its
  interval numbers goes backwards (`TestDeltaBases`).
- [fuzz] Delta and whole-table decoders (`FuzzDecodeTable`, `FuzzDecodeDelta`): what they accept
  encodes back to the same bytes. A truncated delta, an entry for a PG past `pg_count`, a
  decreasing interval number, a leaving member in a recovered interval, a pool's split after the
  delta's epoch or an unknown entry flag is Malformed (`TestMalformedDeltas`), as is a new or resized pool
  without exactly `pg_count` entries, refused before the table is allocated: a 50-byte delta naming
  2³¹ PGs costs nothing (`TestDeltaCarriesEveryNewPG`).
- PG epochs spike B1, a homelab year on 10 nodes: 104 to 105 MB of deltas against 399 MB to 2.25 GB
  of whole tables. F2, one flap with refill staged one member per table: 1,202 tables. A delta costs
  a 38-byte header for one pool and 34 bytes per changed `rep3` entry, 20 more with its previous
  interval's members, 5 more during a move (`TestDeltaSize`).
- A step past its byte budget, `max_ctl_txn_bytes` with each entry counted as its encoding and
  16 bytes: the activations, down marks and refill after `refill_after` of a `rep3` pool at its
  default `pg_count` on 246 disks losing every third node (the refill 1.43 MB), and those of a
  4,096-PG `ec16-2` pool whose lost disks then leave the pool, each commit over tables within the
  budget, the refills over at least two, and end at the table one unbounded `Next` gives
  (`TestAStepOverItsBudgetSpreadsOverTables`). A pool that doubles, or changes `min_live`, beside
  another pool's down marks, together past the budget, changes whole in the first table though the
  order starts at the other pool, and the tables after change only the other pool
  (`TestAPoolWhoseHeadChangesStaysInOneTable`). After a table that stopped at PG p, the next
  one, given p, takes the down marks left before the activations of the PGs the first changed
  (`TestTheNextTableResumesWhereTheLastStopped`).

**[property] tests.** `TestPlacementKeepsItsRules`, 1,000 seeds in `scripts/seeds.sh`, about 40 ms
each; 10,000 passed once in 227 s on 2 processes. Each seed draws a layout from the matrix in
Testing strategy, 3 or 5 nodes of 1 or 4 disks of 0.5 to 8 TB, some holding another pool's data, under `none`, `rep2` or `rep3` with a random
`min_live`, places it, and computes 30 tables after random events: a disk added or removed, a disk
or node marked down, up or in `maintenance`, a drain set or cleared, time passing, primaries asking,
activations folded with recovered reports where every member but a leaving one is up and late reports for earlier such intervals, `replicas` or `min_live` changed, `pg_count` doubled, or a PG reordered and
pinned, each table allowed 0, 1, 5 or every balance move.

After every table:

- Every PG keeps its pool's width and at most `maxMembers` members once any leaves, or more,
  never more than the table before, beside its leaving members after `replicas` went down, with at
  most `max_per_domain` per domain but the leaving members and no disk twice.
- No table raises an interval it need not, and every table raises one it must, by exactly 1, by
  the table above; no last activated interval goes down.
- A member removed and added back gets a new interval.
- A live leaving member is removed in the first table after a recovered report for its PG's
  current interval that marks no other member down or in `maintenance`, and never before.
- An entry is recovered exactly while its interval has had such a report, and a move adds a member
  only to a PG whose entry was recovered or got such a report in that table.
- No live member that holds all of a PG's data, one it started with or one a recovered report
  covered that has stayed live since, leaves unless the members left that hold it still number the
  width; an edit may remove any member.
- A delta reproduces the whole table and its CRC.

Then every disk comes back up, undrained and unpinned, and tables are computed, each once the last
one's moves have copied and activated, until one proposes no move and records every PG recovered, as
`Unbalanced` is evaluated; then a disk is added to the pool holding data, and the same again. Once the loop stops:

- It settles within a few computations, at most 8 over 10,000 seeds: one after the moves copied
  proposes more only where the one before found every PG it would move from a disk still moving,
  since a PG makes one move at a time, and a PG's next move waits a table more, for the report of
  the interval its removal started.
- It has converged: no disk is outside its fill margin.
- Available + held is at least balanced ÷ (1 + the largest margin of the pool's disks) and never
  above balanced.
- The members a disk addition moves stay near the minimum: at most a quarter above the lower bound,
  the larger of the members above and below the disks' margins, plus the sum of the disks' margins.
  Moving from the disk furthest above its target even inside its margin costs those extra moves:
  when a disk joins a domain whose capped share rises, the disks of other domains that are just
  above their targets feed that domain's other disks, and a disk far above its target feeds the
  new disk in its own domain until it falls under the rest. Over 10,000 seeds the moves were 0.69%
  above the lower bound in all, none above a quarter more.
- Over a run of at least 200 seeds, the members disk additions move total at most 5% above the
  sum of their lower bounds. Fewer seeds swing too far: of the 1,250 runs of 8 seeds from 0 to
  9,999, 23 exceed 5%, seeds 7,752 to 7,759 reaching 16.85%, and runs of 40 reach 4.69%; any 200
  consecutive seeds stay within 1.66%, and any 800 within 0.95%. Each process checks it over
  its own seeds, so only one given at least 200 does: `scripts/seeds.sh`'s 1,000 seeds on up to 5
  processes, never `go test`'s 40.

`Unbalanced` [property], `TestAddedDiskNeverUnbalances`, on layouts drawn as the study's test U
draws them: 200 random layouts each for `rep2` and `rep3`, 3 to 6 nodes of 1 or 2 disks of 0.5 to
8 TB, some partly used by other pools, one disk added to a random node of a converged table:

- No addition raises `Unbalanced`, at fills of 0, 50, 70 and 90% of balanced; the worst leaves
  available + held 6.9% under balanced (9.4% in the study's draws), a small disk one member above
  its target.
- `Unbalanced` keeps its value while the computation proposes moves.

`Unbalanced` [property], `TestSettledOnlyOncePlacementIsDone`: 200 random layouts each for `rep2`
and `rep3`, split, then a disk added. Once a computation proposes no move and records every PG
recovered, the next one, every report in, changes no entry. Counting only no move and no leaving
member settled every run while the split's PGs, not yet reported, could not move.

**A refill keeps a possible last source** (`refill_leaving_test.go`; property 18 of the
[Epoch change model](#epoch-change-model), `ci-refills`, `neg-refill-sole-holder`,
`neg-stay-sole-holder`)

- A member merely down, refilled, stays as the PG's leaving member beside its replacement, one
  member wider, an hour on as at once; the recovered report for the current interval removes it, and
  so does its disk leaving the pool (`TestARefilledMemberLeaves`).
- A second member missing while one leaves is refilled the same way, so a PG holds as many leaving
  members as went missing. Each goes when its own disk leaves the pool, the other staying a source
  (`TestASecondMissingMemberLeavesToo`); `dropAllLeaving`, which takes them all, strands a write
  (`neg-drop-all-leaving`, `TestDropAllLeavingStrandsAWrite`). A member missing at `maxMembers`
  stays an ordinary member (`TestRefillStopsAtMaxMembers`), and a leaving member with no room lets
  a refill pass (`TestALeavingMemberWithNoRoomLetsARefillPass`).
- Rep3 on 6 disks, a second disk lost during the copy, together with the first, or the refill
  member itself: repair ends on three copies with no disk returning
  (`TestASecondFailureFinishesRepair`). A drain finishes past a dead disk
  (`TestADrainFinishesPastAFailure`).
- Rep2 on 5 disks, the two old disks lost one after the other: a new write is answered within two
  minutes, X reads unfound, and a returning disk heals it (`TestRep2ServesPastTwoFailures`).
- A disk declared lost goes with its leaving member, and the other leaving member stays the source
  it is (`TestADiskDeclaredLostLeavesThePool`). Both old disks declared lost: the PG ends at its
  width and serves, what they alone held unfound until an operator gives it up; given up, the chunk
  is dropped, takes a write as an empty chunk, reads zeros before it, and keeps the write across its
  members' crash and restart (`TestAChunkOnlyLostDisksHeldStaysUnfound`). Both lost together and
  declared lost: peering still needs the last activated interval, so the PG stays stopped, reads and
  writes refused, until given up: peering then skips the lost intervals and the PG takes writes
  (`TestTwoDisksLostTogetherStayStopped`).
- An operator's give-up (property 23 of the [Epoch change model](#epoch-change-model), registered
  as `invOnlyLost`): refused with nothing unfound, with
  both old disks down and not declared lost, and on an interval an edit started that has not
  activated; under `giveUpFound`, `giveUpWithCandidate` and `giveUpNotStopped` each commits and
  breaks `invOnlyLost` (`neg-give-up-found`, `neg-give-up-candidate`, `neg-give-up-not-stopped`,
  `TestPlantedGiveUpBugsLoseWrites`). After the stopped give-up, Z acknowledged on member B alone
  while A is in `maintenance` reads back once A leads with B in `maintenance` and B returns; under
  `skipPastGiveUp`, A's peering skips B's interval and Z reads back lost (`neg-skip-past-give-up`,
  `TestPeeringPastAGiveUpKeepsLaterWrites`). After X's give-up, A lists only Z, written since; A
  restarts with the give-up in its first table and keeps the listing, so with B declared lost Z
  reads unfound, not zeros (`TestARestartKeepsTheListingOfAWriteAfterAGiveUp`). A give-up staged with
  an edit replacing both members is left out of that table, and Y, which it does not record, reads
  back (`TestAGiveUpWithAnEditKeepsTheChunksItDoesNotRecord`). Seeded, on the real control-plane
  group: writes to three chunks while disks are cut off, come back, are declared lost and restart,
  and give-ups at random, each declaration and give-up committed through `Control.Lost` and
  `Control.GiveUp`; no committed give-up breaks `invOnlyLost` and no chunk written since every
  give-up of it reads zeros (`TestGiveUpsUnderFaultsLoseOnlyWhatIsLost`). Most of its give-ups are
  refused, as they should be: 4 commit over its 20 seeds a commit and 18 over the 200 of
  `scripts/seeds.sh`, about the stand-in's 15. Each give-up bug planted in the control plane's check
  breaks `invOnlyLost` there, over seeds 0 to 39: `giveUpFound` in all 40 (seed 0 in the test),
  `giveUpWithCandidate` in seed 10 alone and `giveUpNotStopped` in 2, the first seed 13
  (`TestPlantedGiveUpBugsBreakTheGiveUpRun`).
- A give-up commits interval k+1 as a copy of k: next to a settings change, an edit, a mark
  change, a refill, a balance move or an activation of its PG it is left out of the table, alone
  it commits (`TestAGiveUpCommitsOnlyWithItsMembersUnchanged`). A store's drop leaves a write
  ordered while it persists, of a later interval, the chunk's version, across a restart too
  (`TestAWriteOrderedDuringADropOutlivesIt`); a drop of interval 4 over a chunk listed in interval
  5 keeps it, with a write of interval 4 ordered meanwhile the newest version in the store and the
  index alike (`TestADropKeepsAChunkListedLater`), and a replica sends no such drop
  (`TestAGiveUpSendsNoDropOfAChunkListedLater`). The index's drop leaves a chunk with a later
  version or listing alone (`TestADropLeavesAChunkWithALaterIntervalAlone`); a drop round-trips
  the disk log, interval 0 or a version refused (`TestDroppedEntryErrors`, `FuzzDecodeRecord`).
- A refilled primary returns behind the others, and does not lead while one of them is up
  (`TestARefilledPrimaryReturnsBehindTheOthers`).
- A leaving member that is up takes the place of a member merely down, which leaves in turn
  (`TestStayKeepsTheMissingMember`).
- Rep2, X on both disks, no write in flight: one disk out past `degraded_refill_after`, then the
  other before the refill member copied X. Both come back whole, X reads OK, and the recovered report
  takes the PG back to its width. Copying stays off for the outage with the `noRecovery` plant, since
  in the simulator it finishes in under a tick (`TestARefillKeepsTheLastSourceOfAPG`).
- Rep2: Y acknowledged on one old disk and on the refill member, which lists the chunk; the other old
  disk returns lacking Y; the disk with Y goes for `refill_after` and the leaving disk takes its
  place. The disk with Y stays, leaving (`TestAStayKeepsTheLastSource`).
- Invariant: an acknowledged write a disk can serve, a member can serve. `refillSoleHolder`, which
  deletes a member merely down, breaks it in both runs (`TestPlantedPeeringBugsBreakTheOracle`).

**A member on a full disk moves before the report** (`park_full_test.go`,
`placement_missing_test.go`; [design](design.md#epoch-changes-and-failure-detection);
[Epoch change model](#epoch-change-model), `ci-parks`, `ci-parks-lost`, `neg-swap-full`,
`neg-park-unpaired`)

- Placement: a `Stuck` PG's member its primary reports short, on a disk at its log reserve, is
  parked leaving beside a member on the eligible disk furthest below its target, in one table and
  with no recovered report, and the recovered report of that interval removes it. It stays as it is
  with no eligible disk, with only the added disk eligible but at its own reserve though under
  `write_limit`, with the report's bits naming other members, with a report of an earlier interval,
  and with the PG not `Stuck`; with the PG's only spare disk an up leaving member, that member does
  not take the full member's place; a PG not `Stuck` beside it is untouched
  (`TestAFullMemberOfAStuckPGIsParked`).
- Rep2 on five disks, X acknowledged on both members: the second member's disk at its reserve and
  short, a third disk joins and the full member is parked beside it; the first member's disk is then
  declared lost and replaced before the third copies anything, and the parked member still serves X
  (`TestAFullMemberParkedKeepsWhatItHolds`). `swapFull`, which deletes the full member in the table
  that adds its replacement, strands X there.
- Rep2 on two disks, both members at their reserve and short, no disk eligible: neither moves
  (`TestFullMembersWithNoEligibleDiskStay`). `parkUnpaired`, which parks a member with no
  replacement, parks both, and the recovered report removes every member, which the run's removal
  invariant reports. Both plants fail `TestPlantedPeeringBugsBreakTheOracle`.
- A report whose bits of short members disagree with its count of lacking copies is malformed
  (`TestWireReportLeads`).

**Errors**

- Refill that finds no eligible disk never panics, keeps the failure-domain rule, and leaves the
  member marked down. One example: `rep3` on 3 nodes after one node fails
  (`TestRefillWithNoEligibleDisk`).
- A PG with no eligible disk for refill raises `Stuck` once it has copied nothing for 60 s, and
  `rock-solid pool status` states the layout fact (`rep3` on 3 nodes: losing a node leaves its PGs
  degraded until it returns). It never raises `CannotReprotect`.

## Replica primary

`internal/chunkstore`, with a simulated single authority standing in for the control plane. k.n is
version (interval k, counter n), as under [Wire messages](#wire-messages).

**Versions**

| Chunk state when a write arrives at a primary in interval k | Version given |
| --- | --- |
| Absent (version 0), k = 7 | 7.1 = `0x0000000700000001` |
| Newest ordered 7.5, still pending | 7.6 |
| Newest committed 6.9, nothing pending, k = 7 | 7.1, which orders above 6.9 |
| Parent PG split at interval 9, chunk at 9.4, child starts at 10 | 10.1 |
| Newest ordered 7.(2³² − 1) | The write waits: the PG's pending writes commit, the primary asks for interval 8 and re-peers in it (no lease wait, since the primary stays), then the write gets 8.1 |

- 1.(2³² − 1) orders below 2.1.
- A chunk at 7.(2³² − 3) takes 5 writes. Writes 1 and 2 get 7.(2³² − 2) and 7.(2³² − 1). Write 3
  waits until the PG's pending writes commit and interval 8 is peered, then gets 8.1. Writes 4 and 5
  get 8.2 and 8.3. Other PGs see no refusal. A 32-bit counter lasts 1.2 hours at 1 M writes/s to one
  chunk and 50 days at 1,000 (PG epochs spike C1).

**Interval check at a member whose table has PG 7 in interval 42**

| Tag | Sender's table epoch | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 42 | Older or newer than the member's | Accepted |
| 41 | Any | Refused, with the member's table epoch and 42 |
| 43 | Newer | The member fetches a table at least as new as the sender's; if PG 7 is then at 43, accepted |
| 43 | Newer | As above, but PG 7 is at 44 after the fetch: refused with 44 |
| 43 | Older | Refused with the member's table epoch and 42: no correct sender sends it, and a refusal costs nothing |

**Client writes at primary B, whose term began in interval 42; PG 7 is now at 44 after two replica
swaps**

| Client tag | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 42, 43 or 44 | Accepted |
| 41 | Refused with 44; the client fetches the table |
| 45 | B fetches the table first |

- A client write that B held when interval 43 ended under it is ordered again, once B has re-peered
  in 44, with a version of interval 44.
- Held across a whole table: B holds a write in interval 2 and next adopts a table at interval 4
  whose past intervals show B leading 3: the write is ordered as 4.1 once B has re-peered. When
  they show another primary leading 3, the write is refused with 4.

**Commit, map and read**

- A write goes to every member in parallel while the primary appends it to its own log, and is
  acknowledged once every live member holds it: the pass that orders it sends it to both replicas
  and writes the primary's disk. With one member cut off, the write is not acknowledged, the other
  two hold it, and a read returns the version before it.
- A version that fails at a member or on the primary's own disk fails with every later pending
  version of its chunk; their clients are refused with the newest table the primary knows of, and
  none is mapped.
- A failed version ends the interval. Disk 3 refuses 1.1 of an absent chunk: the client is
  refused, the primary asks for interval 2 once no version of the PG waits for a member or its own
  log, holds the next write,
  and writes nothing over the absent chunk. Once peering, standing in, drops 1.1 and the primary
  activates in 2, the held write is 2.1 on every member, merged on zeros.
- A write waiting behind a base read when its interval ends is refused at once and never ordered,
  whether a table ends the interval or a write to another chunk of the PG spends its counter; with
  the interval 2 table adopted and `Settle` tried while the read is in flight, the next write is 2.1
  merged on 1.1 on every member. A waiting write whose PG leaves the table is refused, never sent.
- Disk 2 in `maintenance` and disk 3 refusing 1.1, the only member it went to: the client is
  refused and the primary goes on.
- 1.2 commits, its acknowledgments in, while 1.1 still waits for disk 3, which then refuses 1.1
  (a resend after a lost acknowledgment): the primary still asks for interval 2, and `Settle` at 0
  drops both, the committed 1.2 included, their clients refused.
- A gated version whose records all fail keeps the chunk at its number: it is never handed out
  again. The primary's own disk failing 1.2's write refuses 1.2 and 1.3 behind it, and the primary
  asks for interval 2 once.
- A PG whose entry lists more up members than a primary fans out to (8 besides itself) has its
  writes refused, not the primary panic; a table listing one disk twice in an entry is malformed.
- The primary maps the write into its index at commit, not when its own log entry is durable. A
  replica maps it when durable.
- A read without `at_ver` while 7.6 is pending returns 7.5's blocks without waiting. Once 7.6
  commits, the read returns 7.6.
- `at_ver` of a frozen version is served by any member holding it and never waits for a writer.
- `at_ver` of a version still pending at a replica never returns its bytes: a replica serves only
  frozen versions, and `at_ver` of a version neither frozen nor committed is refused.
- `expect_ver` is compared with the newest ordered version, pending ones included. 7.6 is pending:
  a write with `expect_ver` 7.6 is ordered as 7.7, and one with 7.5 fails with a mismatch and
  changes nothing.
- Commits that arrive out of version order are still mapped in version order. A planted variant that
  maps them in arrival order must fail, as chunk epochs spike R2 did; replay itself is covered by
  the [Chunk index](#chunk-index) section's R1 case.
- A chunk's writes go to each member in version order. After a `PeerLost` and reconnect they are
  sent again from the oldest unacknowledged one, in the same order. Invariant, checked after every
  step of the replica tests: no `NetSend` of k.(n + 1) to a member before k.n on one connection.
- A write ordered between a `PeerLost` and the resend waits behind the resend: 1.1 is written while
  disk 3 is cut off, the cut heals, and 1.2 is written before the resend is due; disk 3 gets 1.1
  and then 1.2, and maps both.
- A member answers a version sent again while its first copy is still being logged with that
  copy's outcome, and logs it once. A member whose disk fails the first copy of 1.1 refuses both
  copies. 1.1 sent again once its copy is done is refused, and so is 1.2 after it.
- A member that failed to log k.n of a chunk refuses the chunk's later versions in interval k: 1.1,
  a punch whose edge block finds the pool full, then 1.2 arriving later; and 3.2 already waiting
  behind 3.1 for write admission when 3.1 fails before it is logged. A member that refuses a
  version of its current interval for any other reason, as under a table marking it in
  `maintenance` at that interval, refuses the later ones too, even once its table marks it up
  again: disk 3 refuses 1.1 under such a table and then 1.2 under the table marking it up
  (`TestAMemberThatRefusesAVersionRefusesTheLaterOnes`).
- A member restarting from its disk refuses 1.1 and 1.2 while its store recovers, and 1.3 once it serves, which
  follows the failed 1.1; each `MemberFail` record says `unready`.
- Disk 2 answers 1.1's first send, which a lost connection left unanswered, after the primary sent
  1.1 again: the primary keeps the buffer until the second send is answered too (driver contract).
- `Settle` refuses a chunk with a gated write's record in flight (`ErrUnresolved`), settling
  nothing, and takes it once the record is durable; it refuses a chunk whose PG the primary has
  activated (`ErrActive`).
- `Activate` waits for every pending version to be settled. Disk 2 in `maintenance`, disk 3
  refuses 1.1 of an absent chunk, so no member holds it: in interval 2, `Activate` refuses with
  `ErrUnresolved` and `Unsettled` lists the chunk; once `Settle` at 0 drops 1.1 the PG activates,
  and the next write is 2.1 on every member, merged on zeros.
- A demoted primary is a member. Disk 1 orders 1.1 while disk 3 is cut off, and interval 2 makes
  disk 2 primary with disk 1 an up member: disk 1 refuses 1.1's client, maps 1.1 as a member maps
  what it logs and frees its buffer, and disk 2's 2.1 of the chunk is answered once the cut heals.
  A write whose counter ran out after its PG's lead moved away is refused.
- An index rebuild is a restart to the primary. Disk 1's index rebuilds while 1.1 waits for
  cut-off disk 3: the store answers 1.1 in doubt (`ErrInDoubt`) and a late commit maps nothing
  twice, since the rebuilt index maps 1.1 as a restart's replay would; disk 1 refuses 1.1's client,
  refuses pg0's reads and asks for interval 2. That the primary then serves no version peering
  dropped needs its persisted missing list, under [Peering and read leases](#peering-and-read-leases),
  and recovery, under [Recovery per PG](#recovery-per-pg).
- Peering's decision on a chunk (`Settle`), as the store takes it: with 4.1 to 4.3 pending, keeping
  4.2 maps and acknowledges 4.1 and 4.2 and drops 4.3, whose client is refused; the next interval's
  first write is 5.1, merged on 4.2's bytes. At the primary, 1.1 waiting for a member that interval
  2 marks down is acknowledged once peering keeps it.
- A dropped version that froze snapshot epoch 1 gives the freeze back: the next write at epoch 1
  freezes the kept version again, and epoch 1 reads it. Superseding dropped versions in the logs
  that hold them is under [Recovery per PG](#recovery-per-pg).
- Writes 1.1 and 1.2 of one chunk and 1.1 of another, sent while a member is cut off, reach it in
  that order once it is reachable again, and all commit. A planted variant that sends them again
  newest first breaks the send-order invariant.

**Partial blocks** (sub-block writes spike). Block 5 is committed at 7.7.

| Write | Base | Sent to members |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bytes 0 to 99 of block 5, nothing pending | 7.7's block 5 from the live map, CRC32C checked | One merged whole block, 7.8 |
| Bytes 100 to 199 of block 5 while 7.8 is pending | 7.8's merged block | Whole block 7.9 holding both writes' bytes; 7.9 is acknowledged only after 7.8 commits |
| As above, but a member refuses 7.8 (its session fenced, or a new interval reached the member first) | 7.8 never commits in interval 7 | 7.9 is refused too and interval 7 ends; peering decides both, and the client retries in the next interval |
| Bytes 0 to 99 of a block never written | Zeros | Whole block |
| Bytes 0 to 99 of a punched block | Zeros | Whole block |
| Bytes 100 to 8,291 of a chunk (blocks 0 to 2) | Edge blocks 0 and 2 only; block 1 is whole | Three whole blocks; at most two edge blocks are merged per write |
| Whole blocks 3 and 4 | None | Two blocks, no base read |
| Partial write whose base is in the disk's merged-block cache | The cache, no disk read | Whole block |
| Partial write whose base read fails its CRC32C | Fetched from another member before merging; the chunk's later operations wait behind it, in order | A block merged on the good copy, never on the rotten one |
| Partial write whose two edge blocks' bases both fail their CRC32C | Each fetched from another member | Both edges merged on the good copies |
| Punch of bytes 100 to 8,191 | Block 0 merged with zeros; block 1 gets a punch entry | One record |

- Sub-block spike M1 and M9 as seeds: 2 clients, 8 writes pipelined each, 24 writes each, of 1 to
  300 bytes (up to 3 blocks in M9) at random offsets in the first 3 blocks of a chunk, on 3
  simulated nodes, the history completed from the primary's replies. No seed of 500 leaves any
  member's disk different from the acknowledged writes applied in version order. M6's primary
  changes need peering and run under [Peering and read leases](#peering-and-read-leases).
- M2 and M3 as planted bugs: merging on the committed version fails at least one seed of 500, with
  one client pipelining 4 writes or two clients with one write each. Both fail at seed 0, as the
  spike's model failed every seed.
- A base fetch with every member's copy rotten fails the write, refused.
- A rotten base asked of disk 2, which is cut off: once the connection is lost the primary asks
  disk 3, and the write merges on its copy.
- Member faults as seeds (`TestReplicatedWritesSurviveFaults`, 1,000 in `scripts/seeds.sh`): 2
  clients pipeline up to 8 writes and punches each, 24 each, of up to 300 bytes or 3 blocks in the
  first 3 blocks of two chunks of PG 0, with records of at most 3 blocks so most versions take
  several. A seeded schedule cuts members off for up to 30 ms, crashes them, most often while they
  hold a version in part, then sometimes cuts them off for 40 to 80 ms so a resend reaches them
  recovered, fails a disk write (the member is crashed and restarted once its store stops), has a
  member refuse through a table that puts it in `maintenance`, rots a block of the primary's copy,
  half the time cutting off disk 2, which a base fetch asks first, fails the primary's disk in about
  one seed in ten, after which every write is refused, and starts the PG's next interval; the
  primary's own asks start one too. The run's authority is the real control-plane group of
  [Control-plane placement faults](#control-plane-placement-faults): its leader's detector marks the
  disks and starts the next interval of each PG whose marks it changed, and it answers the replicas'
  asks; a member whose disk failed restarts only once the committed record marks it down, and after
  two failed restarts stays up with its store failed, kept down.
  Member crashes and disk failures also land while the PG peers, at a tenth of the rate: each
  restart waits 4 s, and at the full rate peering would never end. The run ends once the table
  follows the committed marks and every disk not lost is up. A primary crash, index rebuild or
  move joins the schedule under [Recovery per PG](#recovery-per-pg): each leaves versions peering
  may drop mapped on the next primary until recovery supersedes them. Invariants, checked after
  every step: a member acknowledges a version only once it maps every block of it; every client
  write or punch gets one reply, and all are answered by the end; the primary maps exactly the
  writes and punches it answered OK, applied in version order, so a refused one is never read back;
  and the epoch checks of [Placement faults and invariants](#placement-faults-and-invariants).
  Answering a resent version OK because the member's newest is at least it fails a seed of 1,000.

**`min_live` and `maintenance`**

| Pool, members down | Writes |
| --- | --- |
| `rep3`, `min_live` 2, one down | Accepted on the 2 live members |
| `rep3`, two down | Rejected until recovery restores a member |
| `rep2`, `min_live` 2, one down | Rejected |
| `rep2`, that node in `maintenance` | Accepted on one copy; resync on return is under [Recovery per PG](#recovery-per-pg) |

**`write_limit` admission.** The pool's `write_limit` is 90%. Member disk X reports 91% fill with
its acknowledgments and heartbeats.

| Write | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Adds live data to a PG with X as a member | Refused with `NoSpace` |
| The same, with every member under 90% (outstanding grants counted by each disk's share) | Admitted |
| X at 88%, 20 blocks of 1,000 granted on the pool, X's share 1 | Refused: 880 + 20 reaches 900 |
| The same with 19 blocks granted | Admitted |
| Flush under a space grant, marked granted in the update's flags | Admitted on the grant alone |
| Overwrite of blocks held live, written after the chunk's latest freeze, held as copies, no freeze due | Admitted; the check costs one index lookup per run of blocks |
| Overwrite of live blocks 3 and 4 plus never-written block 5, in one write | Refused with `NoSpace` (it adds live data) |
| Overwrite of a block a snapshot shares (a freeze is due) | Refused like a new write |
| Punch | Admitted |
| Recovery copy | Admitted |
| Any write while no member is past the limit | No overwrite lookup is made |
| Pool P1 (limit 95%) and pool P2 (limit 90%) on one disk at 92% total fill | P1 admitted, P2 refused: each checks its own limit against the disk's total fill |

- Tables applied as deltas and fetched whole after a gap or CRC mismatch: the cases under [Placement
  computation](#placement-computation), seen from the primary: a delta that follows its table is
  applied, and a gap or a CRC mismatch leaves the table as it was and asks for the whole table.
- A member's acknowledgment carries its disk's live blocks, which the primary then holds as its
  fill.
- A space grant's flush is marked by its client in the update's flags; the primary trusts the mark
  until phase 4's control-plane group gives it the grants to check it against.

## Peering and read leases

`internal/lease` for the leases, `internal/chunkstore` for peering. Constants for every lease case
below and in the other sections: `primary_lease` 4 s (4,000,000 ticks), `lease_drift` 1%, a
heartbeat every 1 s, `rate_window` 10 s, `rate_gap` 100 ms, `max_margin` 50%, 1 tick = 1 µs. k.n is version (interval k, counter n).

**A kept version's client at activation**

- `rep3`, `min_live` 2, disks 1, 2, 3 holding X. Disk 2 drops out. Disk 1 logs W and sends it to disk 3, which is cut off before logging. Disk 2 returns as disk 3 is marked down. Disk 1 peers with disk 2: W is kept and listed for disk 2, disk 1 is its one copy, and the client is refused. The resend lands on disks 1 and 2 and is answered OK. Once recovery has made disk 2 clean, disk 1 is lost for good: X and W read from the others.
- The same with a refill in place of the returning disk, on `rep2` and `rep3`: every other member is cut off, the refill brings the PG back to `min_live`, W is refused, its resend reaches both, recovery makes the refill clean, and a second refill that removes the first disk leaves W readable.
- `rep3`, `min_live` 2, W on disks 1 and 2 when disk 3 goes down: the client hears OK at activation, with two copies.
- `rep2`, `min_live` 2, the second member in `maintenance`: the primary's one copy and the member in `maintenance` make two, and the client hears OK, as it would on a write in that interval.
- A `rep3` pool with `min_live` 1: one copy is enough and the client hears OK, unless the primary lists the chunk: it then counts no copy, so its client is refused and sends the write again.
- `rep1`: W has no member to wait for, so it commits on its own log, and the client hears OK across an interval that ends under it.
- A version that committed on every member it was sent to, behind a failed version: it keeps its OK at activation, whatever the count.
- A refused version whose one holder then dies: the chunk reads unfound, X below it included, though X was acknowledged and is whole on the other two disks, and reads again only when the disk returns. Were it lost for good, X would stay unfound with no operator path.
- A write to a chunk with one clean copy: W1 lands on disks 1 and 2, disk 2 goes down, and disk 3 returns listing the chunk. W2 waits unordered until recovery makes disk 3 clean, and only then is answered OK, so losing disk 1 for good and disk 2 returning leaves W2 readable. Planted away (`noDegradedHold`), W2 is answered OK on disks 1 and 3, disk 1 its one clean copy, and once disk 1 is lost the chunk reads unfound though disk 3 logged W2, until disk 1 returns.
- The wait, measured in the primary-change run over seeds 0 to 99 (`rep3`, `min_live` 2): 2,074 of the 8,833 client writes ordered, in 86 seeds, were held for too few clean copies or while the primary listed the chunk. They waited 6.2 ms at the median, 15 ms at p90 and 4.0 s at p99 and at most; those ordered in the interval they arrived in, 1,859, within 20 ms at p99 and 22 ms at most. The 39 slowest, in seeds 18 and 24, waited out the interval change a member's crash brought. 132 more were never ordered by the replica that held them, which crashed or lost the lead first. In the fault run over the same seeds, 771 of 4,498 were held: 8.1 ms at the median, 1.0 s at p90 and 5.5 s at p99, at most 9.0 s; within their interval 6.1 ms at the median and 1.0 s at p99, the retry after a failed recovery read.

**Serving reads**

- A `rep3` primary holding B's grant but not C's serves no reads, and still takes writes.
- C is marked down in a new interval. Once the primary has re-peered, C's grant is no longer needed.
- A grant that lapses during a pass: the read in that pass is refused.

**Lease time.** The holder counts from when it asked and ends the lease when either clock shows 2.96
s: 4 s less `lease_drift` and less `core.ResumeThreshold`, 1 s, left for a suspend that delivers no
`Resumed`. The grantor counts from when it granted and keeps the grant until both clocks show 4 s.
The request is sent at real time 0 and granted at 0.5 ms. Rates are relative to real time. The
single-clock column is what counting on `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` alone would give (clock slew spike), from a
holder's end of 3.96 s, since that second belongs to the suspend.

| Holder `BOOTTIME`, raw | Grantor `BOOTTIME`, raw | Holder ends (real s) | Grantor ends (real s) | Single-clock |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| exact, exact | exact, exact | 2.960 | 4.0005 | Same |
| +22.6%, exact | exact, exact | 2.414 | 4.0005 | Same |
| −22.6%, exact | exact, exact | 2.960 | 4.0005 | Holder 5.116: 1.12 s overlap |
| exact, exact | +22.6%, exact | 2.960 | 4.0005 | Grantor 3.263: 0.70 s overlap |
| exact, exact | −22.6%, exact | 2.960 | 5.168 | Same |
| −22.6%, exact | +22.6%, exact | 2.960 | 4.0005 | 1.85 s overlap |
| −8.33% (chrony), exact | +8.33%, exact | 2.960 | 4.0005 | 0.63 s overlap |
| exact, −1% | exact, +1% | 2.899 (margin 2.52%: the bound sees the raw clocks 2% apart) | 4.0005 | |
| −100 ppm, −100 ppm (no daemon) | +100 ppm, +100 ppm | 2.9603 | 4.0001 | |
| −1%, −1% (no daemon), before the first bound | +1%, +1% | No lease taken | | |
| −1%, −1%, first lease, from grants `rate_gap` apart, 100 µs round trips | +1%, +1% | By 2.921 (margin up to 2.72%) | 3.961 | |
| −1%, −1%, after a full window | +1%, +1% | 2.928 (margin 2.52%) | 3.961 | |

- With a grantor's `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` 22.6% slow, a crash waits up to 5.2 s for the lease, past
  `node_down_after`.
- A grantor's wait is a timer on `ctx.Now`. If it fires while `ctx.Raw` shows less than the lease,
  the grantor sets another timer for the remainder and joins no peering before it.
- A holder cut off from a grantor whose clocks run 0.5% fast, spending the margin's headroom,
  suspends 0.999 s 1 s after its lease formed, `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` gaining nothing and no `Resumed`
  coming: its lease ends before the grant, and with a second 30 ms shorter it would not
  (`TestTheResumeMarginCoversAHiddenSuspend`; it passes from 0.979 s).
- [property] 10,000 seeds with random rates per node (`BOOTTIME` ±22.6%, raw ±100 ppm) and random
  renewal timing: no holder's lease ever ends after its grantor's. With raw ±4%, and `BOOTTIME`
  slewed or at the raw rate (no daemon), the same holds from the first lease.

**Rate bound.** A grant carries the grantor's raw reading `g`; the holder records its own raw `s`
(request sent) and `r` (grant received).

```text
bound = (g_b − g_a) / (s_b − r_a)
```

The holder keeps a window per grantor node and run ID. When a window's first grant arrives it
asks again `rate_gap` later, and it takes no lease from that grantor until it has a bound. It pairs
the shortest-round-trip grant of the first third of the window's span with that of its last third.
It widens its margin for that grantor by the excess of the bound over 1 + `lease_drift` / 2 = 1.005,
and reports the pair; a margin of `max_margin` or more gives no lease. Times are in µs, and G0 =
50,000,000.

| Case | s_a, r_a, g_a | s_b, r_b, g_b | Bound | Margin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exact rates, 1 ms round trips, `g` read at the worst ends | 0, 1,000, G0 | 3,333,333, 3,334,333, G0 + 3,334,333 | 1.000600 | 1% (600 ppm overshoot) |
| Exact, 100 µs round trips, worst ends | 0, 100, G0 | 3,333,333, 3,333,433, G0 + 3,333,433 | 1.000060 | 1% |
| Grantor raw 1% fast, 100 µs, `g` at midpoints | 0, 100, G0 + 50 | 3,333,333, 3,333,433, G0 + 50 + 3,366,666 | 1.010030 | 1.503%, reported |
| Grantor 0.6% fast | As above | g_b − g_a = 3,353,333 | 1.006030 | 1.103%, reported |
| Grantor 0.4% fast | As above | g_b − g_a = 3,346,666 | 1.004030 | 1%, nothing reported |
| Grantor 1% slow | As above | g_b − g_a = 3,300,000 | 0.99 | 1%: the margin never drops below `lease_drift` |
| Every grant in the first third took 50 ms, worst ends | 0, 50,000, G0 | 3,333,333, 3,333,433, G0 + 3,333,433 | 1.015259 | 2.026%: a false widening, in the safe direction |
| One 50 ms grant among 100 µs ones in the first third | The shortest is chosen | | 1.000060 | 1% |
| The pair started 6 s ago: thirds of the 6 s span, 100 µs, worst ends | 0, 100, G0 | 4,000,000, 4,000,100, G0 + 4,000,100 | 1.000051 | 1% |
| First grant of a window | 0, 100, G0 | | none | No lease from this grantor; a request is sent at r_a + 100,000 |
| Second grant, sent `rate_gap` after the first arrived, 100 µs, worst ends | 0, 100, G0 | 100,100, 100,200, G0 + 100,200 | 1.002000 | 1% |
| The same with 1 ms round trips | 0, 1,000, G0 | 101,000, 102,000, G0 + 102,000 | 1.020000 | 2.5%: the first lease ends 2.90 s after the ask |
| A grant with a new run ID after a reboot, g = 1,200 | | | none | A new window starts and the old run's lease ends; no lease until its second grant |
| Grantor raw about 50% fast | | g_b − g_a = 1.505 × (s_b − r_a) | 1.505 | 51%, past `max_margin`: no lease, reported |

- Open (clock-skew study, recommendation 2): naming the miscalibrated node by majority at the
  control plane is not adopted.

**Pause detection.** The holder's last grant is `a`: s_a = 1,000,000, r_a = 1,001,000, g_a =
50,000,500. The lease taken from `a` has margin m. A heartbeat arriving at holder time r trips the check when
g − g_a > (r − s_a) / (1 − m). The rows use m = 1% unless they say otherwise.

| Event | Check | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heartbeat r = 2,001,000, g = 51,000,500 | 1,000,000 ≤ 1,001,000 / 0.99 = 1,011,111.1 | Nothing |
| The same with g = 51,011,611 | 1,011,111, not > 1,011,111.1 | Nothing |
| g = 51,011,612 | 1,011,112 > 1,011,111.1 | Ends every lease |
| Grantor raw 2% fast, m = 2.5%; g = 51,020,500 | 1,020,000 ≤ 1,001,000 / 0.975 = 1,026,666.7 | Nothing, on every heartbeat |
| `a` is a window's first grant, which gave no lease; grantor raw 4% fast, the second grant at r = 1,101,000 with g = 50,104,500 | None: no lease was taken from `a` | The bound forms and the lease is taken |
| The holder's VM stopped 10 s on kvm-clock, its clocks frozen; heartbeat r = 2,001,000, g = 61,000,500 | 11,000,000 > 1,011,111.1 | Ends every lease |
| A heartbeat with the grantor's new run ID, or with g below the last reading | None: the readings span two runs | Ends the lease taken from that grantor's previous run; a new window starts |
| `Resumed` after a suspend | | Ends every lease |
| `Resumed` after the VMClock marker changed | | Ends every lease |
| `Resumed` at a node that only grants | | Keeps its grants and its waits |

- After any detection the holder sends a grant request to every grantor at once and restarts its
  rate window, asking again `rate_gap` after the first grant arrives. About 100 ms of reads on
  each grantor's leases is lost, and no later bound counts the pause as a fast grantor.
- Peer messages come before reads. In one pass, a queued heartbeat that trips the step check and a
  client read that arrived after it: the trace shows the leases ended before the read, and the read
  is not served on the old lease.
- VM pause spike T6 as simulator seeds, 100 pause phases per length from 0.5 to 30 s. A planted bug
  must fail at least one seed:

| Pause handling | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| The rate bound alone, pauses of 3.5 s and longer (T6a) | Up to 0.99 s of stale reads: a planted bug |
| The rate bound alone, after a pause, with no window restart (T6a) | Every lease shortened for up to 4.0 s: a planted bug for the restart rule |
| Step check on grants only (T6b) | Up to 0.99 s of stale reads: a planted bug |
| Step check on every heartbeat, messages lost, no marker (T6c) | Up to 0.94 s of stale reads: a planted bug |
| Marker alone, messages queued (T6d) | 0.99 s of stale reads: a planted bug |
| Marker and step check, messages queued or lost (T6e) | 0 stale reads at every length; about 100 ms (`rate_gap` plus a round trip) blocked |

**Support epochs and the restart wait**

- A is primary of PG 17 and holds B's grant under support epoch 7.
  - A partition lasts 10 s.
  - A stops serving at 2.96 s on its own clocks.
  - B's grant lapses on both of B's clocks. B moves to support epoch 8 and helps peer interval 42,
    which moves PG 17 to C.
  - The partition heals before A sees that table.
  - A asks to renew, and B answers under 8, not 7: nothing A held under 7 survives, and A counts
    the grant as a fresh lease under 8.
- A grant under a lapsed support epoch is never renewed, whatever the message delay. A duplicated
  old request arriving after the bump gets a grant under 8, never one under 7.
- A holds B's grant and reaches B but not the control plane. B adopts a table that moves PG 17's
  primary away from A; A's heartbeats still report the older table. B refuses A's renewals until A
  reports a table at least as new, so A's lease on B lapses within one `primary_lease` and A serves
  no read of PG 17 after it. Once A fetches the table, B renews again.
- A node that starts at t = 100 s grants no vote and joins no peering before 104 s. The wait is a
  grantor's, so it lasts until both clocks show 4 s: with its `BOOTTIME` 1% fast, not before its raw
  clock shows 4 s too.
- The restart wait also delays a restarted primary's own peering: its own disk answers its peering
  like any member's, so a primary restarting at t = 100 s activates its new interval at about 104 s.
  It asks for no lease during the wait, so it serves reads about `rate_gap` later, once it holds
  its members' grants anew (`TestARestartedPrimaryAsksForNoLeaseDuringItsRestartWait`).
  A member restarted 0.5 s before a new interval of its PG is published holds that interval's
  activation back until its wait is over.
- A fresh grant takes the same table check as a renewal: B holds PG 17 in interval 42, A asks
  afresh with 41's table, and B refuses it until A reports a table at least as new, so A
  gets no lease for PG 17. A planted variant that exempts fresh grants
  (`neg-fresh-grant-no-table-check`) fails "no PG serves reads from two primaries at once".
- A primary asks a lease of each other up member's loop as the membership record names it when it
  learns the loop, not only when it adopts a table: disk 1 adopts a table while it still places disk
  3 at disk 2's loop, then learns disk 3's loop, and keeps serving reads
  (`TestAPrimaryAsksAMemberLearnedAfterItsTableForALease`).
- One grant covers every PG the pair shares and is renewed by the pair's heartbeat. With 2,048 PGs
  on 5 nodes, a pair sends one grant per heartbeat, not one per PG, and the count does not change
  when `pg_count` doubles.

**Leases and peering**

- A grantor joins no peering of a new interval that moves the primary off the holder until its grant
  expires on both clocks, or until the holder has adopted that interval, which its next lease
  request shows by reporting a table at least as new as the grantor's. Interval 2 moves PG 0's
  primary from disk 1 to disk 2: if disk 1 adopts the table too, peering waits at most a heartbeat
  (a planned move); if it does not, the grantors refuse its renewals and join peering once their
  last grant to it ends, 3 to 4 s later.
- A new interval that keeps the primary, such as a replica replaced or a counter bump, needs no
  lease wait. The primary keeps serving reads of committed versions, a chunk its last peering found
  unfound still answered unfound, and holds writes until it has re-peered: interval 2 keeps disk 1
  as primary and a member's list acknowledgments are lost, so it does not activate, yet it reads 1.1
  (`TestAPrimaryThatKeepsLeadingServesReadsWhileItPeers`).
- Peering across several intervals adds no wait: only the last activated interval's primary, or the
  primary of later intervals that kept it, can have served reads, and peering reaches a live member
  of each of those intervals.
- A primary serves no reads in an interval with fewer than `min_live` live members. PG 7 is `rep2`
  [B, C], activated; C is marked down (42), so B would need no lease; C comes back (43) and the
  primary moves to C (44) while B, cut off from the authority, holds 42's table. Peering skips 42,
  and B must not be serving: the planted variant that lets it read breaks "one read-serving primary
  per PG".

**Stopping earlier intervals.** PG 7's last activated interval is 41.

| Intervals since 41 | Members peering must get to adopt k |
| --- | --- |
| 42 only, the usual case | One member live in 42 |
| 42 (never activated), now 43 | One live in 42 and one live in 41 (`TestPeeringStopsEveryIntervalSinceTheLastActivated`) |
| 42 had fewer than the `min_live` it ran under | 42 skipped |
| 42 was short of `min_live` only by members in `maintenance` | 42 stopped and read like any interval that accepted writes |
| No member of an interval to stop is reachable | The PG waits (down) until one returns; it accepts no writes, this is not an error, and declaring its disks lost does not end the wait (`TestTwoDisksLostTogetherStayStopped`) |

- A past interval is judged by the `min_live` it ran under, which the table keeps with its members:
  interval 2 runs under `min_live` 1 with only disk 1 live and takes 2.1; interval 3 raises
  `min_live` to 2 and moves the primary to disk 2. Peering waits for disk 1, crashed and then in its
  restart wait, and keeps 2.1 (`TestPeeringJudgesAPastIntervalByItsOwnMinLive`); judged by the
  pool's current value it activated without disk 1. Refill keeps such a member the same way
  (`TestAwaitedMemberStays`).
- Activation report lost. 42's primary activates and its heartbeat report is lost, then 43 starts.
  43's peering still reaches members of 41 and 42, since the last activated interval is still 41. A
  report for 42 that arrives after 43 was recorded does not lower it.

**Keep rule.** The last activated interval is L = 41 and the new primary peers in 43. A, B and C are
live in 41 unless a row says otherwise. "Lacks" means the member neither holds the version nor lists
it on its missing list.

| A | B | C | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unreachable | 41.8 | 41.7, lacks 41.8 | Drop 41.8; keep 41.7, with C authoritative |
| Unreachable | 41.8 | Down for all of 41 (41 = A, B) | Keep 41.8 |
| Unreachable | 41.8 | 41.8 | Keep 41.8: it may have been acknowledged |
| Unreachable | 41.8 | 41.7, lists 41.8 (written by a peering of 42 that never activated) | Keep 41.8 |
| Unreachable | 41.8, 41.9 | 41.8, lacks 41.9 | Drop 41.9, keep 41.8: a suffix |
| 41.7, lacks 41.8 | 41.8 | 41.8 | Drop 41.8 |
| Unreachable | 39.3, lists 39.4 | Lists 39.4 (L's peering kept 39.4) | The chunk is unfound; 39.3 is never served |
| Unreachable | 41.8, and lists 41.7 from 42's peering, which activated but whose report is lost | Live in 42 only, holds 41.7 | Keep 41.7: 42's decision is the newest one a reached member persisted, and 41.8 is below it only in number |
| Live in 41 only, lacks 41.8 | Not reached | Live in 42 only, lists 41.8 from 42's peering | Keep 41.8: deciding it by 41's members would drop what 42 kept |
| Any | Any | Any; D, new in 43 and not live in 41, holds nothing | D does not affect the decision; recovery gives D the kept versions |
| Unreachable | 41.8 | 41.7, and 41.8 in part | Keep 41.8, with B authoritative: C, listed whatever is kept since its 41.7 has 41.8's records on top, is no source and has no say. Dropping 41.8 would list B too and leave the chunk unfound (`TestAMemberHoldingAVersionInPartDoesNotVetoIt`: a member crashes holding part of Y, the other two hold Y whole, and an edit moves the primary) |
| 41.1 in part over 40.7, live in 43 | 41.2, down in 43 | 40.7, down in 41 and 42 | Keep 40.7, with C authoritative: A gives way only to a member up in 43 that holds 41.2 clean, and there is none. Keeping 41.2 would list A and C and leave the chunk unfound with C up |
| Lists 40.7, live in 43 | 41.2, down in 43 | 40.7, down in 41 and 42 | Keep 40.7, with C authoritative: a member that lists the chunk gives way on the same condition |
| 41.1, and 41.2 in part | 40.7, and 41.1 in part | 40.7, down in 41 and 42 | Keep 40.7, with C authoritative: A holds 41.1 but, holding 41.2 in part, is listed whatever is kept, so is no source of it, and B keeps its say. Keeping 41.1 would list all three |
| 41.7, and 41.8 in part, the one member up in 43 | 41.8, down in 43 | 41.8, down in 43 | Keep 41.7, which A, the primary, holds as its image |

- A disk formatted again or replaced comes back as a new disk, not as the member it was: on
  41.8 acknowledged by A, B and C, C's disk is formatted again and its node reports a new log ID.
  The authority gives it a new disk ID, keeps C's old disk ID down, and peering keeps 41.8 from B.
  The planted variant that keeps C's old disk ID for the new log drops acknowledged versions in the
  primary-change seeds (below): 20 of 500 seeds fail, the first, seed 15, on "no acknowledged version
  is ever dropped".
- A member answers only peering messages that name its own disk. Disk 3, which took 1.1, is
  formatted again and comes back as disk 4 at the same loop while the table still lists disk 3 up
  there; interval 2 moves PG 0's primary to disk 2, and peering waits for disk 3 rather than taking
  disk 4's empty answer and dropping 1.1 (`TestADiskFormattedAgainAnswersNoPeeringForItsOldID`).
  Recovery reads too: disk 1, down in interval 2, misses 2.1 and leads interval 3 with disk 2
  down, so disk 3 is its only source; disk 3 is formatted again as disk 4, which answers no
  recovery read for disk 3, and disk 1 keeps the chunk listed rather than taking disk 4's empty
  image over 2.1 (`TestADiskFormattedAgainAnswersNoRecoveryReadForItsOldID`; the primary-change
  run's seed 34 found it).
- A log ID reported on another device than its disk's, up or down (a cloned drive), is refused,
  and the disk that reported it first keeps its ID; a down disk reported from another node on its
  own device has moved, and keeps its ID (`TestDisksAreKnownByTheirLogIDs`).
- Before the primary activates, each member persists its missing list: for each chunk it lacks or
  holds a dropped version of, the kept version it must get. With one member's acknowledgments of
  its list lost, the primary reports no activation and answers no held write until one arrives
  (`TestNoActivationBeforeEveryMemberPersistedItsList`); the planted variant that activates before
  every member persisted its list is `neg-activate-before-durable` under [Placement faults and
  invariants](#placement-faults-and-invariants). Reads and removal of entries
  are under [Recovery per PG](#recovery-per-pg).
- A member's log holds a chunk's versions in order, so a kept version never follows a dropped one;
  the simulator checks this after every step.
- A partial-block write to a chunk whose kept versions are not yet on the new primary waits: once
  it has settled the chunk, its index maps a version other than the kept one, lacking it or, after a
  restart, mapping a dropped one, or its own store listed the chunk before the decision. Disk 3, down
  in interval 1, leads interval 2 and lacks 1.1, which peering keeps from disk 2: a partial write to
  the chunk waits, as does a whole-block write to it, the primary listing the chunk, while a partial
  write to another chunk goes ahead (`TestAPartialWriteWaitsForTheKeptVersion`). Disk 3, down in interval 2, misses 2.1 of block 0 and
  lists it in interval 3, where a whole-block write to block 1 brings its copy to 3.1; leading
  interval 4, which keeps 3.1, it still lists the chunk, and a partial write to block 0 waits rather
  than merging on 1.1 (`TestAPartialWriteWaitsWhileThePrimaryListsTheChunk`; found by the
  primary-change seeds). A primary that kept leading and dropped its own pending version, never
  mapped, lists the chunk, since replay would map it, and still merges on it
  (`TestAFailedVersionEndsTheInterval`).
- A read of a chunk the primary's peering found unfound is answered unfound.
- A primary whose store failed refuses the writes it holds and every one not yet answered, and takes
  no more: its PGs peer on another primary, which decides whether their versions stay.
- A version whose client the primary refused when it failed at a member can still be kept: a member
  that logged it and refused it when it was sent again holds it. The replica primary's seeded fault
  run checks that the primary maps exactly the versions it answered and those the next peering kept.
- Sub-block spike seeds on replicas, the primary-change seeds
  (`TestPeeringKeepsAcknowledgedWritesAcrossPrimaries`, 500 seeds in `scripts/seeds.sh`): two
  clients pipeline 8 sub-block or whole-block writes each to two chunks of PG 0 while a stand-in
  authority, knowing disks by `DiskRecord` and computing every table with `Next`, records the
  activations and asks the replicas report, marks the primary down and moves it to a member it picks,
  marks replicas down and up, restarts the primary and formats a member's disk again. In half the
  seeds the primary moves only to members that stayed live throughout (M6); in the rest a member
  marked up again may lead though it missed writes. In a quarter of the seeds these changes also land
  while the PG peers, at a tenth of the rate: at the full rate a primary restarts every ~40 steps and
  the run spends its time taking new intervals. Every acknowledged version is kept, no two
  members hold different data under one version, and every member that lists nothing maps the kept
  writes applied in version order. M9's writes up to 3 blocks long are the replica primary's
  byte-oracle seeds.
- Planted variants fail the primary-change seeds (`TestPlantedPeeringBugsBreakTheOracle`), each
  checking its invariant alone, where the spike's model failed 500 and 458 seeds of 500 for M7 and
  M8. The epoch change model's counterexamples planted in these seeds are under [Placement faults
  and invariants](#placement-faults-and-invariants).

| Planted bug | Seeds of 500 failing | First | Invariant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M7: peering drops a subset of a chunk's pending versions, not a suffix (`Settle` drops the first kept one below the newest; `TestSettleMapsTheKeptVersionsAndDropsTheRest` fails at once) | 26 | 60 | "a member listing nothing maps the kept writes applied in version order" |
| M8: a partial-block write merges before the primary holds the versions peering kept | 11 | 16 | The same |

- A restarted primary asks for a new interval of each PG it leads, peers in it, then serves
  (`TestARestartedPrimaryTakesANewIntervalBeforeItServes`); only a store opened at start, not one
  formatted, asks.
- Activation is reported on the next heartbeat, and on every heartbeat after until a table records
  it. The authority records the last activated interval in a later table that starts no interval,
  and trims the past intervals' member lists.
- Before it activates, the new primary hands its store the decision on every chunk with versions
  still pending from an earlier interval (`Replica.Settle`): a primary that kept leading after a
  version failed at a member keeps or drops that version and the chunk's later ones by the keep
  rule, maps the kept ones and answers their clients, and its next write to the chunk merges on the
  newest kept version.
- A member back from an outage shorter than `refill_after` is marked up in a new interval and, after
  peering, receives only the versions on its missing list: in a seed where it missed 100 writes to
  a PG of 10,000 chunks, recovery copies those 100 chunks' blocks and no others.
- Open: peering's duration. It compares every chunk's newest version from every member, so it grows
  with the chunks a PG holds (open question "Peering's cost"). Measure it on 3 nodes with several TB
  each before setting a bound.
- The phase 1 trace rules `peering-before-write` and `peering-before-read` require a reply from
  every peer a loop asked, which replica peering does not meet: it asks every up member of the
  interval and of each past interval it must stop, then decides once every up member of the interval
  and one up member of each such past interval answered. They check no replica trace; the
  primary-change seeds and the per-wait tests above check replica peering.

## Failure and fail-slow detection

`chunkstore.Detector` stands in for the control-plane leader's failure detection. The tables run it
alone, fed heartbeats, `member_timeout` reports and probe answers on its own clock, with tables
computed from its marks by `Next` (`detector_test.go`); the scripted cluster rows run it on a
simulated node of its own that three rep3 replicas heartbeat over the simulated network, beside the
stand-in authority of [Peering and read leases](#peering-and-read-leases), which publishes a table
whenever its marks change (`detect_cluster_test.go`). The seeded row runs on the real control-plane
group of [Control-plane placement faults](#control-plane-placement-faults) instead: its leader's
detector marks the disks, and the row reads each mark from the committed disk record. `node_down_after` 5 s, `member_timeout` 1 s,
`slow_disk_factor` 10×, `slow_disk_window` 1 minute, `refill_after` 10 minutes, `flap_count` 5,
`flap_window` 10 minutes.

**Node failure and hung disks**

| Events | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Heartbeats every 1 s, the last at t = 10.0 s | Marked down at t = 15.0 s, in a table that starts a new interval of every PG with a member on the disk, and no other |
| A heartbeat at 14.9 s | Not marked; the 5 s count restarts from 14.9 s |
| A primary reports member M after waiting 1 s; the direct probe answers that M's log failed | M is marked down at once, not after 5 s; a second report while the probe is out sends no second probe |
| The same report; M's node and loop are up, but a write M's disk took 1.2 s ago has not completed | The probe answers from memory with age 1.2 s; M is marked down at once |
| The disk's oldest unfinished I/O is one of its log's format writes or flushes, or a flush whose round a later flush already made durable | The log ages it like a round's write, so the probe reports it (`disklog` `TestOldestAgesEveryFormatWriteAndFlush`, `TestOldestAgesAFlushALaterFlushRetired`) |
| The same report, and the answer names another log | M is marked down |
| The same report, and M's loop does not answer within 1 s | M is marked down 1 s after the probe, as silent: it is marked up at its next normal heartbeat |
| The same report reaches a new leader before M's first heartbeat to it | No probe: M's heartbeat, due within a second, stands for it, and a healthy one leaves M up |
| The same report, and the probe answers with no I/O older than 1 s | M is not marked |
| A report naming a disk the record does not know, or an answer to no probe out | Ignored |
| No report; a disk's heartbeat shows its oldest unfinished I/O 1 s old (the primary's own disk, or one holding only shard replicas) | Marked down from that heartbeat |
| A disk's heartbeat shows its open log failed | Marked down from that heartbeat, until heartbeats show a working log for a whole `slow_disk_window`, which takes recovery |
| A discard has been unfinished for 3 s; no read, write or flush is older than 1 s | The store's oldest age is 0: discards are left out (`detect_store_test.go`) |
| A stalled disk whose marking leaves a PG below `min_live` | Marked down anyway |
| A stalled disk whose I/O completes; then normal for 50 s, then a whole minute | Stays down for 50 s; rejoins after the whole `slow_disk_window` |
| `rep2` with `min_live` 2 on three disks; disk A stalls once, then heartbeats normally | Marked down, and up at its first normal heartbeat: its PGs are below `min_live` without it, so they serve nothing either way. No member moves, though the third disk could take A's |
| A stalled disk normal for 58 s, then stalled again, then normal for a whole minute | The second stall restarts the window; it rejoins a whole minute after it |
| A new control-plane leader whose lease starts at t = 30 s; disk A is never heard from again | A is marked down at 35 s: the count starts from the lease, not from A's last heartbeat under the old leader |
| A new control-plane leader at t = 10 s; disk A was marked down as stalled at 3 s | A stays down since 3 s, as the disk record holds it, and rejoins after a whole `slow_disk_window` of normal heartbeats, the record marking it up then |
| The detector's own node stops for 4.5 s, counted by its clocks, and the heartbeats sent meanwhile arrive together after it, its timer firing late or not | Nothing is marked: an event more than two heartbeats after the detector's last, or `Resumed`, gives every disk one more heartbeat |
| Every disk falls silent at once after t = 10 s | All are marked down by 16 s, within a heartbeat after `node_down_after` |
| A disk flapping: silent 5 s, then heartbeating, every 10 s | Marked down at its 1st to 5th flap and up at its next heartbeat after the first four, each flap starting two intervals of every PG with a member on it (F1); in a `rep3` pool and in a `rep2` pool never refilled, since no outage reaches `refill_after` or `degraded_refill_after`. At the 5th mark within 10 minutes it stays down |
| The damped disk then heartbeats normally for 9 minutes, then 10 | Stays down for 9 minutes; marked up after the whole `flap_window`. In `rep3` its members, down for `refill_after` meanwhile, have been refilled |
| A disk marked down as stalled 5 times within 10 minutes | Stays down until its heartbeats have been normal for a whole `flap_window` |
| `rep2` on two storage nodes; disk B damped at its 5th mark, then heartbeating normally | Marked up at its first normal heartbeat, since its PGs would otherwise stay below `min_live` with no disk to refill onto |
| `rep2` with `min_live` 1 on three disks; disk B goes down, then disk A, which ran their PGs alone, is damped at its 5th mark | Marked up at its first normal heartbeat, though the third disk could take its members: peering waits for A in those PGs, so placement would not refill it |

Cluster runs, each with a client keeping six one-block writes in flight over all four PGs:

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Seeded, 9 seeds a commit and 500 in `scripts/seeds.sh`: one disk's node cut off from every other node, its disk hung, or its log failing a write; in every other nine seeds, clocks slewed and drifting, delivery jittered up to 20 ms, and the control plane's node stopped for up to 4.5 s before the fault | Marked down within 1 to 5.1 s of the cut (sooner than `node_down_after` when a primary waits on it: its probe goes unanswered), 1 to 2.5 s of the hang, or 1.5 s of the failure, a quarter wider either way on noisy clocks; before it, primaries report their members' latencies; its mark is the only one that ever changes, and no other disk is ever marked down ("the detector marks down only a disk whose node was cut off, whose I/O stalled or slowed, or whose log failed", registered with `sim.Invariants`); the PGs take writes again within 5 s afterwards |
| A disk's node is cut off for 2.5 s while writes wait on it | Marked down as silent when its probe goes unanswered, and up within 2 s of the heal |
| A primary is cut off from one member only, which still answers the detector's probes | The primary reports the member once per `member_timeout` for as long as its write waits: three reports in 3.5 s |
| A primary is cut off from a member for 0.5 s under a write, which it sends again after the heal | The member's acknowledgment of the resend gives no latency: the reconnect is not the disk's |
| A member's disk hangs under a write | The primary reports it, the member's loop answers the probe from memory, and the member is marked down within 2 s of the write: by the probe, or by its next heartbeat when the hung write was not yet 1 s old as the probe arrived; the write is answered; a member that never acknowledged has no latency |

- The new primary of the PGs a crashed node led peers once its grantors' grants to the node have
  ended on both of their clocks, which [Peering and read leases](#peering-and-read-leases) tests
  (`TestAGrantorJoinsNoPeeringMovingThePrimaryOffAHolder`); with a grantor's `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` slewed
  −22.6%, the 4 s grant ends 5.2 s after it was given, so up to about 0.2 s after the down table.
- Open: the link between a primary and member M is down while both reach the authority. The primary
  reports M, the probe answers healthy, and the PG's writes wait while the link stays down (open
  question "A link down between a primary and one member"). Today's expected result is that wait;
  the row changes with the rule the open question picks.
- Open: the 1 s stall threshold is a default, not a measurement (open question "The stall
  threshold").
- Open: node A crashes with writes in flight, and writes to PGs with no member on A never wait. The
  three-node `rep3` cluster cannot express it, since every PG has a member on every node; a cluster
  of more nodes than the pool is wide can.

**Fail-slow.** Disk X is in a pool of 6 disks. Each second, every disk heartbeats and a primary
reports each disk's 99th-percentile acknowledgment latency, X's at the stated ratio to the others'.
The simulated disk's fail-slow cannot stand in here: the scheduler moves its one clock to each
completion it takes, so a slow disk delays the other disks' completions in flight as much as its
own ([Testing strategy](design.md#testing-strategy)).

| X's p99 against the other disks' median | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 12× for 60 s | Marked down as if failed |
| 12× for 59 s, then normal | Not marked |
| 9× for 10 minutes | Not marked |
| 12× for 2 minutes, but marking X down would leave a PG below `min_live` | Not marked; `Detector.Slow` lists X for the pool to report |
| X and Y both 12× for 60 s, in one primary's reports, where marking both down would leave a PG below `min_live` | One is marked down; the other is kept up and listed by `Detector.Slow`: the guard counts the detector's own marks, not only the last table's |
| 12× at 1 s and at 61 s, with no figure for X between | Not marked: a gap of more than two heartbeats between figures restarts the window |
| Marked down, then heartbeats normal for 59 s | Stays down: a disk marked down takes no writes, so its heartbeats judge it |
| Marked down, then normal for a whole 60 s | Rejoins, with a new interval of its PGs |
| Alternating 50 s slow and 10 s normal for 10 minutes | Never marked, and its PGs' intervals never churn |
| A latency for a disk the record does not know | Ignored |

- The primary's figure: 1,000 acknowledgments, 10 of them slow, give the fast bucket as the 99th
  percentile, and an 11th slow one the slow bucket; every latency up to 2^20 µs falls in a bucket
  whose lower bound is at most a third below it, and buckets rise with latency.
- The median is over the pool's other disks that are up and have a figure at most two heartbeats old, the lower
  of the two middle ones for an even count, so a pool of 2 compares a disk with the other; a disk
  with no fresh figure from the others is not judged.

## Recovery per PG

- Most degraded first. PG 12, led by disk 1 like PGs 4 and 9, misses two members and they one
  each: recovery's first write is PG 12's though it is the highest PG, and PG 9, last among the
  equally degraded, starts only once PG 12's have (`TestTheMostDegradedPGRecoversFirst`). A member still listing a chunk counts
  like one not up, and equals go to the lower PG.
- Resync copies only what the returning member missed. Disk 3 misses a write to chunk a while down;
  marked up again, it lists a alone, and recovery copies a's blocks to it alone, never touching chunk
  b, which it missed nothing of, nor disk 2. The primary then reports the interval recovered, and
  again on each retry until a table records it (`TestAReturningMemberGetsOnlyTheChunksItMissed`).
- A dropped version is superseded on every member that logged it, the new primary included, by a
  recovery write logged under an existing version
  (`TestRecoverySupersedesADroppedVersionOnEveryMemberThatLoggedIt`):
  - Chunk epochs spike R3: without recovery, a restart's replay gates the dropped write and drops
    it again at the dropping peering's decision marker.
  - R3b: with it, replay ends at the recovered block.
- Replay rollback: a primary's versions outlast a restart or a lost lead gated, and its image with
  them. The shape is `rep2` with X acknowledged on both members and Y, never acknowledged, on the
  primary alone; each test then has the other member's disk die and be declared lost, and reads X
  back from the primary and Y's block as zero:
  - The primary restarts with Y pending, and replay leaves Y gated for the next peering to drop
    (`TestARestartedPrimaryRollsBackItsPendingWrite`, seeds 1 to 3); it restarts after the peering
    that dropped Y, and its flagged entry gives back its image
    (`TestAPrimaryRestartedAfterItsDropServesFromItsFlag`, seeds 1 to 3), also across a decision
    of its own after the restart (`TestARestartedPrimaryKeepsItsDropsAcrossItsNextDecision`).
  - The primary's disk is marked down and up, a bounce, with Y pending
    (`TestABouncedPrimaryWithItsWritePendingRollsItBack`) and after Y was dropped
    (`TestABouncedPrimaryKeepsTheImageOfItsDroppedWrite`). An operator edit that puts the other
    member first leaves the old primary's disk an up member, and its image goes
    (`TestAnUpMemberUnderAnotherPrimaryCarriesNoImage`).
  - A decision persisted and not activated before the next peering drops Y at the persist
    (`TestADecisionPersistedAndNotActivatedKeepsItsDrops`), and the primary's entry for its
    dropped Y carries the image flag, before and after a restart
    (`TestThePrimarysEntryForItsDroppedWriteCarriesTheImageFlag`, the entry kind's round trip in
    `TestImageEntryRoundTrips`). A demoted primary keeps its pending versions gated until its next
    decision (`TestADemotedPrimaryKeepsItsPendingVersionsGatedUntilItsNextDecision`).
  - Planted: `mapOnReplay`, `replayForgetsDrops`, `ignoreImageFlag`, `mapOnDemote` and
    `forgetImageDown` each lose X on the shape that needs its rule
    (`TestReplayRollbackPlantsLoseX`).
  - After a restart the versions replay holds gated, a whole one and one a crash tore, keep the
    replay point before their records and their segments from the cleaner until a decision
    settles them (`TestReplayGatedVersionsKeepTheirSegmentsAndTheReplayPoint`).
  - A leaving member down when its move completes and then restarted: `rep2` on the slot geometry drains a
    member to a third disk, writes a whole chunk Z once the move's interval recovered, crashes the leaving member
    as the table removing it is published and restarts it, its first table naming it only in a past interval.
    Replay gates Z, pinning its slot and holding the replay point short of its record; once the interval without
    the member activates and a table names it in no interval, it drops Z: nothing gated, no slot pinned or in use,
    and the replay point past Z's record and its segment's newest (`TestALeftMemberDropsItsGatedWritesOnceNoIntervalNamesIt`,
    seeds 1 to 3). The drop is in memory: an index rebuild after it gates Z again, and the replica drops it again
    under the same table (`TestALeftMemberDropsItsGatedWritesAgainAfterARebuild`). A table that arrives while a
    write of Z's chunk has records in flight leaves Z gated until they are durable, then the replica drops it
    (`TestALeftMemberDropsItsGatedWritesOnceTheirChunkIsResolved`). With `leftNeverSettles` Z stays gated
    (`TestALeftMemberThatNeverSettlesKeepsItsGatedWrites`).
    In the store, a version replayed gated and settled to nothing frees its record's segment to the cleaner once later
    writes roll it closed and a checkpoint passes it (`TestADroppedGatedWriteLeavesItsSegmentToTheCleaner`). A slot
    write's record lies in the slot lane's open segment, which closes only once later slot writes fill it. In the
    cluster, once the left member dropped Z, a later move puts its disk back into the PG, and the whole-chunk
    writes it takes there, with checkpoints due every 16 MiB, get Z's segment freed by the cleaner, the replay
    point past Z's record, within 2,000 writes, 685 on seed 1 (`TestALeftMembersDroppedWriteSegmentIsCleanedOnceItTakesWrites`).
    The rcluster's stores otherwise take a 1 TiB replay budget, so they never checkpoint, and a run of about 410
    whole-chunk writes fills the slot geometry's 512 segments on the primary, whose gated writes take no slot.
  - `neg-settle-left-early`'s trace on `rep2` disks 2 and 3, seeded: W is acknowledged in interval 1, which
    activates; disk 3 restarts, its replay gating W, and interval 2 replaces it with disk 1, whose messages to the
    primary are held up, so interval 2's peering hears disk 3 through interval 1, the last activated. Under the
    correct rule disk 3 keeps W gated and the decision keeps W; with `settleLeftEarly`, or with the past intervals
    counted only above the last activated, disk 3's reply without W vetoes it and `invAckedKept` fails
    (`TestALeftMemberSettledEarlyLosesAnAcknowledgedWrite`, seeds 0-19, 200 in `scripts/seeds.sh` in 70 s).
  - Seeded: the primary-change run with each leaving member crashed as the table removing it is published
    (`TestALeftMemberDownAtItsMovesEndKeepsAcknowledgedWrites`, seeds 0-9, 200 in `scripts/seeds.sh` in 18 s) keeps every
    acknowledged write and breaks no invariant, `invLeftGated` included, which judges naming from the cluster's
    table, not the replica's; it logs how many seeds had a restarted
    disk drop a left PG's gated writes, 4 of seeds 0-9 (2 on the real group), and fails if none did. `leftNeverSettles` breaks
    `invLeftGated` at 89 seeds of 500, seed 4 first (`TestALeftPGNeverSettledBreaksItsInvariant`).
  - The stranded-move shapes move the primary instead of restarting it, as the epoch change model's
    negatives do: an operator edit that removes the leaving disk and puts the new member first
    (`TestKeepPastMemberLeavesAMoveUnfound`, `TestNeverUnfoundBreaksTheSourceInvariant`,
    `TestWriteOnUnfoundEndsTheWayBack`, `TestAnEditNamingTheRemovedDiskHealsAnUnfoundChunk`), and
    for the lister a swap of the first two members (`TestListerVetoesLeavesNoMemberASource`). Their
    guards take both shapes, a restart and a move (`TestAnAcknowledgedWriteReadsAfterAMove`,
    `TestALeadChangeDuringRecoveryKeepsASource`).
  - A torn member, holding the kept version whole and part of a later one, is listed, and recovery
    rewrites it (`TestAMemberHoldingAVersionInPartIsListed`); with `unlistTorn` it is left off the
    list and maps the part of Y it holds, on all 20 seeds (`TestUnlistTornMapsADroppedVersion`).
- A recovery write is logged under the version of the interval's last write of the chunk before
  it, or under the kept version, by the members that list the chunk alone. In the store, a member's
  recovery write replaces its chunk with the image past the dropped versions and alone removes the
  entry, across a restart too (`TestARecoveryWriteReplacesAMembersChunk`); the primary's leaves out
  what the interval covered, a whole-chunk punch of the interval leaving it nothing to carry
  (`TestAPrimarysRecoveryWriteLeavesOutWhatTheIntervalCovered`). A gated write the store fails
  before ordering it, for want of a pool buffer, covers nothing and lends the recovery write no
  version (`TestAWriteFailedBeforeItIsOrderedCoversNothing`). A member refuses a recovery write
  under a version it does not stand at: another of the interval than its newest, or the kept one
  once it holds a write of the interval (`TestAMemberRefusesARecoveryWriteAtAVersionItLacks`).
