| Every write of a fenced lock holder that completes is ordered before every write of the next holder; no fenced session's write is applied; a dead client's locks are free within `session_lease` on the leader's clock plus one heartbeat interval while the leader holds its lease and has measured the client, `dead_wait` instead when it has not, or once an unreachable storage node is marked down | Leader side registered by [Control-plane sessions](#control-plane-sessions) (`TestNoSessionIsFencedWhileItsClientsLeaseRuns`): a lock reaches its next holder only once every node with a disk up holds its old holder's fence, and a dead client's locks are free within `dead_wait` (the measured bound is `TestAFenceStretchesByTheMeasuredRate`'s), under acknowledgements that lag, storage nodes cut off for 2 to 27 s, some of them marked down, and failovers. Storage side registered by [Session fencing on storage nodes](#session-fencing-on-storage-nodes) (`TestNoFencedSessionsWriteIsApplied`): a fenced client that writes on for up to 2 s while the fence reaches each node after its own delay, storage nodes cut off, paused and rebooted, and the rejoin gate in the session run |
| On every disk of a pool, (1 + k) times the grants outstanding plus the flushes not yet in fill reports never exceed the disk's gap above the larger of its fill and `write_limit`, and no flush under a grant is refused for space | Registered by [Space grants](#space-grants) (`TestNoGrantedFlushIsRefusedForSpace`) on the leader's counts, with the run's own daemons standing in for [Write-back buffer under space grants](#write-back-buffer-under-space-grants): the pool reaching `write_limit` while daemons buffer and other nodes write through; grant heartbeats lost or delayed, requests and replies; a control-plane failover while daemons stream; a client partitioned from the control-plane leader but not from storage, streaming under its grant; daemon deaths. A daemon crash in the middle of a reuse window is scripted (`TestARestartedCountKeepsTheOldBudgetInF`); a refill moving members onto the fullest disks while grants are out is not in the run |
| An inode ID is never reused; no file's `mtime` goes backwards except by `utimensat`; a file's keys and its directory's entry are in one slot, unless a link or a cross-directory rename put the entry there; no directory is its own ancestor ([Filesystem schema](#filesystem-schema)) | Registered by `TestTheFilesystemWorkloadKeepsItsInvariantsAcrossElections` (`internal/meta`), on the leader's state after every `Txn`: three daemons run every filesystem operation through a three-replica shard, one or two requests proposed in one round, and in 1 step of 6 one daemon's two requests built from one read: two sibling directories renamed into each other, or two `SetAttr`s of one file, applied in either order; the volume's root, inode and slot reservations go through the shard too, and the shard's slots end at 20, so later directories share their parent's slot. Faults: per send, the leader cut off and a new one elected (1 in 10), a replica restarted before or after the round settles (1 in 10), each answer lost (1 in 10); a daemon reconnected without its reservations, its requests resent (1 in 60 steps); a daemon crashed and restarted under a new session, its requests never resent (1 in 120 steps); and the root's creation resent (1 in 40). "Never reused" is read at allocation: no inode ID, the root's included, is handed out twice. The workload has no `utimensat`, so no `mtime` may go backwards. A file's entry outside its slot passes only once a link or cross-directory rename that put it there has committed; directories are not held to their parent's slot. Each invariant fires within the run's 100 per-commit seeds when the code is broken: `Rename` without its ancestors' live checks (36 of the first 120 seeds), `SetAttr` without its check of the attributes it read (74), an inode reservation overlapping the root (92), and inode IDs placed in the wrong slot (120) |
| A replayed request returns its first result and changes nothing | Registered by `TestTheFilesystemWorkloadKeepsItsInvariantsAcrossElections`, under the faults of the row above: a request is resent up to three times, across leader cut-offs, elections, replica restarts, lost answers and its daemon's crash. A resend's result equals the request's first final one; a round holding only the resend leaves the state unchanged; a check failure that is not final leaves no record. `TestReplayedRequestsReturnTheirFirstFinalResult` and `TestResentFSOpsReturnTheirFirstFinalResult` resend at random later points against one state |
| No learner is promoted to voter before it has caught up with its leader's log | Registered by [Voter replacement](#voter-replacement) (`TestVoterReplacementRunsReplayFromTheirSeed`; planted by `TestPromotingALearnerBeforeItCaughtUpBreaksTheInvariant`): a voter replaced while another is down, the replaced voter returning mid-swap, compacted logs, drops and partitions on the learner's links |
| An internal `Txn` repeated after an election changes nothing it did not read | The control-plane leader's builders: [Control-plane sessions](#control-plane-sessions)' seeded run (`TestNoSessionIsFencedWhileItsClientsLeaseRuns`) puts a session start in flight at half its failovers, applying after the new leader's machine read the table, whose first Txn, another start, must fail its check of the table's head (planted without that check by `TestASessionTxnWithoutItsHeadCheckGivesAnIDTwice`, 475 of 500 seeds, as a session ID given twice); the table step's checks are scripted by `TestARacingCommitFailsItsChecks`, `TestAStagedPoolIsCheckedAgainAfterAReload`, `TestATableIsCheckedAgainstEveryPoolItReads` and `TestALostAnswerIsHandedOutAgain`. The filesystem's own: `TestTheFilesystemWorkloadKeepsItsInvariantsAcrossElections` resends the root's creation, which checks the root is absent, unchanged across elections and lost answers, and builds the inode and slot reservations again after a lost answer; those are unchecked atomic increments (`Update` with `Add`), each handing out a fresh range, and the run shows no ID handed out twice. `TestInternalTxnsRepeatedAfterAnElectionFailTheirChecks` scripts a purge entry's guarded delete and a hand-built version bump, each repeated after an election, failing their checks. Owed by phase 6's purger, which builds it: a seeded run with elections while the purger has transactions in flight, and a truncate merging into a purge entry the purger is consuming |

Each invariant is shown to fire: a planted bug for each must fail at least one seed of a scan of about 5 / (its rate over 500 seeds), so a change that re-rolls the draws fails the scan less than 1% of the time, or every time in a scripted scenario. The bugs:

- two leaders allowed in one term, by a vote granted to every candidate, and lease reads served by
  a follower while it supports its leader, both planted under [Leader leases](#leader-leases);
- an entry acknowledged before its flush;
- replay skipping the last record;
- a restart that forgets its vote (planted by [Raft storage in the disk log](#raft-storage-in-the-disk-log));
- a flock `Txn` without its compare;
- a control-plane session `Txn` without its check of the table's head
  (`TestASessionTxnWithoutItsHeadCheckGivesAnIDTwice`);
- a fence committed at the holder's lease end without its margin;
- grants not capped by the gap, and a shrink counted before a heartbeat echoes it (planted under
  [Space grants](#space-grants));
- on the daemon's side, owed by [Write-back buffer under space grants](#write-back-buffer-under-space-grants), which builds it: grants reusable for the
  whole session lease; a reuse window counted from the reply's receipt instead of the request's
  send; flushes reported since the last sent heartbeat instead of cumulatively; a floor grant that
  can be reused;
- in the filesystem run (`TestFilesystemPlantsAreCaughtAcrossElections`): a replay record ignored (caught
  on 500 seeds of 500), a check failure that is not final stored as the request's result (500 of 500),
  and the root's creation without its check, so a resent creation resets the volume's inode and slot
  counters (`FS.resetRoot`, 497 of 500, as an inode ID handed out twice);
- a purger's `Delete` without its `Check`, scripted by
  `TestInternalTxnsRepeatedAfterAnElectionFailTheirChecks` and owed in a seeded run by [Purger](#purger);
- a learner promoted at once (planted by [Voter replacement](#voter-replacement));
- the [Epoch change model](#epoch-change-model)'s two rows for property 2: no support-epoch bump on
  lapse (`neg-no-epoch-bump`), and a leader transfer that keeps the old leader's lease
  (`neg-transfer-keeps-lease`), planted under [Leader leases](#leader-leases);
- the [Sessions and fencing model](#sessions-and-fencing-model)'s leader-side rows: renewals
  answered without the leader lease (`neg-answer-without-lease`), no full lease after a failover
  (`neg-no-full-lease`), counting on the leader's own clock (`neg-count-on-own-clock`), only
  `session_lease` for an unmeasured session (`neg-dead-wait-lease`) and an eviction fenced at once
  (`neg-evict-at-once`), planted under [Control-plane sessions](#control-plane-sessions); and two
  holders of a lock after an eviction fenced at once (`neg-two-holders`), a lock released at the
  fence's commit, while the old holder's session is still listed (`neg-release-on-commit`), and an
  acknowledged version that counts only reachable nodes (`neg-ack-reachable-only`) or waits for
  nodes marked down (`neg-ack-waits-down`). Its storage-side rows are planted under [Session
  fencing on storage nodes](#session-fencing-on-storage-nodes).

## Off-heap slabs

- Slabs are mapped with `unix.Mmap`, outside the Go heap, and every buffer's and every carve's
  address is 4 KiB-aligned (`O_DIRECT` and io_uring need it). A page is viewed as `*[4096]byte` by
  slice conversion, with no `unsafe`.
- The Buffer pool section's scenarios run on the slab pool and the simulator pool alike, from one
  shared suite (`internal/core/pooltest`): explicit capacity, PoolExhausted with requested and
  available, rounding to whole blocks, a reused slot with a new generation, `AllocZeroed` returning
  zeros, the live-buffer limit, freed and stale handles, and exhaustion as an ordinary outcome.
  Poison on `Alloc` is the simulator pool's only.
- Seeded, seeds 1-50 (10,000 in `scripts/seeds.sh`): over 400 random allocations of 1 to 4 blocks
  and frees, in a pool of three regions of 8, 8 and 5 blocks, every allocation lands where a plain
  first-fit scan puts it, and no buffer crosses a region, as both pools share one allocator. A pool
  refuses, by panic, a region under a block, a last region larger than the first, and a short
  region before the last, since its slot arithmetic could not address them.
- Review criterion: a stale handle is caught. A freed handle, and a handle whose slot was reallocated
  (generation mismatch), panic before any byte is read or written, in every build, as the
  simulator pool does: a machine holding one has broken its own state.
- Review criterion: the Go heap stays flat while slabs fill. With 512 MiB of 4 KiB buffers and
  512 MiB of 1 MiB page slabs, every byte written, `runtime/metrics` heap object bytes rise by no
  more than the pool's handle table (8 bytes a block) plus 64 KiB, and the fastest of five forced
  collections is within 1 ms of the fastest of five with empty slabs. Measured: 1.06 MB against
  1.11 MB allowed; 172 against 206 µs.
- A pool over regions: 5 blocks in regions of 2 put a 2-block buffer after a 1-block one at slot 2,
  not across the boundary at slot 1, and the next 1-block buffers at slots 1 and 4; each buffer
  reads back what was written to it.
- Growth: a slab of 3-block regions carving 2 blocks then 2 more maps a second region; the first
  carve's address and bytes are unchanged. Carving more than a region panics.
- Closing a pool unmaps it and empties it in place: a handle live at `Close` panics as past the
  pool's end (0 blocks), through the pool and through a `*core.Pool` kept from before, and the
  closed pool allocates nothing. A slice taken from `Bytes` must not outlive its handle.
- The memtable's page store on slabs: a tree whose `Config.Pages` is a loop slab carves its page
  slabs from it and reads back 20,000 entries written in shuffled order. Every LSM tree test runs
  with its trees' pages on a loop slab ([Slabs for every tree](#slabs-for-every-tree)). A full collection with 20 million entries in
  slabs, half in runs, takes 0.4 ms (`BenchmarkCollection -lsm.entries 20000000`, under the 1 ms of
  the LSM tree section).
- Slabs never hold a Go pointer: a slab and the pool hand out only `[]byte`, and the sans-IO
  analyzer refuses `unsafe`, so no other type can be stored in one.
- Hot-path allocation and free allocate nothing: `testing.AllocsPerRun` of 64 frees and
  allocations is 0, and `BenchmarkAllocFree` reports 0 allocations (10 ns per pair).

## Slabs for every tree

- `Tree.Close` gives the tree's page slabs back, and a slab carves a returned piece again: a tree
  on its own slab, closed, leaves the next tree carving the same pieces without mapping more
  (`TestATreeTakesItsPagesFromConfigPagesAndGivesThemBack`), and a slab hands a returned piece to
  the next carve of its size (`TestASlabCarvesAgainWhatItWasGivenBack`).
- Every dropped tree closes, checked by counting the page bytes out where tests drop stores and
  shards (`looptest.Pages`): the chunk store harness's reopen and small-disk runs, the replica
  cluster at each reboot, a node's device starts that format or fail, the chunk index tests'
  trees, the MetaStore group's restarts and the control-plane host's. Planted: without `Restore`
  closing the tree it replaces, `TestASnapshotHoldsTheEntriesHandedOverInItsCall` fails; without
  recovery closing the index it replaces, `TestRecoveryAndRebuildEqualLiveIndex` does; without a
  failed device closing its store, `TestADeviceWhoseFormatFailsGivesItsPagesBack` does.
- Every LSM test runs its trees on one off-heap slab per test binary (the package's `TestMain`),
  seeded runs included: each seed of `TestMetamorphic`, the range-removal model, the memtable model
  and the copy-on-write views closes its trees and checks its page bytes out are back to zero.
  `TestMetamorphic`'s peak resident memory is the same over 100 and 400 seeds, 483 MiB.
- The chunk index's trees take their pages from slabs: every chunk index scenario passes with
  them. Under the seed flags the chunk store's and MetaStore's trees count their pages on the Go
  heap instead, since a seed's last stores are dropped unclosed at its end.
- Collection takes 0.0% of CPU under request garbage, read as: a tree on slabs adds no collection
  work per cycle and no heap goal over a one-entry tree, within noise, where the same entries as Go
  objects multiply both. `TestATreeOnSlabsCostsCollectionNothing` holds it with ten forced
  collections each: a tree of 500,000 entries on slabs must cost at most twice the one-entry tree's
  CPU per collection plus 1 ms, and raise the heap goal by at most 8 MiB, while a pointerful map of
  the same entries (`map[uint64]*struct{k, v []byte}`) must cost more than that bound, or the
  measure could not fail. Measured on an M4 Pro: 0.24 to 0.41 ms on slabs against 0.28 to 0.48 ms
  for one entry and 34 to 39 ms for the map, heap goal 4 MiB for both trees. Planted: the same tree
  with its pages on the Go heap raises the goal to 42 MiB and fails.
- `BenchmarkCollectionUnderGarbage` shows the same under load: a goroutine makes 256 MB/s of
  short-lived garbage beside lookups, `GOMEMLIMIT` 512 MiB above the live heap, and runtime/metrics
  gives collection's share of CPU, its cycles, its CPU per cycle and the heap goal at the end. Cycle
  counts differ between runs, since a bigger live heap collects less often, so the bar is read per
  cycle and on the goal. At `-cpu 4 -benchtime 4s -lsm.entries 2000000`: one entry 0.26 ms a cycle,
  goal 19 MiB; 2 million on slabs 0.36 ms, 19 MiB; the same with pages on the Go heap 0.41 ms but a
  188 MiB goal, the cost slabs remove; the pointerful control 97 ms a cycle and 476 MiB.
- The daemons hold `GOMEMLIMIT` at `-memory` less the slabs mapped, never below 64 MiB: with a
  256 MiB budget, a 64 MiB pool at start sets 192 MiB and each 64 MiB page slab region then 128 and
  64 MiB, and two more regions keep it at 64 MiB with one log line; a 192 MiB budget takes a 64 MiB
  pool and one page slab to come, while 191 MiB, or two page slabs, is refused; with no budget no
  limit is set (`TestTheHeapLimitIsTheBudgetLessTheMappedSlabs`).
- A removed shard leaves the round driver told nothing more ([Round driver](#round-driver),
  `TestRoundRemovedShardIsToldNothing`), and an ask about a replica its node does not hold is
  answered by `raftshard.Gone` ([Voter replacement](#voter-replacement), `TestAReplicaItIsNotIsAnsweredGone`).

## Event loop

Pass order, the read budget, `writev`, backpressure, the queue cap and the block decision run
stepped, on `looptest` (`internal/loop/looptest`); 1,000 connections, every syscall in the trace, a
slow reader, a loop asleep at the queue cap, goroutines, allocations, the inbox under `-race`, timers
that really sleep and cgroup sizing run on the real kernel (`internal/loop`, Linux only, in `docker run` on a Mac). The loops' own tests frame messages
with `looptest.Wire`, a 2-byte length and the message; the open-loop load run needs a TCP server and
belongs to the TCP network driver.

Review criteria, each a test:

- Stepped, seeds 1-50 (1,000 in `scripts/seeds.sh`): a run of 8 loops over socketpairs, run twice,
  gives the same results and the same event order per loop, and so does a run of 1 loop; the two
  runs' traces are `cmp`-equal, and every pass of both holds one `epoll_wait`, at most one `writev`
  per connection and no more than the read budget per connection
  (`TestSteppedLoopsReplayFromTheirSeed`). Its backpressure run sends bursts of 24 frames of 251
  bytes to one loop over sockets with 2 KiB buffers, so writes stop with `EAGAIN` and mid-frame,
  connections wait for `EPOLLOUT`, and reads fill the 512-byte budget; every message still arrives. Traces name connections by the IDs the loop assigns, not
  by descriptor number (`TestSteppedTraceNamesConnectionsNotDescriptors`).
- Stepped: a loop that calls `Wait` with `block` set while `Pending` reports work (a queued inbox
  item, a due timer, a connection that filled its read budget) fails the run at once
  (`TestSteppedRunFailsALoopThatBlocksWithWorkPending`, on a planted loop).
- Stepped: a pass reads peer connections before clients, whatever order the kernel reports them in
  (`TestSteppedPassReadsPeersBeforeClients`), so a lease holder that lost time ends its leases before
  it serves a read that waited behind the grantor's messages (VM pause spike).
- Stepped: while the bytes queued for writing are at or over `QueueCap` (16 MiB by default), a pass
  reads peers but no client, and the next pass under the cap reads the client
  (`TestSteppedLoopStopsReadingClientsAtTheQueueCap`). Open: the cap's value.
- Real kernel: at the cap the loop modifies its clients to no read interest, so it sleeps rather than
  spinning on a readable client it will not read: with 4 MiB queued behind a peer that does not
  read and a client frame waiting, it makes at most 10 passes in 100 ms, and as many again after the
  muted client hangs up, which closes it (`TestALoopAtTheQueueCapSleeps`).
- Real kernel: a client that reads its replies slowly, then keeps up, gets all 3,000 echoes in
  order; meanwhile the loop's writes block and stop mid-frame and it mutes and unmutes the client
  at a cap of 40 frames (`TestASlowReaderGetsEveryFrameInOrder`).
- Stepped: a frame the driver queues when a write fails and closes a connection (a `PeerLost` the
  machine answers by sending elsewhere) is written in the next pass
  (`TestSteppedFrameQueuedWhileFlushingIsWritten`).
- Stepped: a timer a handler arms again at `Now` fires once per pass, not again within it
  (`TestSteppedTimerArmedAgainAtNowFiresInTheNextPass`).
- `Queue` refuses a frame of no bytes or longer than its buffer
  (`TestQueueRefusesAnEmptyOrOversizedFrame`), `AddConn` a blocking descriptor
  (`TestAddConnRefusesABlockingDescriptor`), and a read that finds nothing leaves the connection
  open (`TestAReadThatFindsNothingKeepsTheConnection`).
- Real kernel: under 1,000 connections, the recorded trace of every pass shows one `epoll_wait`, at
  most one `writev` per ready descriptor, and no more than the read budget read per descriptor, and
  some pass finds all 1,000 ready (`TestAPassUnder1000Connections`). Example of a passing pass:

  ```text
  2000000 1 syscall pass=40 epoll_wait ready=2
  2000001 1 syscall pass=40 read fd=40 bytes=262144
  2000002 1 syscall pass=40 read fd=41 bytes=8192
  2000003 1 event pass=40 NetRecv peer=3 msg=write
  2000009 1 syscall pass=40 writev fd=40 iov=12 bytes=49536
  2000010 1 syscall pass=40 writev fd=41 iov=1 bytes=64
  2000011 1 syscall pass=41 epoll_wait ready=0
  ```

  A pass reading connection 40 past 256 KiB, or writing it twice, fails.
- Real kernel: no syscall a pass makes is missing from the trace
  (`TestNoSyscallOfAPassIsMissingFromTheTrace`). The test counts the seam's `epoll_ctl`,
  `epoll_wait`, `timerfd_settime` and close calls, and takes the thread's `read` and `writev` counts
  from `/proc/thread-self/io` around each pass; both match the trace's records, the reads `Wait`
  makes to drain the eventfd and the timerfd falling under its `epoll_wait`.
- `runtime.NumGoroutine` is the same with 1 and with 1,000 connections
  (`TestGoroutinesDoNotGrowWithConnections`).
- Under a 2.5-CPU cgroup the daemon's sizing gives 2 loops with `GOMAXPROCS` 3, and `cpu.stat` shows
  no throttled periods in 3 s of idle loops (`TestCgroupSizing`, run under
  `docker run --cpus 2.5 -e RS_WANT_LOOPS=2 -e RS_WANT_PROCS=3`, both in the container's own cgroup
  namespace and with `--cgroupns=host`).
- `testing.AllocsPerRun` of a pass is 0, on the real kernel (`TestARealPassAllocatesNothing`) and
  on the stepped kernel (`TestASteppedPassAllocatesNothing`).

Sizing from Go's default `GOMAXPROCS`, which is `min(CPUs, max(2, ceil(limit)))` under a cgroup
limit (`TestSizeFollowsTheCPULimit`):

| CPUs | Limit | Go's default | Loops | `GOMAXPROCS` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | none | 4 | 4 | 5, set by the daemon |
| 4 | 2.5 | 3 | 2 | 3, left to the runtime |
| 4 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2, left to the runtime |
| 4 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 3, left to the runtime |
| 4 | 4 (equal to the CPU count) | 4 | 4 | 5, set by the daemon: the limit is missed |
| 2 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 3, set by the daemon: the limit allows every CPU |
| 1 | none | 1 | 1 | 2, set by the daemon |

- The limit is taken from Go's default `GOMAXPROCS` falling below `runtime.NumCPU()`; the runtime
  reads cgroup v1 and v2 up the process's hierarchy, inside a cgroup namespace or not. A limit equal
  to the CPU count looks like none, and the daemon then sets one P more than the quota pays for.
- A limit lowered while the daemon runs leaves it with no spare P, and it reports that until it
  restarts. Open: what it does when the limit is raised.
- The chart asks for an integer limit of at least 3 CPUs or none; a 2-CPU limit runs one loop, and a
  fractional limit is accepted. Open: whether the daemon reports a fractional limit.

Inbox, timers and syscalls:

- Other loops and worker goroutines hand work through a lock-free multi-producer queue and write its
  eventfd only when the inbox holds no wake already: a burst of 64 items from one producer costs one
  eventfd write and one pass (`TestAnInboxBurstWakesTheLoopOnce`, counted by `Inbox.Wakes`; the write
  is the poster's, on any goroutine, so the loop's trace does not hold it). Real kernel, under
  `-race`: 4 producer goroutines post 80,000 items to a consumer loop that really blocks in
  `epoll_wait`, and every item is handled within 10 s (`TestProducersPostToALoopThatBlocks`). Targets
  from the log per core spike: an inbox hop of one item about 13.6 µs of CPU, 8 items 0.73 µs and
  64 items 0.07 µs per item. Open: tolerance.
- A loop with only a timer left blocks until it is due: a 50 ms timer fires no earlier than its
  deadline, within 4 passes, and the trace holds the `timerfd_settime` that armed it
  (`TestALoopSleepsUntilItsTimer`).
- Timers live in a heap per loop with one timerfd armed for the earliest deadline: after any sequence
  of `SetTimer` actions, the timerfd holds the earliest deadline in the heap, armed with at most one
  `timerfd_settime` per pass and none when the earliest deadline did not change (Clock and timers).
- Non-blocking reads and writes use `unix.RawSyscall`; `epoll_wait` uses `unix.Syscall`. Open: a test
  for it; the trace records do not say which entry point a call took.
- Loops are not locked to OS threads, except a loop driving a C library that requires its own thread.
- Output buffers are rings or compacted in place, never grown by `append`: a connection queues at
  most 64 frames in a ring, and `Queue` refuses the 65th.
- `tools/sansio`'s rule set for `internal/loop` and `internal/driver/…` finds no `time.Now`,
  `time.Since`, `time.Sleep`, `time.Timer`, `time.AfterFunc`, channel operation, `select` or `range`
  over a map; only the real kernel behind the seam reads a clock. A planted `time.Now` in a driver
  fails the lint.
- CPU per replicated 4 KiB write is benchmarked nightly against the codegen spike's tuned figure; a
  20% regression is a bug. Open: the figure on the CI host.

## Clock and timers

Each case runs in one tier (design.md, Testing strategy, Driver tests):

- **Stepped**, in `internal/loop/looptest/clock_test.go`, on the simulator's clock model through the
  kernel seam, with each stop scripted between two passes: the slew, `Resumed`, VMClock-marker
  (each row of the table below as a scripted stop), never-decreasing and timer cases.
- **Real kernel**, in `internal/loop/clock_linux_test.go` and run in CI: read cost and allocations,
  the wake-up `Now`, a stop inside the clock read and no false `Resumed` under throttling, the
  timerfd's clock and `timerfd_settime` record, and the VMClock reader on a crafted device file.
- **VM, nightly** (`spikes/vm-pause`'s QEMU and Firecracker drivers): the hypervisor rows of the
  table with the real marker, and the `date -s` step. Not run yet: the harness is not a nightly
  ([VM pause rows nightly](build-checklist.md#phase-5-default-drivers)).

Reading the clocks:

- Each pass reads its clocks after its wait returns, together: `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` into `ctx.Now` and
  `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW` into `ctx.Raw`, in ticks of 1 µs (nanoseconds ÷ 1,000). Real kernel: a loop
  blocked 200 ms in `epoll_wait` and woken by a socket write reads both clocks after the wait, and
  hands that `NetRecv` a `Now` at least 200 ms after the previous pass's
  (`TestAPassReadsBothClocksAfterItsWait`).
- The real `Clocks` reads `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` through the vDSO, `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` and
  `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW` with raw syscalls, `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` again, and reads again while the two
  `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` readings lie more than ε = 1 ms apart, at most 8 times, keeping the narrowest
  read. `Epoll.Bracket` counts the reads wider than ε and the widest gap. The whole bracketed read
  costs 365 ns and allocates nothing (`BenchmarkClocks`, arm64 Docker VM); a real pass allocates
  nothing (`TestARealPassAllocatesNothing`).
- Real kernel, a stop inside the clock read (`TestAStopInsideTheClockReadIsBracketedOut`): a child
  process reads its clocks in a loop while the test stops it with `SIGSTOP` for 20 ms, 200 times. A
  stop between the `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` and `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` reads would move
  `CLOCK_BOOTTIME − CLOCK_MONOTONIC` by 20 ms, as a suspend does. In Docker, 172 of the 200 stops
  landed inside a read and were retried, and no reading moved more than 243 µs; with the retry
  planted out, a reading moved 22.7 ms and the test fails. A real stop must last the 1 s threshold
  to deliver a false `Resumed`, so the test checks the readings, not `Resumed`.
- No false `Resumed` under throttling (`TestNoResumedUnderThrottling`): 100,000 passes beside a
  spinning goroutine per CPU in CI; with `RS_WANT_THROTTLE=1` under `docker run --cpus 0.5`, a
  million passes in 14.5 s through 145 throttled periods. A throttled period stalls about 100 ms, a
  tenth of the threshold, so this run passes with or without the bracket and does not bound ε
  (design.md, open questions).
- Trace records carry the pass's clock reading as their tick; no record has a tick of its own:
  every record of a pass has the same tick (`TestSteppedResumedComesOncePerStop`).
- `ctx.Now` and `ctx.Raw` handed to machines never decrease within a run of the loop: a reading
  below the last one leaves them at their last value and delivers one `Resumed`, and the first
  reading above it moves them again with no second one
  (`TestSteppedClocksThatGoBackHoldAndDeliverResumed`). A wall-clock step of 1 s or 2 s (`date -s`,
  VM nightly) moves neither.
- A time daemon slewing `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` by −10% moves `Now` against `Raw` while `Raw` keeps its
  rate; a 1 s timer then fires after 1.111 s of `Raw`, as the clock slew spike measured, and
  machines see both values (`TestSteppedSlewMovesNowAgainstRaw`).

`Resumed`:

- `core.Resumed(prev, cur, threshold)` reports a suspend when `CLOCK_BOOTTIME − CLOCK_MONOTONIC`
  grew by at least the threshold between two readings, which the kernel does only when it adds sleep
  time, and reports a marker change and a `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` or `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW` reading below
  the last (`TestResumedSeesASuspendAMarkerChangeOrAStepBack`). The loop and the simulator share
  one threshold, `core.ResumeThreshold`, 1 s: above ε and at most 1 s, the margin by which a holder
  ends each lease early for a suspend it may miss, and provisional with ε. Both
  take their first reading when the loop is made, so a stop before the first pass delivers
  `Resumed` in that pass in each.
- **[property]** Over the clock model, 2,000 seeds per commit (`TestSteppedResumedComesOncePerStop`):
  slews of up to ±22.6% and raw rates up to 4% off give no `Resumed`; every suspend whose gain
  reaches the threshold gives exactly one; every marker change gives exactly one; a suspend the
  kernel rounded below the threshold gives none; the loop and the simulator count the same.
- A 2.3 s suspend, which `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` counts as 2 s, delivers one `Resumed` in the first pass
  after it, after its clock read and before any other event, its `NetRecv`s included; every timer
  that fell due during the suspend fires in that pass, in deadline order, before the `NetRecv`s
  (`TestSteppedPausesDeliverResumedAsTheVMPauseTableSays`, "suspend to RAM").
- VMClock: where `/dev/vmclock0` exists the loop maps it and reads the marker each pass (0.8 ns in a
  guest, 2.8 ns from Go natively, VM pause spike). The reader maps the device's first 24 bytes
  read-only, refuses a file without its magic, and reads the marker under the device's sequence
  count (`TestTheVMClockMarkerIsReadFromTheMappedPage`,
  `TestAMissingOrForeignVMClockIsRefusedAndReadsZero`, on crafted files). A read that finds the
  count odd waits for the host to finish its update; a count still odd after 65,536 reads gives a
  marker no device holds, so the loop delivers one `Resumed` rather than hang
  (`TestATornVMClockReadIsRetriedAndAStuckOneReadsAsChanged`). Real kernel: a change of the crafted
  file's marker delivers one `Resumed` (`TestAVMClockMarkerChangeDeliversResumed`); where the
  device does not exist (bare metal, or a host whose kernel lacks the driver), the marker reads 0,
  the loop runs, and `Epoll.VMClock` reports why (`TestALoopWithoutAVMClockRuns`); a device that
  exists but cannot be mapped, or is not a VMClock, fails `NewEpoll`
  (`TestAVMClockThatCannotBeMappedFailsNewEpoll`). Cases
  from the VM pause spike, with the expected loop behaviour; each runs stepped as a subtest of
  `TestSteppedPausesDeliverResumedAsTheVMPauseTableSays`, and on real hypervisors only nightly:

  | Event | Marker | Expected |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | QEMU `loadvm`, or an incoming live migration (1 ms downtime) | Changed | `Resumed` in the first pass after the guest runs |
  | QEMU live migration held 10 s at switchover | Changed; kvmclock counted the hold, the TSC did not | `Resumed` |
  | Firecracker snapshot restore | Changed | `Resumed` |
  | One snapshot restored twice | Changed in each restored guest | `Resumed` in each |
  | QEMU `stop` 10 s and `cont`, guest on `kvm-clock` | Unchanged, every clock frozen | No `Resumed`; the lease's step check on grantor messages must catch it (not this item) |
  | QEMU migration cancelled after 10 s, guest on `kvm-clock` | Unchanged, every clock frozen | No `Resumed`; as above |
  | QEMU `stop`/`cont`, guest on `tsc` (`+invtsc`), or a Firecracker pause | Unchanged; every clock gained 10 s | No `Resumed` from the marker; `Now` and `Raw` both jump |
  | `SIGSTOP` of QEMU 10 s | Unchanged; clocks kept time | No `Resumed` |
  | Suspend to RAM | n/a | `Resumed`; `Now` gained the sleep, `Raw` did not |

Timers:

- `SetTimer` arms the loop's timer heap, a pure function in `internal/core`; the timerfd is on
  `CLOCK_BOOTTIME`, so a timer that came due during a suspend fires after resume, and every overdue
  timer fires in deadline order, equal deadlines by `TimerID` (`TestTimersFireInDeadlineOrderAndReplace`).
- `SetTimer` on an armed `TimerID` replaces its deadline; there is no cancel; a `Timer` event for a
  replaced deadline may still arrive and the loop does not filter it (machines check their own
  deadline).
- Timers fire from the heap, not from the timerfd's readiness: a pass whose `Wait` reported no
  timerfd still fires every timer due by `Now` (`TestSteppedTimersFireFromTheHeapNotTheTimerfd`),
  and `Wait` drains the timerfd's expiration count.
- A client read and a lease-expiry timer that become ready in the same `Wait` are handled after the
  expiry (`TestSteppedPausesDeliverResumedAsTheVMPauseTableSays`: timers before `NetRecv`s).
- `Arm` only when the earliest deadline changes: at most one `timerfd_settime` per pass, none in a
  pass whose earliest deadline did not change, and the timerfd always holds the heap's earliest,
  over passes that fire timers and passes that fire none (`TestSteppedResumedComesOncePerStop`).
- Real kernel (`TestTheTimerfdIsAnAbsoluteBoottimeTimer`): `/proc/self/fdinfo` shows the timerfd on
  `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` with `TFD_TIMER_ABSTIME`, and the one `timerfd_settime` record has an `it_value`
  equal to the heap's minimum. `timerfd_gettime` returns only the time remaining (`fs/timerfd.c`),
  so it is used as a bound: remaining ≤ deadline − a `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` reading taken just before. A
  real 10 ms timer wakes a blocked loop no earlier than its deadline, within 4 passes, and leaves the
  timerfd drained.

## io_uring disk driver

The ring's tests (`internal/driver/uring/ring_linux_test.go`) run on the real kernel with a
file-backed disk, under `go test` and `-race`, natively or in a container: Docker's default seccomp
profile refuses `io_uring_setup` with `EPERM`, so container runs use
`--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`. The pure tests (`sqe_test.go`) run everywhere.

- Event mode: the ring's completion eventfd sits in the loop's epoll set, and the driver never waits
  inside `io_uring_enter` (trace: every `io_uring_enter` records the `min_complete` it was passed,
  0, and took every entry it was asked to); a pass with nothing to do blocks in `epoll_wait` until
  the eventfd wakes it, and the loop's read of the eventfd is traced. An `io_uring_enter` that fails
  is traced with the entries it took, 0, and its errno. `TestAWriteAndItsLinkedFlushGoInOneEnter`,
  `TestAFailedEnterIsTraced`.
- A write and its `IORING_FSYNC_DATASYNC` emitted together go linked (`IOSQE_IO_LINK`) in one
  `io_uring_enter` (trace: one `io_uring_enter` submitting 2), and the bytes read back are the bytes
  written. `TestAWriteAndItsLinkedFlushGoInOneEnter`. A linked flush behind another disk's write,
  on a `flush` or a `fua` disk, breaks the action contract and completes with `DiskIO` at once,
  submitting nothing, while the writes go alone. `TestALinkedFlushBehindAnotherDisksWriteFails`.
- A chain the kernel cuts never lets a flush run before its write: the test asks `io_uring_enter` to
  submit 1 of a chain of 2, which leaves the kernel where a failed request allocation does (the
  head taken and run alone, the rest in the submission queue). The driver takes the rest back and
  submits nothing until the head completes; then the flush goes alone, or completes with `DiskIO`
  unsubmitted when its write failed, and a trim's header write goes after its failed discard and
  still zeroes the header alone. `TestAFlushCutFromItsWriteWaitsForIt`,
  `TestAFlushCutFromAFailedWriteFails`, `TestAHeaderWriteCutFromItsDiscardStillRuns`. The cut is
  read from the submission queue's head, so it holds when the syscall's count is lost
  (`TestACutIsReadFromTheSubmissionQueueHead`, which throws it away). A cut between two chains,
  the kernel taking a write and its flush of the three entries asked, makes nothing wait: the read
  after them goes at the next `Submit` (`TestACutBetweenTwoChainsWaitsForNothing`). Entries taken
  back go in front of those that did not fit, in the order executed: 4 of 6 reads copied into a
  ring of 4 and 1 taken leave the queue at reads 2 to 6 (`TestEntriesTakenBackGoInFrontOfTheQueue`).
- Vectored writes: a `DiskWrite` with a `Vec` of pool buffers writes them in order as one `WRITEV`;
  with `Vec` empty, or a `Vec` of one, it writes `Buf` with `WRITE_FIXED`. A vector whose lengths do
  not sum to `Len`, an element not in whole blocks or past its buffer, or more than 1,024 elements is
  refused with `DiskInvalidRange`, as is any range off the disk or not in whole blocks.
  `TestPrepareBuildsEachSubmission`, `FuzzPrepare`.
- A failed write fails its linked flush: both complete with `DiskIO`, the write first.
  `TestAFailedWriteCancelsItsLinkedFlush`. A write refused before submission fails its linked flush
  with `DiskIO` at once, and nothing is submitted. `TestARefusedWriteFailsItsLinkedFlushAtOnce`.
- A short count is an error: a read or write that moves fewer bytes than asked completes with
  `DiskIO`, and so does every negative result and a flush or trim with any result but 0.
  `TestAShortReadIsAnError`, `TestCompleteDecodesEachResult`, `FuzzComplete`.
- `durability: fua` as a per-disk setting: writes carry `RWF_DSYNC` and no flush is submitted; an
  unlinked flush completes at once, a linked one with its write. On the measured consumer drive FUA
  cost 2.2 ms per 4 KiB write against 0.95 ms for write plus flush, so `flush` stays the default.
  `TestAFUADiskSubmitsNoFlush`; `FuzzPrepare` fuzzes the setting.
- A full ring defers, never drops: 64 reads into a ring of 4 entries all complete once, no
  `io_uring_enter` submits more than 4, and nothing is left in flight. A link chain goes into the
  submission queue whole or waits whole for the next pass, and entries in flight never exceed the
  completion queue, so it never overflows. `TestAFullRingDefersSubmissions`.
- File-backed disks are written in full when created, every block allocated, so later writes are
  overwrites that commit no file system journal; a trim never changes the file's allocation.
  `TestAFileIsWrittenInFullAndATrimZeroesOnlyTheHeader`.
- A trim zeroes the segment header: on a file it is a write of 4 KiB of zeros over the trim's first
  block alone; on a device a `BLOCK_URING_CMD_DISCARD` with that write hard-linked behind it, the
  trim completing with the write's result whatever the discard's. A trim's blocks after the first
  read back unchanged on a file. `TestAFileIsWrittenInFullAndATrimZeroesOnlyTheHeader`,
  `TestADeviceTrimIsADiscardThenAHeaderWrite`; `TestAFailedDiscardStillZeroesTheHeader` sends the
  discard to a file, where the kernel fails it, and the header still reads back as zeros.
- Fixed buffers and files: the loop's pool is registered once (`IORING_REGISTER_BUFFERS`) in regions
  of at most 1 GiB, reads and writes of one buffer use `READ_FIXED`/`WRITE_FIXED`, and the disk
  descriptors go into a table of 16 fixed files; the status reports both.
  `TestAWriteAndItsLinkedFlushGoInOneEnter`.
- Fallback: with an 8 MiB memory-lock limit and no `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, registering a 64 MiB pool fails
  with `ENOMEM`; the status reports it, and a write, its flush and the read back still pass on plain
  `READ`/`WRITE`. `TestTheRegistrationFallback`, run under `--ulimit memlock=8388608` and with the
  test lowering its own soft limit.
- A failed ring is a failed disk: an `io_uring_enter` error other than `EINTR`, `EAGAIN` or `EBUSY`
  (the test puts `/dev/null` behind the ring's descriptor of a ring of two entries) completes every
  operation in flight, queued or executed later with `DiskIO`, each once, sets `Status.Failed`, and
  the completion queue is never read again. Once the log frees every buffer, the pool hands out
  every block again but those of the read the kernel held and the write copied into the submission
  queue; the read left queued in the driver and the one executed after the failure get theirs back.
  `TestAFailedRingCompletesEveryOperationWithDiskIO`. `Close` quarantines the buffers of the
  operations the kernel holds the same way, and the buffers of those still queued go back to the
  pool. `TestCloseQuarantinesWhatTheKernelHolds`.
- A disk file whose size is not whole blocks is refused at `Open` with `ErrNotBlocks`.
  `TestOpenRefusesAFileNotInWholeBlocks`.
- Nothing allocates per operation: a vectored write with its linked flush and a single write, with
  the GC off. `TestARoundTripAllocatesNothing`; `BenchmarkAWriteAndItsFlush` reports 0 allocs/op.

## Format discards every segment

- Format writes zeros over the superblock's copy then the superblock, each flushed, trims every
  segment but segment 0, 64 trims in flight at a time, flushes, and only then writes the superblock
  and its copy, each flushed; the driver zeroes each header behind its discard. A disk that is a
  file is not trimmed and gets no zeros first. `TestFormatZeroesTrimsThenWritesBothSuperblocks`.
- A used disk formatted again and crashed after each of format's first eight and last six actions,
  every unflushed write landing or none, starts as the old log whole, as no log or as the new one,
  never as the old superblock over headers the trims zeroed (`log corrupt at LSN 1` before the
  zeros). `TestAUsedDiskCrashedMidFormat`. In a cluster, a disk formatted again that crashes
  mid-trims opens unformatted, and its node formats it again under a new log ID: it comes back as a
  new disk (seed 47 of `TestPeeringKeepsAcknowledgedWritesAcrossPrimaries` before the zeros).
  `TestADiskCrashedMidFormatComesBackUnformatted`.
- A disk whose segments' first blocks hold another log's valid segment headers or random bytes is
  formatted, and no start, the first or a later one, reads any segment in full.
  `TestFormatLeavesNoSegmentReadInFull`.
- A trim of format's that fails costs only its discard: format finishes, and every start reads that
  segment, whose first block still holds what the earlier use left, in full and recovers the new
  log's records. `TestAFailedFormatTrimCostsOnlyAReadInFull`.
- The disk log's crash sweep (`TestCrashAtEveryAction`) crashes before and fails each of format's
  zero writes, trims and flushes: a crash leaves a disk with no log, a failed trim a log that runs
  on, and a failed zero write a failed format.

## io_uring on a raw device and NVMe

The tests that need a block device or a real drive run as root on a spare drive, which they
overwrite: `RS_RAW_DEVICE` names it, always by its `/dev/disk/by-id/` path, as `nvme0n1` and
`nvme1n1` can swap across reboots, and without it they skip. Before any write each checks that
the path is a block device that an `O_RDWR|O_EXCL` open finds free, and fails otherwise: named a
mounted loop device, the benchmark and every device test fail and the loop's file is unchanged
(before the check, the benchmark's prefill overwrote the file system), and the OS disk's
`by-id` path, its partitions and its md array are refused with `EBUSY`. A partition or disk that
nothing holds, mounted nowhere and in no array, passes the check. The file-backed measurement needs
`RS_URING_DIR` on a file system on that drive. All rows ran on a WDC SN720 512 GB (client NVMe,
volatile write cache, DLFEAT 1: deallocated blocks read as zeros), Linux 7.0, Xeon E-2236 (6 cores, 12 threads):

```sh
go test -c -o uring.test ./internal/driver/uring/
D=/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-…                     # the spare drive, whole
sudo RS_RAW_DEVICE=$D ./uring.test -test.run 'RawDevice|TheChunkStoreSuite'
for t in linear error flakey delay log-writes; do
  sudo RS_RAW_DEVICE=$D RS_CRASH_TARGET=$t ./uring.test -test.run '^TestCrashOnARealDisk$'
done
sudo RS_RAW_DEVICE=$D ./uring.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench BenchmarkRawDevice -test.count 6
mkfs.ext4 $D; mount $D /mnt/rs                 # then, on the file system
RS_URING_DIR=/mnt/rs/u ./uring.test -test.run TestDurableWritesIntoAFileCommitNoJournal
```

- A raw device is opened `O_DIRECT` and `O_EXCL` and sized with `BLKGETSIZE64` (its blocks match
  sysfs's `size`); a second `O_EXCL` open fails with `EBUSY`, and a second ring's `Open` too, at
  once, and once the first ring is closed `Open` succeeds at once. That last step
  failed until `Close` unregistered the file table: the kernel drops it with the ring later, in a
  worker, and it held the claim. `TestARawDeviceIsOpenedExclusively`.
- The suite's open waits out a claim that is about to go, such as a killed process's, retrying
  `EBUSY` for up to 2 s as the daemon does: with no retry, the crash test's first child on `linear`
  failed to open the device with `EBUSY`, and with it every child of every target opens it. `TestCrashOnARealDisk`.
- A trim of a raw device is a `BLOCK_URING_CMD_DISCARD` with the header write behind it, in one
  `io_uring_enter` submitting 2: the device's discard count (`/sys/class/block/…/stat`) rises by
  the trim's sectors, the header reads back as zeros, and on this drive so do the blocks after it.
  `TestATrimOfARawDeviceDiscardsItThenZeroesTheHeader`.
- The [Shared ChunkStore suite](#shared-chunkstore-suite) runs on the device's first 256 MiB,
  written with zeros (`BLKZEROOUT`) before each case as a new disk file is, and passes: 9 cases in
  3.3 s, the 3 simulator-only cases skipped. It passes the same on a loop device
  (`losetup --direct-io=on`) over a file on the drive, and the raw-device tests above too.
- File-backed disks: 1,000 durable 4 KiB writes (write and linked flush) into a disk file on ext4
  on the drive have a p50 of 0.36 to 0.52 ms and a p99 of 1.4 to 1.6 ms over three runs, and the
  ext4 journal commits 0 times across them (`TestDurableWritesIntoAFileCommitNoJournal`, which
  allows one per 5 s commit interval). fio's 4 KiB write and `fdatasync` agrees on a prewritten file
  (sync p50 0.47 ms); into a fresh `fallocate`d file it takes 0.96 ms and commits the journal once
  per write (999 commits). The NVMe flush spike's drive took 0.95 ms and 2.5 ms: this drive flushes
  about twice as fast, and the ratio holds.
- Benchmarks, 4 KiB `O_DIRECT` reads and writes at random offsets in the device's first GiB from
  random slots of a 64 MiB pool, 6 reps of 2 s (`BenchmarkRawDevice`, 0 allocations per I/O); the
  medians of `cpu-ns/op`, the process's user and system time per I/O, against the
  [registered buffers spike](design.md#appendix-io_uring-registered-buffers-spike):

  | Case | Plain | Fixed buffer and file | Spike |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | QD 32, read | 2.99 µs | **−0.12 µs** (−0.11 buffer alone), every rep | −0.11 µs (1.88 → 1.77) |
  | QD 32, write | 2.12 µs | **−0.08 µs** (−0.06 buffer alone), every rep | −0.10 µs (1.63 → 1.53) |
  | QD 1, write | 6.07 µs | **−0.24 µs**, every rep | −0.24 to −0.29 µs of 3.7 to 4.7 µs |
  | QD 1, read | 35 µs | −1.7 to −3.8 µs, inside rep-to-rep noise of 5 µs | |
  | Registration | | 16.1 ms per GiB already touched | 17 to 70 ms per GiB |

  The savings match the spike's. The totals are higher, most at QD 1, because the benchmark waits
  in `poll` and reads the eventfd, as the loop does, rather than in `io_uring_enter`: a sleep in
  `io_uring_enter` counts as iowait, which keeps the core's clock up and its idle states shallow,
  and a sleep in `poll` does not. The box runs `intel_pstate` on `powersave` with C-states down to
  C10. Waiting in `io_uring_enter` (`min_complete` 1) instead, a QD 1 read took 69.5 µs against
  104 µs and 6.4 µs of CPU against 35 µs, in the same cycles (`perf stat`: 1.26 GHz against
  3.7 GHz); a QD 1 write 10.5 µs against 12.0 µs and 4.5 µs of CPU against 6.1 µs. `GOMAXPROCS`
  12, 2 or 1 changes a QD 1 read's CPU little (35, 36, 48 µs), so it is not the Go runtime's other
  threads. Under the `performance` governor the same QD 1 read, still waiting in `poll`, took 71 µs
  and 8.3 µs of CPU, and a write 11.7 µs and 5.8 µs (3 reps of 3 s): the governor alone makes the
  difference. So `cpu-ns/op` at QD 1 compares clock speeds, not work. Open: tolerance.
  Open: polled completions (`IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL`) are an open question, not built.
- Many reads in flight: recovery's segment-header reads (4,096 to 262,144 per disk) go out at the read
  depth recovery asks for and the ring defers what does not fit, never drops it. Open: ring depth.
- The [crash test](#crash-tests-on-real-disks) on device-mapper targets (root; in Docker,
  `--privileged`): with `RS_CRASH_TARGET` set the disk is `/dev/mapper/rs-crash`, the raw device's
  first 256 MiB behind the target, and each kill comes with its fault. Seed 1, 150 cycles each, every
  restart a prefix holding every acknowledged change, every history linearizable:
  - `linear`, the raw device alone: 23 s.
  - `error`: at the kill point the table swaps to `error` (`dmsetup suspend`, `load`, `resume`), the
    driver sends 8 more changes and the child is killed 50 ms later. Every child answered a change
    with an error first (150 of 150), no change sent after the swap was acknowledged, and recovery
    after swapping back is a prefix: 37 s.
  - `flakey`: the history clients are stopped, then the table swaps to `flakey` with `drop_writes`
    and the driver stops counting acknowledgments: every write from then on completes and is lost,
    as on a power cut of a drive whose cache is durable. 149 restarts kept a change never
    acknowledged: 42 s. It adds little over `linear`: the suspend before the swap finishes every
    write in flight and every later one is lost, with no acknowledgment counted, so the disk it
    leaves is the one a kill at the swap leaves, and an acknowledgment before the flush goes
    unseen. It stays for the 20 ms the store runs on after its writes stop landing, reading back
    blocks older than it wrote, which no other target gives, at 13 s for 50 cycles.
  - `delay`: every I/O 5 ms late; nothing fails, and the run takes 289 s.
  - `log-writes`, the power cut that loses every write not yet flushed: `dm-log-writes` logs each
    write with its data and each flush into another window of the drive, and after the kill the
    test puts back a copy of the window taken before the cycle and replays only the writes logged
    before the last flush. 135 s; 19,736 writes replayed behind 15,720 flushes, and 6 completed
    writes never flushed were dropped.
  - The plant `log-writes` exists for, applied by hand and never committed: in
    `internal/disklog/groupcommit.go`, where a round's record write completes, right after
    `l.sendFlushes(out)` add
    `if i == 0 { if r.flushSent { l.stale = append(l.stale, r.flushIO) }; l.retire(out); l.startRounds(ctx, out) }`,
    so the oldest round is reported durable once its write completes, before its flush. Built
    into a separate test binary, it fails on `log-writes` at cycle 74, 70 and 95 of seeds 1, 7 and
    11 (the restarted child's read of a chunk finds a malformed header or a bad magic), and passes
    all 150 cycles of `linear`. A kill lands between a write's completion and the issue of its
    linked flush only rarely, and a flush already issued is not stopped by the kill: the ring's
    teardown waits for it and `dm-log-writes` logs it before the cut. A 10 ms flush delay under
    the logged window (`dm-delay`, `delay <raw> 0 0 <raw> 0 0 <raw> 0 10`) drops more writes, 26
    to 30 per 150 cycles, but the plant then passes all 150 cycles of the same three seeds, so
    the rig has no delay. Open: a cut where the kill lands, such as a `dm-log-writes` mark sent
    before the kill, only the flushes logged before it replayed and the acknowledgments after it
    ignored.

## TCP network driver

Tests in `internal/driver/tcp` and `internal/meta/wire_test.go`; the socket tests run on the Mac
under the stepped kernel and on Linux in Docker, plain and with `-race`.

- One connection per pair of event loops, opened by the first send or accepted, both ways over it
  (`TestMessagesCrossOneConnectionBothWays`); two loops that dial each other at once keep one
  connection (`TestLoopsDialingEachOtherAtOnceKeepOneConnection`).
- A request that reaches the wrong loop, after a shard moved, is forwarded through the inbox and its
  reply names the new owner; the sender's next request goes to the new owner directly. The owner map
  is a hint: with a stale map every request still completes. Not yet tested: no dispatch forwards
  through the inbox yet.
- A 10-node cluster of 8-loop nodes holds at most 576 sockets per node.
- Framing: a 12-byte header with a version, both lengths and a CRC32C over header, inline bytes and
  data ([Runtime in Go](design.md#runtime-in-go)); frames decode from any split of the stream
  (`TestFramesDecodeFromAnyPieces`); a bad version, kind, length or checksum is refused
  (`TestBadFramesAreRefused`) and ends the connection as a `PeerLost`; the decoder is fuzzed (`FuzzDecoder`). Messages up to
  256 bytes travel inline; bulk data travels in pool buffers. A message before the hello ends the
  connection, on a dial too (`TestAMessageBeforeTheHelloOnADialIsRefused`), and a send to the loop
  itself panics without dialing (`TestASendToTheLoopItselfPanics`).
- A received frame's data is read straight into a 4 KiB-aligned pool buffer, the message's data
  buffer (`TestDataIsReadStraightIntoItsAlignedBuffer`), with no allocation per message on either
  path (`TestSendingAndReceivingAllocateNothing`, `BenchmarkSend`, `BenchmarkReceive`: 0 allocs).
  Small frames arrive in batches, 300 in one read (`TestManySmallFramesArriveInOneRead`), and in a
  stream of large frames each copies at most 4 KiB out of the read-ahead
  (`TestALargeFrameCopiesAtMostCopyMaxOutOfTheReadAhead`).
- Messages are batched per connection: everything ready for one connection in a pass goes in one
  `writev` (as under Event loop).
- MetaStore requests ([Sharded API](#sharded-api-one-shard)): a `Txn` and an `Answer` cross the
  wire whole, inline or in a pool buffer, every error code included
  (`TestTxnsAndAnswersCrossTheWireWhole`), with fuzzed decoders (`FuzzDecodeTxnMsg`,
  `FuzzDecodeAnswerMsg`); a `Txn` sent to a follower is answered `NotLeader`, resent to the loop
  hosting the leader's replica and answered under the client's token
  (`TestATxnCrossesTheWireToTheLeader`); every `Txn` a server hears is answered, a node with no
  replica with `NotLeader`, a bad body with `ErrMalformed` (`TestEveryTxnTheServerHearsIsAnswered`);
  a send to a lost peer ends in a dropped answer (`TestAClientTxnToALostPeerIsDropped`); an answer
  that promises nothing (an error with no code, an applied `Txn`'s answer the server's pool had no
  buffer for, an answer that does not decode, a lost peer) is never resent
  (`TestAnAnswerOfUnknownOutcomeIsNeverResent`); a restarted client's tokens differ from its
  earlier start's, so an answer to an earlier start's `Txn` settles nothing
  (`TestARestartedClientIgnoresItsEarlierStartsAnswers`); only a
  server proposes under a token with bit 63 set (`TestOnlyAServerProposesUnderAServerToken`); and
  the router's shard map is fed from `ctl/`'s (`TestTheClientRoutesByTheShardMapUnderCtl`).
- Dial and listen are functions the driver is given, so stepped tests hand it AF_UNIX socketpairs
  and skip the TCP-only socket options; the TCP-specific cases below use real loopback.
- Any transport error becomes exactly one `PeerLost` for that peer and the driver reconnects, made
  on loopback: a reset by closing the peer with `SO_LINGER` 0 (`TestAResetIsOnePeerLostThenReconnects`),
  an EOF by `shutdown` (`TestAnEOFIsOnePeerLostThenReconnects`), a peer that stops reading
  (`TestAPeerThatStopsReadingIsOnePeerLost`), and a dropped socketpair
  (`TestADroppedConnectionIsOnePeerLostThenReconnects`). A partial frame at a reset is never
  delivered (`TestAPartialFrameAtAResetIsNeverDelivered`). Every send to a loop that cannot be
  reached ends in its `PeerLost`, during the backoff too (`TestEverySendToAnUnreachableLoopEndsInPeerLost`),
  and by the next pass without the loop blocking when a failed write's `PeerLost` handler made the
  send (`TestAPeerLostFromAWriteFailureIsDeliveredWithoutBlocking`).
- A connection ID kept past its connection names nothing: frames read ahead on a connection a
  handler closed are never delivered as from the connection dialed into its slot
  (`TestReadAheadIsNeverDeliveredAsTheNextConnectionsPeer`), and two write failures in one pass are
  each their own peer's `PeerLost`, though the first one's handler dials two new peers
  (`TestTwoWriteFailuresInAPassAreEachTheirOwnPeerLost`).
- A send finding 32 MiB queued on its connection ends it as a `PeerLost`
  (`TestAConnectionQueuesAtMost32MiBAndOneFrame`); an accept error that lasts (`EMFILE`) pauses the
  listener for a backoff rather than waking the loop every pass, and connections are accepted after
  it (`TestAnAcceptErrorThatLastsPausesTheListener`).
- Buffers (driver contract): a `NetSend`'s buffer is released before the peer's reply is delivered,
  and all of a peer's buffers are released before its `PeerLost` is emitted; a `NetSend` marked
  `Reply` has its buffer freed by the driver once sent, or before that peer's `PeerLost`; one buffer
  sent to several peers is freed once every one is done: the pool's live count is zero after a
  fan-out to three peers where one is lost (`TestAReplyBufferSentToThreePeersIsFreedOnceWhenOneIsLost`).
- A peer answers every request that carries data, even to reject it.
- The core keeps its own deadlines: the driver sets no transport timeout, keepalive or
  `TCP_USER_TIMEOUT` that fails a request on its own.
- A frame the receiving loop's pool has no buffer for ends its connection, as the simulator breaks
  one.
- The read budget per connection per pass and the replication queue cap apply as under Event loop.
- Under the open-loop latency spike's load generator (16 connections, writes timed from their
  scheduled send), a replicated-write server on the event loop and this driver drops no request up to
  100,000 writes/s, the rate the spike's bounded harness served (the generator's own limit), and its
  output buffers stay under 20 MB (`TestTheLoadGeneratorDropsNothing`, which runs when `RS_LOADGEN`
  names the built generator): in Docker capped at 4 CPUs, 9,910 to 115,115 writes/s offered with
  none dropped, p99 1.45 to 3.91 ms, 12.3 µs of server CPU per write at the top rate, and the
  primary's queued output at most 7.8 MiB ([Runtime in Go](design.md#runtime-in-go)).
- TCP first: RDMA upgrades the same connection's peers in phase 9; nodes without rdma-core stay on TCP
  with no error.

## Round driver

Review criteria, as stepped trace checks in `internal/loop/looptest/round_test.go`: producer loops
with stand-in shards (`stub`, one blob of 128 B proposals a round, one round in flight, as a Raft
shard keeps), an owner loop on a simulated disk with a 0.95 ms flush, one pool per loop. The trace
check (`checkRounds`) reads the owner's ring, the one order both directions share. The latency
measurement below runs on real loop goroutines.

Hand-off, with 1, 2, 4 and 8 producer loops (`TestRoundsHandOffOncePerRoundAndFlushOncePerRound`):

- Between two round writes the owner takes at most one batch from each producer loop and wakes it at
  most once; durable notices to a loop strictly increase in LSN and in batches counted; every batch
  sent is counted durable, in order; no two blobs are told the same place. With 8 loops some batch
  is taken after its loop's pass ended, and that loop is woken for it.
- One `DiskFsync` per `DiskWrite`, whatever the number of producer loops.
- One round holds a batch from every producer loop (the log per core spike wrote 39 items per flush
  with 8 producers, 8 with a log per loop), and commit latency's p99 with 8 loops is within one round
  of one loop's.
- A shard on the disk's own loop skips both inbox hops: the owner's inbox wakes only for the
  proposer's first timer (`TestRoundOnOwnerSkipsTheInbox`).
- With room in the owner's pool for two batches' copies, batches wait for it and none fails, every
  proposal becomes durable, and the trace holds a `PoolWait` for the batches that waited and none
  with room (`TestRoundFullOwnerPoolDelaysBatches`). With 16 shards on the owner beside a producer
  loop's 16 and room for 20 blocks, a waiting batch is retried every pass, not only when another
  batch arrives, and every proposal on both loops becomes durable
  (`TestRoundWaitingBatchesShareTheOwnerPool`).
- Mail and dead blobs cross loops: a replayed blob, with its bytes, and a cleaner's rewrite request
  reach the shard; the blobs it reports dead leave the owner's log and the rest stay
  (`TestRoundMailAndDeadBlobsCrossLoops`). Mail sent on the owner loop, from its machine's event or
  from a shard's `Durable`, reaches the shard after the sender's own actions run, and those actions
  are kept, and the shard still hears of its next record
  (`TestRoundSendOnOwnerKeepsTheCallersActions`). Hanging the cleaner's moves for a shard's
  runs on this is the work of the item that wires them.
- A Raft shard's rounds through the driver (`raftshard.Rounds`), on a producer loop and on the
  owner, ten rounds of three 1,000-byte entries and a hard state, every third compacting to the
  commit before it: every round is durable in order, and the blobs it reports dead through
  `Loop.Dead` are the oldest, which the log no longer holds, while it holds every other
  (`TestRoundsOfARaftShardDieAsItCompacts`). Taken off its loop with its fifth round in flight and
  its state deleted, the driver reports that round's blobs and `Rounds.Delete` every other: the
  log holds no live block and the loop's pool is back where it started
  (`TestRoundsOfARemovedRaftShardAllDie`). Six rounds of several blobs each, compacted before the
  fourth, and a seventh whose last blob never landed, replayed blob by blob into a fresh storage on
  the base as recovery's mail will hand them: the storage holds the same entries and commit, only
  the torn round's blobs die, and the live blobs are those the writer kept
  (`TestRoundsReplayRebuildsTheStorage`, `internal/raftshard`). A round missing its last blob,
  then the first blob of the next: the torn round's blobs die at once
  (`TestRoundsReplayDropsATornRoundAtTheNextFirstBlob`). A round its loop's pool cannot hold stays
  queued, and once the pool frees and the shard is marked again it and the rounds after it become
  durable (`TestRoundOfARaftShardWaitsOutAFullPool`). A round 0, a write while a round is queued
  or in flight, and `Durable` with none in flight or after `Delete` panic
  (`TestRoundsPanicOnABrokenCallOrder`). A chunk store on its device loop, with a Raft shard on
  the round driver of that loop and one on another loop, seven rounds each compacting every
  third, restarted: each shard is mailed its blobs and the end of the replay, its storage, on the
  base its runs would restore, equals its state before, and the log holds as many live blocks as
  before, the blobs the shards report dead during the replay taken once the log is served
  (`TestRaftShardsOnTwoLoopsRecoverTheirStorage`).
- The owner's machine keeps its own disk completions and, as a `LogMachine`, the events of its own
  log records; an owner machine that is not one panics on a log event the driver did not submit
  (`TestRoundOwnerMachineKeepsItsDiskAndLogEvents`). Two logs on one loop, fed from it and another
  loop, each get only their own completions and every proposal becomes durable; overlapping IO ranges
  are refused (`TestRoundSeveralLogsOnOneLoop`). While a loop serves no log, as while its disk
  recovers, a completion in the log's range reaches the machine; once it serves the log the machine
  recovered, the machine's record comes back as the log's `Durable` and a nil event follows each
  completion, and its earlier read is not handed over again (`TestALoopServesTheLogItsMachineRecovered`).
  A shard on the owner marked while no log is served stays marked and is collected once the log
  is served (`TestAMarkedShardWaitsWhileNoLogIsServed`); a producer loop's batch, sent meanwhile,
  waits in the owner's queue and is written once the log is served
  (`TestAProducersBatchWaitsAtTheOwnerWhileNoLogIsServed`); a Raft blob reported dead meanwhile
  leaves the live blocks of the log served next, not before (`TestRaftBlobsReportedDeadWaitForALog`).
  A record the owner's machine writes and a shard's, made in one pass, go out in one round
  (`TestTheOwnersRecordsShareARoundWithItsShards`). A storage node's device on a blank disk formats it on
  its loop and reports it opened, though the format ends with no log event, only the nil after its
  last completion (`TestADeviceOnALoopReportsTheDiskItFormattedOpened`).
- A marked shard whose `Ready` adds nothing is not told anything durable
  (`TestRoundShardWithNothingReadyIsToldNothing`). A `Keep` buffer bound for another loop's disk
  panics, and one whose submit fails is not freed (`TestRoundKeptBuffers`).
- A failed write or flush, the sixth, with 2 producer loops: every batch resolves, some with the
  error, and every pool is back where it started (`TestRoundFailedDiskResolvesEveryBatch`).
- A shard removed, on a producer loop and on the owner, while its batch is in flight and mail waits
  for it: the batch is written and its Raft blob leaves the log's live blocks, the shard gets no
  `Durable` call and no mail, a shard added after it gets a new ID and only its own mail, and every
  pool is back where it started (`TestRoundRemovedShardIsToldNothing`).
- Over seeds of shape (0 to 8 producer loops, 1 to 32 shards each, the proposal gap, the round cap, at
  times a nearly full owner pool): the driver contract and "durable only once the log is" at every
  step, which fails a durable notice naming other than one place for a shard's one record, an LSN
  not above the shard's last (as a notice sent at take, with LSN 0, would be) or one past the log's
  durable LSN; then the checks above, every proposal durable and every buffer back in its pool
  (`TestRoundsKeepTheirRules`, 400 seeds in `scripts/seeds.sh`).

Collection:

- A round with 1,001 shards and one marked calls `HasReady` once (`TestRoundAsksOnlyMarkedShards`);
  a round's CPU with 10, 100 and 1,000 idle shards is flat, about 18 µs, and allocates nothing
  (`BenchmarkRoundIdleShards`, `TestRoundAllocatesNothing`). Scanning every shard cost 54% of loop CPU
  at 0.1 ms flushes in the raft rounds spike.
- A round is bounded by `max_group_commit_bytes` only: with one producer loop, 48 shards of 2 KiB
  against a 64 KiB cap are collected in marked order over two rounds, and no batch the loop hands
  over holds more than the cap and one shard's records (`TestRoundCapLeavesTheRestInOrder`). With L loops each sending cap-sized batches a loop's batch is
  taken after about L rounds ([On-disk format](design.md#on-disk-format)); no test bounds that.

Latency, against the raft rounds spike (3 nodes × 1,000 groups, 128 B proposals, 4 loops per node),
with a simulated 0.95 ms flush and 1 and 8 producer loops of 16 shards, each proposing every 20 µs.
On real goroutines (`TestRoundLatencyOnRealLoops`, which runs when `RS_ROUND_LATENCY` gives its
length, here 10 to 20 s in Docker capped at 4 CPUs) each loop has its own epoll set and pool, and
`GOMAXPROCS` leaves a spare P, as a node does. Docker Desktop's kernel is built without
`CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS`, so a timerfd fires on the next 1 ms tick (a 20 µs timer was 980 µs late
at p50): a goroutine spinning on its own thread posts the proposals to each loop's inbox, eight to
an event, and signals the disk's completions on an eventfd instead. Latency runs from the pass that
handles a proposal's timer event to the pass that handles its `Durable`, which is commit latency as
the targets define it; it leaves out the time the event waits in the inbox after the posting
goroutine posts it. "CPU a round" is the process's CPU less the posting goroutine's thread, so it
includes the simulated disk, which runs on the owner loop, and the Go runtime's threads, and the CPU
per proposal below overstates the driver's a little. Each stand-in shard checks every durable
notice it gets as the stepped runs do, and the run fails if one was wrong.

| Run | p50 | p99 | CPU a round, all loops | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Raft rounds spike | 2.9 to 3.6 ms | 4.6 to 5.8 ms | | 3 ms / 5 ms |
| Stepped, 1 loop (simulated time) | 2.8 ms | 3.8 ms | | |
| Stepped, 8 loops (simulated time) | 3.1 ms | 4.7 ms | | |
| Real goroutines, 1 loop | 2.9 ms | 4.4 ms | 77 µs | 3 ms / 5 ms |
| Real goroutines, 8 loops | 3.3 ms | 5.0 ms | 480 to 500 µs | 3 ms / 5 ms |

With 8 loops a round held 407 proposals, about 1.2 µs of loop CPU each, and the loops used 0.45
cores. Posted one to an event, the 400,000 proposals a second cost a wakeup each: the posting
goroutine spent its core writing eventfds and offered 250,000, the producers' inboxes refused
56,000 posts in 10 s, and p99 rose to 43 ms. The profile was 83% syscalls (`epoll_wait`, eventfd
reads and writes, clock reads), the round driver's own code under 2%, so the bound is the cost of a
wakeup per proposal, which a node avoids since a connection's read hands a loop many messages at
once.

## Shared ChunkStore suite

- One suite, `internal/chunkstore/storetest`, written once against its `Disk` interface (queue an
  action, wait for completions, restart the process over the same disk) and run unchanged on the
  simulated disk (`storetest`'s own tests), on io_uring over a 256 MiB file-backed disk
  (`internal/driver/uring`, Linux, in Docker with `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`), and on a
  stepped loop that owns the store's log; the driver is the suite's only parameter. Done-when
  checkpoint: the same suite later passes on SPDK (phase 9).
- The suite drives the store directly, queueing its actions as a loop's pass does and handing it
  every completion, with merges and cleaner jobs run inline. io_uring submits the queue in one
  batch; the simulated disk runs one queued action per completion, so a crash can fall between a
  round's write and its fsync. On the loop (`TestSuiteOnALoopThatOwnsTheLog` and, over 4 seeds,
  `TestFaultsOnALoopThatOwnsTheLog`, in `internal/loop/looptest`), a `storetest.Host` disk, the
  loop attaches the log before the store opens it, serves each log the store opens or formats, hands
  the log its completions and TRIM timer and the store the log's events through `Store.OnLog`; each
  case fails if no log event came through the loop, or if the store reports an unfinished I/O with
  nothing in flight. Results are checked against a byte-range model of the acknowledged changes and the
  order of the replies, never against traces.
- The store runs the single-node configuration, every check on and no merged-block cache: the cache
  (`MergeCache`) is a replica primary's, and the replica tests cover it.
- Cases, the Single-node ChunkStore item's behaviours: writes of 1 byte, across a block edge and of
  3 blocks with merged edges, and a punch with merged edges, at rising versions, read back whole and
  unaligned; 8 two-byte writes pipelined to one block, each overlapping the next by a byte, answered
  in order and leaving each byte as the last write over it; `expectVer` that succeeds at the current
  version and fails with `ErrVersion` at a stale one; a flush answered only after its chunks'
  writes; a whole-chunk punch leaving a tombstone, which a restart keeps; a whole 4 MiB chunk write
  mapped as several extents of one version, answered once; a snapshot cut, then a read at the frozen
  version, before and after a restart, and a chunk first written after the cut reading zeros at
  version 0 (its absent freeze).
- Restart, on both drivers: a clean close and reopen (on io_uring the ring and pool closed and
  opened again over the same file) recovers every acknowledged change and each chunk's newest
  version, and a write after it goes above that version; with `max_replay_bytes` at 256 KiB, 400
  changes write checkpoints, and a restart replays to the same reads.
- Fault cases run only on the simulated disk, seeded (`TestFaultsOnTheSimulatedDisk` in
  `scripts/seeds.sh`): a power cut after random changes and a random number of disk actions, with
  each unflushed block or sector landing at random, recovers every acknowledged write, and a write
  not acknowledged, or answered with an error, to a new chunk recovers whole or not at all; the test
  fails if no crash over its own seeds held an unflushed block. A failed disk write answers its
  write with an error, and a restart keeps every acknowledged change; a flipped bit fails the read
  with `ErrBadChecksum`. The io_uring run lists them as skipped, simulator-only, by name.
- Not covered here: a raw device (the suite runs on a loop device in the **io_uring on a raw device
  and NVMe** item); durability on io_uring, where a restart closes and reopens the file and no power
  is cut, so a flush there checks only that it waits for its writes (**Crash tests on real disks**
  owns it); counts per loop pass (no loop runs); and allocations, which the store's benchmarks
  measure on the simulated disk.

## Control-plane host

The host machine, `meta.CtlHost`, on a single-voter control-plane group of ID 257 unless a row says otherwise, each voter's log on a simulated disk whose actions run before a call returns, fed events with no network.

| Input | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| A single-voter Raft shard's timer | It elects itself within two election timeouts, commits a proposal and serves lease reads (`TestASingleVoterElectsItselfAndLeases`, `internal/raftshard`) |
| A message of group 257 (`Txn`, report, session table) read as a chunkstore frame, and a chunkstore frame read as a group message | Each refused by the other's decoder; a Raft message whose first byte is chunkstore's is undecodable (`TestAGroupMessageIsNeverAChunkstoreFrame`, `TestUndecodableMessagesAreDroppedAndCounted`) |
| A node's report, then a client's session start under request 5, sent twice before it commits, then a fetch under token 77 | The host leads and starts one session, whose ID the client hears under request 5; the fetch is answered under token 77 with the session live |
| A session start reaching a leader whose Control does not serve yet, then the same start once it serves | The first never starts a session; the second does (`TestAStartBeforeTheControlServesIsNotTaken`) |
| A session start waiting when the Control drops, then the same start to the next Control | The waiting start is forgotten with the Control, so the start sent again is taken and answered (`TestAStartWaitingWhenTheControlDropsIsTakenAgain`) |
| A node's report naming a disk on loop 4, then steps, then the report again, then a report without it, then one with a new log on its device, then one with the old log again on another device | The first answer names no disk; once the record commits, the answer names the disk with its log at loop 4 of the node and the size and log reserve the report gave; the next names none; the last names the new log's disk alone, the old one being gone (`TestAReportIsAnsweredWithTheCommittedDisks`) |
| A pool's grants out, a disk's size and fill heard, a disk whose node reported no size, then the leader's answer a microsecond before and at `FillFresh` after the fill on each clock | The answer carries the disk's size, log reserve and fill, size 0 for the other disk, and the pool's grants outstanding; the fill is left out once either clock shows `FillFresh` (`TestTheMembershipCarriesFreshFillsAndTheGrants`) |
| Reports from three nodes, then a session that never renews | Once it is fenced, every node that reported gets the table pushed with token 0; a heartbeat behind the version gets it again, one current does not |
| A report naming node 4 from node 3's connection | Dropped: no push ever goes to node 4 at node 3's address |
| A `Txn` to the group | Answered under its token |
| A `Txn` whose round's disk writes have not run, then run | No answer until the disk holds the round; then answered |
| A session started and a pool committed, then a crash and a restart from the disk | The replay rebuilds the state: the table at the same epoch, a new session's ID past the old one's, the next pool's epoch past the last |
| Three voters on disks of their own | They elect a leader, which answers a `Txn`; every voter applies it |
| A disk write that fails under the leader's `Txn` | The host reports the error, drops its Control and takes nothing more: no action for a `Txn`, a fetch, a Raft tick or a step timer |
| A `Txn`, then 0 to 3 of its round's disk actions, then a crash that keeps all or none of the unflushed writes | A `Txn` answered before the crash is applied after it; the restarted host leads and answers |
| Format cut short by a crash after each of its disk actions, keeping all or none of the unflushed writes, then two restarts | A log with no superblock stays `ErrNotFormatted`, for `-format` to make again; a log whose replay gave no record gets the boot round from the voters given, written to the disk, and the host leads and answers a `Txn` after each restart (`TestARestartAfterAFormatCutShortWritesTheBootRound`) |
| A voter of three restarted with a configuration of itself alone | It takes its log's configuration of three, elects nothing alone, and applies the `Txn` the group's leader answers next (`TestAVoterRestartedWithOtherVotersTakesItsLogsConfiguration`) |
| 16 rounds of 40 counter `Txn`s on a log whose `max_replay_bytes` is 64 KiB, on a disk of 16 segments of 256 KiB, each round ending in a crash mid-round or while a checkpoint runs, after 0 to 8 of the next disk actions or once the checkpoint's pieces are durable and its manifest in flight, keeping the unflushed writes or not | The crashes land with no checkpoint running (8), a piece in flight (5) and the manifest in flight (3), and the run fails if a window gets none. The host checkpoints, compacts and frees segments, so the run writes the disk more than twice over. Each restart loads its manifest's runs, takes the base and applied index from their mark and replays after the group's replay LSN: the counter holds every increment answered, and the state at every index equals what it was before the crash (`TestAHostCompactsAndRestartsFromItsManifest`).
