Planted: a restore that takes the base for the applied index applies the entries after the base twice, and the state check fires (`TestARestoreThatReappliesEntriesBreaksTheStateCheck`) |
| 24 rounds as above, each `Txn` putting a 900-byte key and deleting the key put 200 `Txn`s before, so the tree holds about 200 live keys in runs of several pieces, its merges whole | No key an answered `Txn` deleted comes back after a restart, and the state at every index equals what it was before. The crashes land with no checkpoint running (6), a piece in flight (13) and the manifest in flight (5), and the restarts load 193 pieces besides their runs' roots; the run fails if they load none (`TestAHostRestartsFromRunsOfManyPieces`) |
| The same run, its merges in steps of 8 KiB | Each checkpoint takes the next step of a merge until it ends, so the runs stay few and the log keeps room across all 24 crashes (`TestAHostMergesItsTreeInStepsAcrossCrashes`) |
| A leader of three on that log, cut off from both followers after 10 committed `Txn`s, then sent 1,000-byte `Txn`s it cannot commit until the replay floor passes the round holding the first of them, then a crash | A due checkpoint begins only while no round of the group is in flight, so it writes every entry past the compaction again in a full rewrite, and the floor passes that round; the restart holds every entry the leader held, at the same index, term and bytes. Before, the checkpoint began right after the round that passed the bound, still in flight, and `Host.Rewrite` skips a shard with a round in flight, so the floor never moved and the disk filled after about 380 of them (`TestACutOffLeaderRewritesItsEntriesAndKeepsThemAcrossACrash`) |
| Distinct 900-byte keys put on that disk, none deleted, until the tree outgrows it | A checkpoint finds no segment free, the reserve included, and nothing else frees one: the host fails it (`FailStalled`) and stops with `ErrNoSpace` instead of waiting (`TestAHostWhoseCheckpointHasNoRoomStops`) |
| A pool committed, then a node's table fetch, then heartbeats from a node behind the table and one current | The delta goes to every node that reported, the whole table to the node that fetched, and to the node behind alone, as the leader resends after a failover |
| A heartbeat of a later term from another replica at the leading voter, then a fetch | The Control is dropped; the fetch is answered with the leader the replica knows |
| A fetch at a leader whose lease does not run (a three-voter group with no grants) | No Control is read |
| A node's report naming a disk, then that node's replica report of the disk's fill | The disk joins the record; the fill reaches the Control |
| A node's report opening a disk of 2^20 blocks, then a pool of 4 PGs at one replica | Every PG placed with that disk as its primary |
| Two nodes' disks under a pool of 8 PGs, a restart, then one node's report and a second pool before the other node reports | No PG of the first pool moves, and the second places none on the disk not reported yet, which the step gets at size 0 |
| A node's report for another group | Dropped: the node is not recorded |
| Node 2 reports, then node 3 `node_down_after` later, then a pool commits | The delta goes to node 3 alone |
| A chunkstore frame in a pool buffer and a fetch before the group has a leader | The frame's buffer freed, the fetch answered with no leader known |
| A report, a session fetch and a table fetch at a follower of a three-voter group | Each answered with the leader's node |
| Placement and leader messages across the wire | Decode to what was sent; fuzzed (`FuzzDecodeTableMsg`, `FuzzDecodeDeltaMsg`, `FuzzDecodeLeader`), the table and delta from a seed of a pool with two PGs, one with a past interval |

The rows without a test named are unit tests in `internal/meta/ctlhost_test.go`. The process, `rock-solid ctl` in `cmd/rock-solid`, over TCP and io_uring on Linux:

| Input | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| A single voter of group 257 formatting its disk file, its `-max-replay-bytes` 256 KiB, and a node sending its report, a session fetch and a `Txn` adding 1 to a counter every 100 ms, then 2000 `Txn`s one after another | A fetch answered under its token: the voter elected itself, leased and committed its session table; the `Txn`s answered with their counts. Their rounds pass twice `max_replay_bytes` many times over, which the voter could not answer without checkpointing, compacting and reusing the segments it frees (`TestASingleVoterControlPlaneAnswersOverTCPAndSurvivesAKill`) |
| That process killed with `SIGKILL` and started again on its file without `-format` | It loads its manifest's runs, replays the log after them and answers the node's fetches again, and its counter past every count it answered before; a voter that formats at every start fails this |
| `-format` over a file not there, one of zeros, a short one of zeros, one with a byte in block 0 and one with a byte in the superblock copy | The first three made at full size; the last two refused and left as they were (`TestFormatMakesAFileNeverWrittenAndRefusesAnyOther`) |
| The voter stops with `ErrDeleted`, and with any other error | It exits with status 3, which a service manager should not restart; 1 (`TestADeletedVoterExitsWithItsOwnStatus`) |
| A `-max-replay-bytes` of a quarter of a 1 GiB disk, and one byte more | The first taken, the second refused at start: the reserve keeps room for a checkpoint of up to twice it and the records it bounds take up to twice it again, so a larger one stops the voter at about half its disk (`TestTheMaxReplayBytesFitAQuarterOfTheDisk`) |

The node's side, in `internal/node/node_test.go`:

| Input | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| A leader message from the voter the node talks to, naming another voter; naming none; naming a node that is no voter; one from a voter it does not talk to | Moves to the voter named; to the next voter; to the next voter; stays. Each move is in the output, so replicas report to the new voter |
| The connection to the voter it talks to is lost | Moves to the next voter; the next heartbeat goes there |
| Five losses of the only voter, and that voter naming no leader | No move, so no replica is re-pointed |
| Nine losses and nine redirects naming no leader within one `Interval` at a three-voter node; a loss an `Interval` later; a voter naming itself | One move; one more; none |
| A session fetch in flight when the node's voter names another | The fetch goes to the new voter at once, under a new token |
| A placement table or delta from a voter, and one from a node that is no voter | Handed on for every replica; dropped |
| A heartbeat after a table reached the node, then with replicas holding epochs 5 and 4, then both 5; a node with no replica after a delta of epoch 6 | Reports epoch 0, 4, 5 and 6: the oldest its replicas hold, so a leader after a failover resends the whole table only to a node behind it |
| Two replicas ask for the table in one pass, then again an interval later, then after a table arrived | One fetch, one more, then one at once |

## Storage node session wiring

The node's machine, `internal/node`, fed events with no network, and its messages in `internal/meta`.

| Input | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| A table pushed unasked | Handed to every replica with `answers` 0; the same or an older table hands nothing; a replica opened later gets the newest the node has |
| A session table from a peer other than the control plane, with a huge version | Dropped: nothing handed, and the control plane's next table still counts as newer |
| A heartbeat of a node built from its configuration, and of one configured role meta | Both report `Meta`, since every node holds metadata, and the second `MetaOnly` too, so the leader places voters on their disks and drains the second's (`TestTheHeartbeatReportsTheNodesRole`) |
| A heartbeat after a table reached the node | Reports the oldest version its running replicas' stores hold, not the one received; a node with no replica running reports the one received, safe while a store's fence table starts empty in memory |
| Two opened devices, a membership naming only the first's log, and a table at version 5 | The second runs no replica and the report says 5, the version the first holds: a device whose log the control plane refuses never pins the report (`TestAnUnnamedDeviceDoesNotPinTheReport`) |
| A replica asks while a fetch is in flight | No second fetch; the answer hands each replica the ask its fetch covered, and the node fetches again for the asks made after it went out |
| A fetch is unanswered after `Interval` | Fetched again under a new token; the old token's late answer is a table sent unasked |
| The control plane's connection is lost 100 times while a fetch is in flight | No fetch until `FetchTimer` fires after `Interval`, so a driver in backoff cannot spin the loop |
| Two starts of a node | Fetch under different tokens, so one start's answer never stands for the other's fetch; an unformatted device formats under different log IDs |
| A start with devices opened, failed by recovery and failed by format | The first report lists the opened disks and both failed devices |
| A fetch reaches the control-plane leader before it steps under its lease, after it lost its lease, or after it regained it but before stepping | Unanswered; once stepped under its lease, answered with the live sessions and next ID (`TestAFetchIsAnsweredOnlyUnderTheLeaderLease`, `internal/meta`) |
| A fetch reaches a new leader whose applied table lags a start the old leader committed | Unanswered until a session-table Txn of its own commits; a leader with nothing to commit commits the head's check alone, then answers (`TestAMachineThatHasNotSeenASessionStartAnswersNoFetch`, `internal/meta`) |
| A report or session table across the wire | Decodes to what was sent; live IDs that do not rise, a zero ID or one at or above the next ID are malformed; fuzzed (`FuzzDecodeNodeReport`, `FuzzDecodeSessions`) |
| A session start, its answer and a disk membership of 300 disks, with sizes, fills and two pools' grants, across the wire | Decode to what was sent, a fixed membership to its golden bytes; a membership whose disk IDs are zero or do not rise, or whose pool IDs do not rise, is malformed; fuzzed (`FuzzDecodeStarted`, `FuzzDecodeDisks`) |
| No asks, one and 200 across the wire, and a pool over 32 bits | Decode to what was sent; the pool over 32 bits is malformed; fuzzed (`TestAsksCrossTheWireWhole`, `FuzzDecodeAsks`) |
| A replica restarted over its store, handed its membership and a table with its PG | Its ask for a new interval of that PG goes to its authority (`TestARestartedReplicasAskGoesToItsAuthority`) |
| A replica's ask for a new interval reaches the leading host from a node not heard from, then from one heard from; then its activation of the new interval | Nothing moves; the PG moves to a new interval whose delta goes to the node; the next table holds it activated (`TestAReplicasAskAndActivationReachTheControl`, `internal/meta`) |
| Two replicas, one removed; then the device opened again under another log, then a membership naming it | After the removal a table goes to the other alone, the removed one's held version no longer pins the report, and the report names its device once, with the new log, its replica counted only once the membership names it; before the removal it got every table and its version counted (`TestARemovedReplicaGetsNoTableAndLeavesTheReport`) |
| A disk membership from a voter, and one from a node that is no voter | The voter's handed on whole; the other dropped (`TestTheDiskMembershipIsHandedOn`) |
| A blank device's format cut by a crash after each of its disk actions, then a start with another seed | The second start formats under a log ID of its own source, or opens the first's log once its format landed; the device is reported opened, with its device, log, size, reserve and class, only once a format settles; once its store closes, no page slab is out (`TestTwoStartsOverAFormatCutShortDrawDifferentLogIDs`) |
| A device whose block 0 and superblock copy hold junk | Reported failed, both blocks left as they were, no page slab out, and no replica runs whatever the membership says (`TestADeviceWithNoValidSuperblockFailsUntouched`) |
| A blank device whose writes all fail | Its format fails, the device is reported failed and the format's store has given its page slabs back (`TestADeviceWhoseFormatFailsGivesItsPagesBack`) |
| A session table, a placement table at epoch 2 whose PG has disk 5 as primary and disk 4 as member, and the authority handed to an opened device, then a message, then a membership without its log, then one naming it disk 5 and disk 4 at another node's loop | Nothing runs and the message is dropped until the membership names the device's log; then the replica runs as disk 5, holding session version 3 and epoch 2, reports to the authority and, as the PG's primary, peers with disk 4's loop (`TestTheReplicaStartsAsTheDiskTheMembershipNames`) |
| A device the process could not open, as a drive gone from the bus, beside one that opened | Reported failed with no disk action; the node's report lists it failed and the other opened (`TestADeviceThatCannotBeOpenedIsReportedFailed`) |
| A node's start | Sends a table fetch beside its first heartbeat: its replicas start with no placement table, and a leader that sent the node the whole table before a restart within `node_down_after` sends it only deltas (`TestAStartFetchesThePlacementTable`) |
| A node's start whose table fetch gets no answer, among three voters; then a move to another voter; then a table; then a heartbeat and a move | The next heartbeat sends the fetch again, and the move sends it to the new voter; once the table arrives neither sends it (`TestALostTableFetchGoesAgainUntilATableArrives`) |
| A node's start whose table fetch gets no answer; then a delta; then a heartbeat | The heartbeat sends no fetch: a delta ends the resend as a table does (`TestADeltaEndsTheTableFetchResend`) |
| A node and a device wired as the process wires them: the start's table fetch lost, a delta of epoch 3 before the membership names the device's disk, then the membership, then a heartbeat | The device drops the delta, since its replica does not run yet; the replica, starting with no table, has the node fetch the table, and the heartbeat sends the fetch again (`TestAReplicaStartedBehindADroppedDeltaFetchesTheTable`) |
| A node and a device wired as the process wires them: the start's table fetch lost, a write to the device, then the next heartbeat's fetch answered with a table whose PG has the device as primary, then the write again | The first write is refused, since the replica holds no table; the heartbeat sends the fetch again, and the write after its answer is acknowledged (`TestALostTableFetchIsMadeUpBeforeAWriteIsAcknowledged`) |
| A node and a device wired as the process wires them, each one's output cloned into the other's `Take`: a write of session 5 to the device's activated primary while its fence table is empty, then a table pushed with token 0 that does not know session 5, then the fetch's answer, which knows it, and in a second run does not | The write waits and the node fetches; the pushed table answers nothing; the answer acknowledges the write, and in the second run refuses it (`TestOnlyTheAnswerToItsFetchSettlesAWaitingWrite`). A device that answered every ask on any table fails it |
| A device's output (opened, an ask, a table fetch, held version and epoch, failed) handed to the node | The disk joins the report and is handed the newest table, the ask fetches the session table, the table fetch goes out once an `Interval`, the report acknowledges the held version and lists the failed device (`TestADevicesOutputFeedsTheNode`) |
| The node's output (a move, the membership, session tables for this device and another, a placement table) handed to a device; then the same table again; then a Raft group's message | The replica runs, holds this device's table and the epoch, and reports to the voter moved to; the unchanged table outputs no held version or epoch, so a write costs no mail; the group message is dropped and its buffer freed (`TestTheNodesOutputFeedsADevice`) |
| A membership giving disk 6 a size of 1,000 blocks and a fill of 300 and pool 1 grants of 300, then a write to a PG led by the device with disk 6 down beside it | Refused for space, disk 6 at 600 against a 45% `write_limit`; with any of the three left untaken it is not (`TestTheMembershipGivesAdmissionTheDisksAndGrants`) |
| A node's output cloned, then the membership and table overwritten by the next messages | The clones keep what they held (`TestACloneOutlivesTheNodesBuffers`) |

The rows are unit tests in `internal/node/node_test.go`, `internal/node/device_test.go` and `internal/meta/nodewire_test.go`.

The process, `rock-solid node`, runs as a child of the test binary (`TestNodeProcess`) over TCP and io_uring on files, in Docker, with the control plane, `rock-solid ctl`'s voter, in the test process, where the test calls its `Control` on its loop (`cmd/rock-solid`):

- `TestAStartThatFailsReturnsItsError`: a node whose port is taken and a voter whose disk file is missing return their error from the start, never a panic.
- `TestANodeStartsItsDevicesAndTakesItsDisksAndTablesOverTCP`: two blank devices, one whose block 0 is junk and a path with no file. The blank ones are formatted, reported, named in the membership and up in the record; the junk one and the missing one are in `Control.FailedDevices` while the others serve; a pool created at the leader gives a table whose epoch both replicas report holding, and the leader gets each replica's fill from its heartbeats (`Control.Capacity` is ready), which a device with no authority never sends.
- `TestASessionWritesOverTCPAndARestartedNodeWritesToTheSamePGAgain`: once PG 0 of a one-copy pool is activated, a client loop starts a session through the session-start kind and writes to PG 0's primary. No table has reached the node, so its replicas' fence tables are empty and the write waits for the replica's ask to be answered by a fetch; it is acknowledged. The node is killed and started again at once over its opened stores, within `node_down_after`, so the control plane never marks PG 0's member down: the block written before the kill reads back and a new session's write is acknowledged once PG 0 moves to exactly one new interval, the one the restarted replica asked for, activated with its member up. A device that sends no asks fails it. Once the first session's lease runs out unrenewed and the leader fences it, its write is refused.

Two steps of the item are checked sans-IO rather than over TCP, where they cannot be timed: a pushed table refuses none of the waiting writes (`TestOnlyTheAnswerToItsFetchSettlesAWaitingWrite` with `TestAPushedTableGoesToEveryReplicaUnasked`, and in `internal/chunkstore` `TestAWriteFromASessionNoFetchedTableKnowsIsRefused`), and a disk marked down comes up only once its node's heartbeat reports the current session version (the sessions model's `neg-up-with-old-table` plant, `upWithOldTable`, in `TestPlantedLockBugsBreakTheLockInvariants`, `internal/meta`). Parsing the process's flags refuses a pool ID past 32 bits, a node, voter or peer ID in the upper half of 32 bits, which the operator's command line draws its own from, a voter or peer as the node, a peer that is a voter, no device or one named twice, a port with no room for each device's loop and a `-role` other than `storage` or `meta`, and takes `-role meta` as a node holding metadata alone (`TestParseNodeRefusesABadConfiguration`, `TestParseCtlRefusesANodeOutOfRange`).

## Storage node disk startup

- The model: `StartDevice`'s new log ID for an unformatted device is the code of `epoch.tla`'s
  `Format` step, which gives a disk formatted again a new disk ID. Its negative, `neg-keep-disk-id`,
  has its plant in the replica harness (`keepID`, with `formatUnformatted` standing in for the
  node), not in `StartDevice`.
- The decision (`TestADeviceIsFormattedOnlyWhenBothSuperblocksAreZeros`, `internal/chunkstore`):
  a store that serves is opened; `ErrNotFormatted`, wrapped, is formatted, under a log ID no earlier
  of 100 starts drew; `ErrUnrecognized`, `CopyOnly`, a disk read error and `ErrCorrupt` are each
  failed.
- A format that fails (`TestADeviceWhoseFormatFailsIsReportedFailed`, `storetest`): a blank
  device too small for any geometry, and a blank device whose writes fail, are formatted, and
  `StartDevice` given how the format ended reports each failed.
- Formats crashed twice on the simulated disk
  (`TestADeviceCrashedTwiceMidFormatComesBackWholeOrNew`, `storetest`): a store holding a 3-block
  write to chunk 1 under log `0x5eed` is formatted again under a new log ID and power-cut after k of
  format's 4,104 disk completions, for k from 1 to 8, half of them and the last 9; a start that
  formats is cut after k completions too, and a third start runs to the end. Each start that opens
  shows the old log with chunk 1 whole under its old disk ID in the disk record, or a log ID no
  format of the run drew before under a new disk ID with chunk 1 reading zeros; no start formats
  under a log ID drawn before or leaves the device failed, and the run reaches both outcomes. It
  runs with trims and again with `NoTrim`, the format of a disk that is a file.
- Both superblocks damaged (`TestADeviceWithNoValidSuperblockIsLeftAsItWas`, `storetest`): bit 16
  flipped in block 0 and in the copy of a written store; the start is failed with
  `ErrUnrecognized`, and the disk's SHA-256 is the same before and after it.
- Failed after a repair (`TestAFailedDeviceIsWrittenOnlyByItsSuperblockRepair`, `storetest`): bit 16
  flipped in block 0 of a written store, its copy valid, and every read past the copy failing; the
  start is failed, block 0 now equals the copy, and every other block is as it was.
- On io_uring over a file-backed disk (`internal/driver/uring`, Linux, in Docker), with each start a
  child process of the test binary (`TestStartChild`): the same two cases with `kill -9` in place
  of the power cut. `TestAStartKilledTwiceMidFormatComesBackWholeOrNew` kills the child after k
  rounds of format's completions, for k from 1 to 8, half of a format's rounds and the last 9, the
  start's own format after as many, then starts it unkilled, with the same checks. It runs with
  trims, where both outcomes must be reached, and with `NoTrim`, where only a new log must be: with
  no trims a format's first write is the new block 0, which a kill after a round has let land.
  `TestAStartLeavesADeviceWithNoValidSuperblockAsItWas` checks the file's SHA-256 after a start
  reports the device failed.
- The report (`TestAFailedDeviceIsShownAndNeverRecorded`, `internal/meta`): failed devices
  reported by two nodes, one of them with no disk open, are shown by `Control.FailedDevices` by
  node and device, a proposal after them leaves the disk record unchanged, and a node's next report
  without its failed device drops it from the list. A device whose log the record refuses, a cloned
  drive's, is listed too (`TestADiskIsKnownByItsLogOnItsDevice`).

## Operator CLI

The leader's side is `meta.CtlHost` on the single-voter group of [Control-plane host](#control-plane-host), fed an operator's commands from a node it never heard from (`internal/meta`, `admin_test.go`); the command line is `cmd/rock-solid`.

| Input | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| A pool command sent twice under one request, over two reported disks; then the same command again under another | No answer until the pool commits, then one answer with no refusal and the pool's 8 PGs on the two disks; the repeat, which changes nothing, is answered at once (`TestAPoolCommandIsAnsweredOnceItCommits`) |
| A declaration for an up disk and for an unknown one, a removal of a disk not drained, a pool with `data` set, and a command that does not decode | Each answered at once with its refusal, naming `chunkstore.ErrLostRefused`, `ErrUnknownDisk`, `ErrNotDrained` and the `data` setting; no pool and no disk gone (`TestARefusedCommandIsAnsweredWithItsReason`) |
| A declaration that a disk of a node silent for twice `node_down_after` is lost; then the same declaration again | No answer until it commits, then one with no refusal and the disk gone; the repeat is answered at once (`TestALostDiskIsAnsweredOnceGone`) |
| A pool of replicas 2, `min_live` 1, no overcommit and failure domain `disk` over three nodes' disks; then a command setting only `write_limit` 50 | Answered with no refusal; the committed pool keeps every other setting as it was, not at its default (`TestAPoolChangeKeepsTheSettingsItLeavesOut`) |
| The failed devices command after a node reports device `0xbad` failed | Answered with node 2, device `0xbad` (`TestTheFailedDevicesCommandListsThem`) |
| A pool command waiting when the leader drops its `Control` | Dropped unanswered, for the command line to send again (`TestACommandWaitingWhenTheControlDropsIsNotAnswered`) |
| A pool change staged; then another leader's Txn committing the pool at pg_count 16 | The change's Txn fails its check, the reload drops the change, and it is answered with a refusal; the committed pool keeps its `write_limit` (`TestAPoolChangeDroppedBeforeItCommitsIsRefused`) |
| A declaration that disk 2 is lost, staged once it is down; then another leader's Txn committing the membership that had it up | The declaration's Txn fails its check, the reload drops it, and it is answered with a refusal; the disk is not gone (`TestADeclarationDroppedBeforeItCommitsIsRefused`) |
| The failed devices command and a pool command at a leader whose lease does not run | Neither answered, waiting nor staged (`TestACommandAtALeaderWithoutItsLeaseIsDropped`) |
| An operator's command at a follower of a three-voter group | Answered with the leader's node, as a node's report is (`TestAFollowerRedirectsANodeToTheLeader`) |
| A drain of an unknown disk; drains of two disks a node reported, the same request sent once each; then an undrain of the second and a removal of the first | The first answered at once with `ErrUnknownDisk`; the drains only once they commit, with no refusal, both disks drained; the undrain and the removal once they commit, the first disk gone and the second neither drained nor gone (`TestADrainOverTheWireIsAnsweredOnceItCommits`) |
| A drain and a declaration of a down disk, an undrain and a removal of a drained one, and a drain and an undrain of a third, each pair sent before a step | The declaration, the removal and the undrain answered with no refusal; the drain and the undrain of the disk gone refused as declared lost or removed, and the overtaken drain as changed by another command (`TestADrainChangeOvertakenIsRefusedWithWhy`) |
| A drain of one of two disks under a one-copy pool, then a removal; then each step every PG's interval reported activated and recovered; then the removal again | The first removal refused with how many PGs still name the disk; the disk empties with never more than `max_moves` PGs holding a leaving member, and the second removal is answered with the disk gone (`TestADrainedDiskWithMembersEmptiesAndIsRemoved`) |
| Under a two-copy pool, a pin of a PG naming no disk, then a pin naming its members reversed, an unpin, and an edit naming them in their first order; then an edit naming PG 8 of an 8-PG pool, one naming disk 9, a pin naming a member and the third disk, and an edit naming one member | Each of the first four answered only once its table commits, with no refusal, the entry pinned or not as asked with the members in the order named, the PG's own for the first; the rest at once with `ErrUnknownPG`, `ErrUnknownDisk` and `ErrEditMembers` twice (`TestAnEditOverTheWireIsAnsweredOnceItCommits`) |
| Two reorders of one PG sent before a step; then, every PG activated, an edit of each PG naming its members in order sent with a drain of a disk; then a pin of a PG the drain moved | The first reorder refused as overtaken though the PG keeps its disks and pin, the second answered; the edit of each PG the drain moved refused as overtaken, the rest answered; the pin refused at once with `ErrPGMoving` (`TestAnEditOvertakenInItsTableIsRefused`) |
| While the commit of a drain is in flight, a reorder or a pin naming no disk staged for each PG | The step after drops the edit of each PG the drain moved, which keeps its leaving member and stays unpinned, and applies the rest (`TestAnEditOfAPGMovedInFlightIsDropped`) |
| A reorder of the last PG of four 8,192-PG pools staged before a disk's down marks, a step the table budget cuts; then, from a stale leader, the reorder back proposed against a table another commit moved on | The cut table leaves the PG as it was with the edit staged, and a later table applies it; the stale commit fails its check with the edit still staged, and the step after the reload applies it (`TestAnEditWaitsOutACutAndAFailedCommit`) |
| Each command, a pool spec with every setting, and answers with no text, 300 bytes of refusal, 100 failed devices and give-ups, across the wire | Decode to what was sent; fuzzed (`TestAdminCrossesTheWireWhole`, `FuzzDecodeAdmin`, `FuzzDecodeAdminAnswer`) |
| A give-up or a read of a PG the table lacks, a give-up of an interval past the current, and one with nothing lost; then, once the primary's report names two chunks unfound, a read of the PG and a give-up of its interval; then, once the next interval's report names chunks unfound too, the give-up sent again | The first four answered at once with `ErrUnknownPG`, `ErrIntervalMoved` and `chunkstore.ErrNothingLost`; the read with the interval and 2 unfound; the give-up only once it commits, with the interval given up and both chunks dropped, the PG in its next interval; the one sent again with the same give-up, the newer interval not given up (`TestAGiveUpIsAnsweredWithWhatItDropped`, and `TestAGiveUpCommitsOnlyWhatIsLost` on the `Control`) |
| A stopped PG's give-up and an unfound one's, answered, one with more chunks unfound than it dropped | Printed as the interval given up, every chunk kept as its members hold it, and as the count and each chunk dropped, and how many more stay unfound (`TestAGiveUpPrintsWhatItDropped`) |
| `disk lost`, `disk drain`, `disk undrain`, `disk remove`, `disk failed`, `pool`, `pg give-up`, `pg edit`, `pg pin` with and without disks and `pg unpin` with flags before and after their arguments; a disk of 0, a missing `-ctl`, pool settings on a disk command, an unknown preset, a `write_limit` past a byte, a give-up of pool 0 or of a PG that is no 32-bit number, a give-up or unpin with a disk list, an edit without one, an empty or zero disk in the list, and an unknown PG command | The commands parse to what was given; the rest are refused (`TestParseAdminTakesEachCommand`) |
| A blocking connection, as the command line's, to a loop's TCP driver: a message with inline bytes and data, then the loop's answer | The loop receives it from the node the hello named, and the connection the answer (`TestAConnTradesMessagesWithALoop`, `internal/driver/tcp`) |
| A blocking connection under node 9 to a loop, which then dials a second loop; the connection closes; then the second loop sends to the first, and the first to it | The first loop delivers node 9's `PeerLost` and forgets it, keeping one peer; the second loop's message names it, and the first loop's send goes on the connection it dialed, with no new dial (`TestAPeerThatDialedInIsForgottenOnceItCloses`, `internal/driver/tcp`) |
| A blocking connection under node 9 to a loop; the loop sends it a frame past 16 MiB | The send ends the connection, and by the pass's end the loop delivers node 9's `PeerLost` and holds no peer (`TestAPeerThatDialedInIsForgottenWhenASendToItFails`, `internal/driver/tcp`) |
| A blocking connection under node 9 to a loop whose pool is full | The loop cannot answer the hello and ends the connection, delivering no `PeerLost` and holding no peer (`TestAPeerWhoseHelloCannotBeAnsweredIsNotKept`, `internal/driver/tcp`) |

Over TCP and io_uring on files, in Docker, `TestTheOperatorsCommandLineOverTCP` runs the voter in the test process and two storage nodes as children of the test binary, node 2 with three blank devices and one with junk in block 0, node 3 with two blank devices, and the command line in the test process:

- Two shard-map groups set at the leader, neither the control-plane group, each get a voter on node 2 and one on node 3, the two nodes whose heartbeats report they hold metadata.
- `rock-solid pool 1 -replicas 2 -min-live 2 -failure-domain disk -pg-count 16` prints that pool 1 is set, and the committed table places all 16 PGs on two of the five disks the nodes reported and the record keeps.
- `rock-solid pg pin 1 0` prints that PG 1.0 is pinned, and the committed table has it pinned; `rock-solid pg unpin 1 0` prints that it is unpinned, and the table has it unpinned.
- `rock-solid disk drain` of node 2's third blank device's disk, which holds members, prints that it drains; `rock-solid disk remove` of it exits 1 with how many PGs still name it, and, once balance has moved them off, prints that the disk is removed.
- `rock-solid disk lost` for an up disk of node 2 exits 1 printing the leader's refusal, `chunkstore: disk not down`.
- `rock-solid disk failed` prints node 2's junk device, by its device ID.
- Node 3 is killed; once refill keeps one of its disks as a leaving member of a PG, after `degraded_refill_after`, `rock-solid disk lost` of each of its two disks prints that the disk is declared lost, and no PG names either disk afterwards, leaving members included.

## Shared network suite

- One suite in `internal/loop/nettest`, written against its `Net` interface (start and stop a
  node's process, its pool, a pass on its loop, hold its reader, run until a condition holds, its
  redial backoff) and run on the simulated network (`TestSuiteOnTheSimulatedNetwork`, seeded in
  `scripts/seeds.sh`) and on loopback TCP (`internal/driver/tcp`, on macOS and on Linux in
  Docker). Nothing in `Net` is particular to one transport, so RDMA joins by implementing it
  (done-when: RDMA and TCP pass the same suite, and a mixed 3-node cluster negotiates per pair).
- On TCP each node is a stepped loop on `looptest` with its own listener on a port the kernel
  assigns, all on one simulated clock; a run passes the loops round robin until nothing moves.
- Every case ends in one check against a model of every message sent: each message arrives at most
  once, whole (its inline bytes and its buffer, which travels as whole 4 KiB blocks), naming its
  sender, and in the order sent; between two `PeerLost`s a process is handed for a peer, what it
  gets from that peer has no hole (no message missing between two that arrive) and none of it
  comes from the peer's next start; every message a live process sent that never arrived is
  followed by a `PeerLost` for its peer, and every buffer it sent to that peer alone is freed before
  that `PeerLost`; every live process's pool is empty. Both drivers keep order per connection
  (the simulated network with duplicates off), so a replica primary may rely on it.
- Cases, the driver contract's network rules:
  - messages of a 256-byte inline payload, and of 1 byte, 257 bytes, a block and 1 MiB in pool
    buffers, between three nodes, arrive whole, in order, naming their sender, with no
    `PeerLost` (each lower node opens its connections first, since two TCP loops that dial each
    other at once keep the lower's dial, and the other's first sends end in `PeerLost`);
  - one buffer sent to three peers and a fourth that is stopped reaches the three, ends in
    `PeerLost` for the fourth, and is freed once the driver is done with it for all four;
  - a `meta.Client` `Txn` sent to a follower is answered `NotLeader` naming the leader, resent there
    and settled under the client's token;
  - a peer stopped with three `Txn`s waiting hands the client one `PeerLost`, after every buffer sent
    to it was freed, and the client settles all three as dropped; a `Txn` to the peer's next start
    is answered;
  - a peer restarted at once, twice, with 64 messages of 16 KiB from each start, is a new
    connection each time: each start's messages arrive after the `PeerLost` for the start before
    and before the one for its own end. The first restart comes while the other end reads; the
    second while it holds its reader, so on TCP, with a 64 KiB read budget per pass, the new
    connection arrives with the old one still open and unread and replaces it;
  - three nodes that each send to both others before any connection is up, so each pair dials each
    other at once: whichever dial a driver keeps, every send arrives or ends in `PeerLost`;
  - a send to a stopped peer, or to one never started, ends in `PeerLost` with its buffer freed,
    and reaches the peer once it is up and the sender's backoff, which the driver states, is over;
  - a reader that stops while 40 messages of 1 MiB are sent to it: what arrives is in order and the
    rest ends in one `PeerLost` at the sender, whatever the driver's queue bound gives (on TCP the
    32 MiB bound fails the connection and those already in the socket buffers arrive, 4; the
    simulated network has no bound and delivers all 40); a send after reaches the reader.
- Simulated network only, listed as skipped on TCP: a partition fails the connection at both ends
  and nothing crosses it, and a send after the heal arrives; with one message in ten dropped, every
  dropped message ends in `PeerLost` at its sender.
- Not covered here: a timeout keeping its buffer until the reply or `PeerLost`, which is the core's
  request tracking, not the driver's (the [driver contract](#simulated-network) checks it in the
  simulator); `SIOCOUTQ` and deadlines, since the suite waits on conditions and arms no timer.

## Durable write benchmark

`TestDurableWriteBenchmark` in `internal/driver/uring` (Linux, root, a spare drive; it skips
without `RS_RAW_DEVICE`, and its file case without `RS_URING_DIR`, as in
[io_uring on a raw device and NVMe](#io_uring-on-a-raw-device-and-nvme)):

```sh
sudo RS_RAW_DEVICE=$D ./uring.test -test.v -test.run 'TestDurableWriteBenchmark|TestRecoveryReadsAFullDisksSegmentHeaders'
mkfs.ext4 $D; mount $D /mnt/rs
sudo RS_URING_DIR=/mnt/rs/u ./uring.test -test.v -test.run TestDurableWriteBenchmark
```

- Durable writes at queue depth 1 through the full path: an event loop, a disk log formatted on the
  disk and io_uring. A shard proposes 128 bytes; the round writes one record, 8 KiB with its header,
  and its linked flush; once the shard hears it is durable it proposes the next, at once or after an
  idle gap the loop's timer counts: 1,000 back to back, 200 after 10 ms, 50 after 100 ms, 15 after
  1 s. It runs on the raw device (64 MiB segments) and on a 4 GiB disk file written in full on
  ext4 on the same drive.
- Each runs twice: the loop as built, waiting in `epoll_wait` for the ring's eventfd, and with a
  kernel wrapper that waits in `io_uring_enter` (`min_complete` 1) whenever the loop would block
  with I/O in flight, the alternative [Runtime in Go](design.md#runtime-in-go) weighs.
- Reports latency from proposal to durable (p50, p90, p99, max), and per write the loop thread's
  CPU time (`RUSAGE_THREAD`) and cycles (a `perf_event_open` counter on the thread, to which the
  test locks the loop's goroutine; the run fails if the kernel multiplexed the counter), and the
  process's CPU; and the CPU frequency driver, governor, energy preference and idle states. It
  asserts no timing.
- Cross-checked with fio on the same drive: `fio --rw=randwrite --direct=1 --iodepth=1
  --fdatasync=1`, 4 and 8 KiB, back to back and with `--thinktime` of 10 ms, 100 ms and 1 s, on
  the raw device's first GiB and on a 64 MiB file written before.
- Results, WDC SN720 512 GB (client NVMe, volatile write cache), Linux 7.0, Xeon E-2236 (6 cores,
  12 threads), `intel_pstate` with C-states down to C10. Each cell gives the event mode, then the
  wait mode, but for cycles, one range over both; latency is p50, and the CPU rows after idle give
  the 10 ms, 100 ms and 1 s gaps in turn:

  | Case | Device, `powersave` | Device, `performance` | File, `powersave` | File, `performance` | fio 8 KiB, device, `powersave` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Back to back | 0.37, 0.37 ms | 0.36, 0.36 ms | 0.36, 0.36 ms | 0.37, 0.36 ms | 0.48 ms (0.02 + 0.46) |
  | After 10 ms | 0.74, 0.64 ms | 0.58, 0.57 ms | 0.72, 0.72 ms | 0.60, 0.60 ms | 0.50 ms |
  | After 100 ms | 0.80, 0.85 ms | 0.58, 0.46 ms | 0.71, 0.77 ms | 0.58, 0.58 ms | 0.52 ms |
  | After 1 s | 0.99, 1.18 ms | 0.81, 0.67 ms | 1.29, 1.19 ms | 0.59, 0.59 ms | 0.53 ms |
  | Loop thread CPU, back to back | 29, 30 µs | 31, 32 µs | 29, 33 µs | 31, 31 µs | |
  | Loop thread CPU, after idle | 327, 424, 414; 245, 376, 378 µs | 140, 149, 143; 139, 132, 140 µs | 306, 443, 419; 274, 370, 393 µs | 147, 158, 149; 139, 158, 157 µs | |
  | Loop thread cycles, back to back | 111,000 | 114,000 to 123,000 | 115,000 to 117,000 | 113,000 to 122,000 | |
  | Loop thread cycles, after idle | 281,000 to 315,000 | 434,000 to 449,000 | 305,000 to 355,000 | 457,000 to 491,000 | |
  | Process CPU, back to back | 46, 46 µs | 48, 50 µs | 45, 51 µs | 49, 49 µs | |
  | Process CPU, after idle | 776, 1,573, 1,380; 419, 865, 693 µs | 288, 398, 424; 295, 374, 356 µs | 750, 1,461, 1,153; 557, 924, 676 µs | 299, 433, 410; 269, 427, 442 µs | |

  Back to back, p99 is 0.55 to 0.65 ms, but for the new file system below. The idle-gap rows have
  15 to 200 writes, so their p50 moves by about 0.1 ms between runs; the file under `performance`
  ran on a new ext4 still initializing its tables, and its p99 reached 1.45 to 47 ms.
- Against the [NVMe flush spike](design.md#appendix-nvme-flush-spike)'s drive (0.95 ms back to
  back, 1.2 ms after 10 ms, 1.9 to 2.1 ms after 100 ms to 3 s): this drive flushes in about half the
  time and, unlike that one, not slower after idling, so fio stays at 0.5 ms whatever the gap. Back
  to back the full path takes 0.11 ms less than fio, though fio's `fdatasync` alone takes 0.46 ms;
  why is not established. After an idle gap the path is up to 0.3 ms over fio under `performance`
  and up to 0.8 ms under `powersave`, and the loop thread's CPU per write grows 4 to 15 times and
  its cycles 2.5 to 4.3 times. Under `performance` the extra CPU, about 110 µs, is smaller than the
  extra latency, 0.1 to 0.45 ms, so most of that latency is not CPU on the loop thread; its cause
  is an [open question](design.md#roadmap-and-open-questions).
- Waiting in `io_uring_enter` gives no consistent latency gain: p50 within ±0.2 ms either way, the
  faster mode changing between gaps, and back to back the same. It saves CPU only after idle under
  `powersave`: 6 to 25% of the loop thread's and 26 to 50% of the process's in every cell; under
  `performance` the two modes match. The QD 1 read gain the raw-device benchmark saw is the
  governor's ([QD 1 reads](#io_uring-on-a-raw-device-and-nvme)). The loop keeps its event mode, for
  the reasons [Runtime in Go](design.md#runtime-in-go) gives.
- Recovery of a full disk's segment headers: `TestRecoveryReadsAFullDisksSegmentHeaders` formats
  a log over the whole device, writes a valid segment header into each of its 7,630 segments of
  64 MiB, and times recovery over io_uring from its first read to the last header read (two blocks
  each), at read depths 1, 8, 64 (the default) and 256: 0.63 to 0.99 s, 130 to 139 ms, 33 ms and
  33 ms, 4.3 to 4.4 µs a header from depth 64 on, under either governor. A 256 GiB disk's 4,096
  headers would take about 18 ms and a 16 TiB disk's 262,144 about 1.1 s, if the drive keeps that
  rate. Open: no target is given.
- Open: tolerances against fio and between runs; a nightly run, where a 20% regression is a bug.
  The hot path's zero allocations per operation are checked by the round driver's and the
  io_uring driver's benchmarks, not here.

## Crash tests on real disks

`TestCrashOnARealDisk` in `internal/driver/uring` (Linux, in Docker on a Mac). There is no daemon
yet, so the test binary is both: the test is the driver, and it runs itself again as the child
(`TestCrashChild`, with `RS_CRASH_CHILD` naming the disk file), a chunk store over a 256 MiB
file-backed disk through io_uring, `O_DIRECT` writes and their linked fsync, the shared suite's
store configuration with `max_replay_bytes` at 256 KiB so cycles recover from checkpoints and
replay. Commands go to the child on fd 3, a pipe the driver shares with the
[history clients](#real-cluster-histories), each a fixed 30 bytes written whole (a write carries its
data seed, not its data); the driver's acknowledgments come back on fd 4, each client's replies on
its own pipe.

- `kill -9` mid-round: the driver keeps 8 changes in flight over chunks 1 to 4 (writes of 1 byte
  to 3 blocks at random offsets, one in six a punch), and after a number of acknowledgments drawn
  from the seed (1 to 400 per cycle) sends SIGKILL, with the changes it just sent and the rounds
  before them unanswered. Once the child is dead, the driver reads the acknowledgment pipe to its
  end and counts what it finds as acknowledged: the child sent them, so a client would have seen
  them. It restarts the child over the same file, and the child sends back the four chunks it
  recovered.
- The crash oracle is a file the driver writes, outside the child (as RocksDB's crash test keeps its
  expected state and trace): a line per change before it is sent, and per acknowledgment, flushed
  and fsynced before the driver counts the acknowledgment. Each check reads the file's lines since
  the last check, not the driver's memory.
- Every restart recovers, in each chunk, its changes in the order sent up to one at or past the last
  acknowledged one, and none after it: no acknowledged change is lost and no change appears that was
  never sent. The prefix is per chunk because the store orders changes only within a chunk: a
  chunk's changes wait for one another, two chunks' do not, so their log order need not be their
  send order. The next change after the prefix, never acknowledged, may also be kept in part, as
  the [design](design.md#alternatives-considered) accepts for a write of several records, but only
  cut where the store cut it into log items and the kill fell between their rounds: an unaligned
  punch of several blocks logs its head edge block, its middle and its tail edge block as separate
  items, so it may come back with its head edge alone, or all but its tail edge. A write here spans
  at most 4 blocks, one record (the child refuses to start if the store's largest write item is
  smaller), and like an aligned punch it comes back whole or not at all. The first 100-cycle runs
  found a cut punch on seed 1: blocks 591 to 594 recovered with the middle punched and the tail
  block not.
- Repeated: `RS_CRASH_CYCLES` kills (150 by default, about 35 s in Docker, in which 3 to 8 restarts keep a cut punch) on
  `RS_CRASH_SEED` (1 by default), which draws, in streams of their own, the changes and their data,
  each cycle's kill point (a count of acknowledgments, then a pause under 0.5 ms) and the pauses
  between sends, so a run's timing does not shift what the seed draws; the timing of the kill against the child still varies. A failure
  prints the replay command and the oracle file's path, and saves the recovered chunk beside it;
  both stay when `RS_CRASH_DIR` names the directory. The test logs how many restarts kept a change
  never acknowledged, lost one, and kept the first rounds of one (the kill fell with a change's
  later round in flight, the only count that proves a round was cut). CI's test job runs seed 1 and
  its seeds job seeds 2 and 3.
- The oracle file, one record per line, numbers in decimal:

  ```text
  write <seq> <chunk> <off> <len> <data seed>   sent; the bytes are core.NewRand(data seed).Fill of len
  punch <seq> <chunk> <off> <len>                sent
  ack <seq>                                      acknowledged, fsynced before counted
  kill <cycle>                                   the child was killed
  kept <chunk> <seq>                             the restart kept the chunk's changes up to seq (0: none since the last kept)
  torn <chunk> <seq> <blocks>                    and the first blocks of the next change, seq
  ```

- What a `kill -9` does not test: the process dies but the kernel lives, so the page cache and the
  drive's write cache keep everything written; even with `O_DIRECT` and fsync on the path, it tests
  rounds in flight, not writes lost to a power cut. So a store that acknowledges a round once its
  write completes but before its flush passes here; the simulator's
  [crash oracle](#crash-oracle) (`TestRecoveriesMatchTheCrashOracle`) catches it, and so does the
  `log-writes` target of [io_uring on a raw device and NVMe](#io_uring-on-a-raw-device-and-nvme). Power cuts come with [Real-cluster file runs](#real-cluster-file-runs).

## Real-cluster histories

The [crash test](#crash-tests-on-real-disks) records its run in the
[history recorder](#history-recorder)'s words, as the [design](design.md#testing-strategy) sets
out: each process stamps its own operations on `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`, invocation rounded down and
completion up, and appends them to the run's history file, `history` beside the oracle.

- Several client processes: beside the driver, two history clients per child (`TestHistClient`,
  the test binary again with `RS_HIST_CLIENT` naming the history file), started with it and stopped
  by its kill, each one operation at a time: a write of a new 8-byte value, or a read, of a slot,
  the first 8 bytes of one block in chunks 5 and 6. A cycle's clients use 8 new slots and the
  previous cycle's 8, so every slot's history spans a kill and stays short enough to check.
- Every operation is recorded: the driver's changes too, invoked before the command is sent and
  completed when its acknowledgment is read, including those drained after the kill; a client's
  operation in flight at the kill, or sent into a dead pipe, stays with no completion.
- The run ends with `lincheck.Illegal` over the file, read by `sim.ReadHistory`, with a register
  per slot; the driver's changes are left to the oracle. Seed 1, 150 cycles: about 6,800 slot
  reads and 7,000 slot writes, varying with timing, from 302 client processes, 302 never completed,
  linearizable.
- Planted in a scratch copy of the child, the check names the operation at fault on 10 cycles:
  a stale read (every 20th read answered 0) as "client 6's r of slot 21 (written 0x0, read 0x0)",
  and a lost acknowledgment (every 20th slot write acknowledged and not applied) as the later read
  that still saw the value before it, "client 6's r of slot 28 (read 0x60000000a)".
- The history file reads back as the operations written to it, from several clients interleaved,
  and refuses a torn event, an invocation twice and a completion with no invocation
  (`TestAHistoryFileReadsBackAsItsOperations`, `FuzzReadHistory`).
- **Benchmarks:** `BenchmarkHistFile`, one invocation and completion appended to the file, zero
  allocations per operation (876 ns, two clock reads and two writes, in Docker on arm64).
- Clients on several hosts, with their stamps mapped by a measured offset and a history file per
  host, come with [Real-cluster file runs](#real-cluster-file-runs); the crash test runs on one host.

## FUSE protocol codec

From [Daemon restart and upgrade](design.md#daemon-restart-and-upgrade) and the FUSE restart and
handoff spikes.

- Golden frames for each opcode the item names, request and reply, and for the three
  notifications, built by `internal/fuseproto/testdata/golden.c` from the structs of Linux
  6.18.44's `linux/fuse.h` (FUSE 7.45), so the codec's offsets are checked against the kernel's
  header rather than against themselves. Their values are the spikes' `rawfs.c` and `hofs.c`
  exchanges: a resent `LOOKUP` of `hang1` and `MKDIR` of `mkhangdir`, their `unique` built from
  `FUSE_UNIQUE_RESEND`, `FOPEN_DIRECT_IO` opens, 128 KiB `max_write`. Every request decodes to its
  fields, every reply echoes the request's 64-bit `unique` whole, and `inval_inode`, `inval_entry`
  and `NOTIFY_RESEND` encode byte for byte (`TestGoldenRequestsDecode`, `TestGoldenRepliesEncode`).
  The resent requests carry `UniqueResend` over their identity
  (`TestResentRequestsCarryUniqueResend`), and the `READDIRPLUS` reply holds names of 8 and 16
  bytes, which take no padding. A `SETXATTR`'s value, which holds zero bytes, stays in its frame
  after its name, and the body is the 8-byte one a mount without `FUSE_SETXATTR_EXT` gets.
- A `CREATE` carrying the supplementary-groups extension decodes as one without it, the
  extension cut off by the header's `total_extlen`; an `INIT` of 16 bytes, an older kernel's,
  decodes without `flags2`.
- Saved `INIT` parameters round-trip, and changing any one field of the kernel's offer or the
  daemon's answer gives parameters that decode to the change and compare unequal
  (`TestParamsRoundTripAndDifferInEveryField`).
- A truncated header, a length that disagrees with the frame or with `total_extlen`, an unknown
  opcode, a name without its terminating zero, bytes after a name, a `WRITE` or `SETXATTR` whose data
  disagrees with its size, a `BATCH_FORGET` count past the frame and every fixed body one byte short or long
  are errors with the header still decoded, so the request can be answered `ENOSYS` or `EIO`,
  never panics (`TestMalformedFramesAreErrors`). **[property]** `FuzzDecode` from every golden
  request and `FuzzDecodeParams`: no panic, names without a zero, a `WRITE`'s data its size, and
  saved parameters re-encoding to their bytes. `FuzzDecode` also decodes each input with its
  header's length patched to the input's, so a shorter or longer body reaches the body decoders.
- The kernel's side, which the [simulated FUSE clients](#simulated-fuse-clients) speak:
  `AppendRequest` encodes `INIT`, `LOOKUP`, `GETATTR`, `OPEN`, `READ`, `WRITE`, `FLUSH`, `RELEASE`
  and `FSYNC` to their golden frames byte for byte (`TestGoldenRequestsEncode`), and
  `DecodeReply` with the entry, attribute, open, write, `INIT` and `inval_inode` decoders reads
  the golden replies back to what encoded them (`TestGoldenRepliesDecode`). A frame whose length
  disagrees with its header and a body one byte short or long are `ErrReply`
  (`TestMalformedRepliesAreErrors`). **[property]** `FuzzDecodeReply`: no panic, and every body a
  decoder takes re-encodes to its frame.
- A `WRITE`'s data stays in its frame, at the offset the kernel put it; `READ` and
  `READDIRPLUS` replies are built in place behind a header written last.
- **Benchmarks:** `BenchmarkWrite`, decoding a `WRITE` and encoding its reply, 8.6 ns;
  `BenchmarkLookup`, decoding a `LOOKUP` and encoding its entry, 16 ns; 0 allocations each, as
  `TestDecodeAndReplyAllocateNothing` checks for those, `READDIRPLUS`, `STATFS`, `INIT` with its
  saved parameters, `LINK`, `TMPFILE`, `ACCESS`, `FSYNCDIR`, `RENAME2`, `STATX`, the four xattr
  opcodes and the notifications (Apple M4 Pro).

## Simulated FUSE clients

From [Testing strategy](design.md#testing-strategy) and the [FUSE coherence
spike](design.md#appendix-fuse-coherence-spike).

`sim.Mount` is the kernel side of a mount without `writeback_cache`, each rule citing the function
of `fs/fuse` (or `mm/filemap.c`) it follows in Linux 6.18.44, the spikes' kernel; where torvalds'
v6.18 differs, as in a direct write dropping its pages again after its `WRITE`s, it follows
6.18.44. It sends `INIT` first and requests as frames (`fuseproto.AppendRequest`), which the
daemon reads with `Read`, and takes replies and `inval_inode` through `Write`, refusing a malformed frame, a reply to no request and any other
notification. Its `Process`es open the root directory's files by name, or by node ID without a
`LOOKUP` as a reopen through `/proc/self/fd` does (`OpenInode`), and read, read through a mapping,
write, `fsync` and close them, one system call at a time, each recorded in the history recorder:
the kind and node ID in the first input word, the errno first in the output, then a write's bytes
written, or a read's bytes returned and what its 8-byte words say. The tests' daemon is scripted
in `fuse_test.go`, over files every node's daemon shares; it can hold a reply and write it later,
as a slow daemon thread does. Not modelled: readahead (each missing page is its own `READ`),
`FORGET`, `O_APPEND`, creates, other notifications, and `O_TRUNC` or any shrink of a file, which
the close-to-open check cannot yet express: it takes every writer to cover the whole file, so a
read past a shrunk end would count as short.

- **T1 to T6 replayed** (`TestTheCoherenceSpikeReplays`), in the spike's order on its file of
  64 KiB of A, with its daemon's hour-long timeouts and the data version as `mtime`, give the
  spike's outcomes: a cached handle stale after another node's write (T1), fresh after
  `inval_inode` (T2), refilled by its old handle and stale again (T3), a new direct handle fresh
  and the old cached one stale until the node's own direct write (T4), revalidated on each read
  with an attribute timeout of 0, one `READ` and two `GETATTR` for two reads (T5), mapped pages
  stale until `inval_inode` (T5b), a churned change counter revalidating a write that kept the
  version (T5c), and stale pages dropped by an open without `keep_cache` (T6).
- **The page cache** (`TestWritesGoThroughThePageCache`, `TestASizeChangeDropsThePages`,
  `TestEntryAndAttributeTimeouts`): a whole page written is cached, a part of an uncached page is
  read from the daemon later, the read after a write fetches the attributes again, a direct write
  drops the pages under it before its `WRITE`s and again after them, so a page a cached read
  filled while they were out goes too (`fs/fuse/file.c` `fuse_direct_io`), a size change drops
  every page with `mtime` unchanged, and a name is looked up again once its entry timeout passes
  and attributes once theirs does.
- **A read's record** (`TestAReadRecordsWhatItsWordsSay`): the least ID among its words that are
  not zero, a word holding another offset counting as ID 0, and the offset of its first zero word,
  or of its end if none is.
- **The close-to-open check** (`sim.CloseToOpen`): every word a handle writes is
  `id<<32 | offset/8`, its ID rising from one writing handle of a file to the next; one handle
  writes a file at a time, over every byte it holds. A read in a handle opened after the close of
  a handle that wrote the file returns as many bytes as that close left in its range, every word
  below that close's end the close's or a later writer's, and every word at its own offset; a
  word past the end may be zero, as a reader beside a writer extending the file sees.
  `TestTheCloseToOpenCheck`: a read of the close's data passes, and so do zeros past its end;
  one with an older word, a zero word before the end or short of the close's size fails, and
  either passes in a handle opened before the close returned; a word at another offset fails
  whenever the handle opened.
- **The size at open** (`TestAReadAfterAnotherNodesCloseSeesItsSizeOnlyWhenTheOpenLooksItUp`): A
  grows a file from one page to three and closes; on B, which cached the size of one page, a
  writer opens and writes two pages, its `WRITE` held, and a reader opens and reads the third
  page. With entries cached for 1 s the read returns nothing and fails the check, whether the
  daemon answered without `keep_cache` alone or also sent `inval_inode` for the attributes, whose
  `GETATTR` the kernel discards while the write past its size is out; with an entry timeout of 0
  the open's `LOOKUP` brings the size and the read returns the page.
- **A reopen without `LOOKUP`** (`TestAReopenWithoutLookupHoldsTheNodesSizeForAWhile`), Tier 1's
  known limit: after A grows the file from one page to three and closes, a reader on B reopening
  it by node ID reads one page, failing the check as the limit allows, and all three of A's once
  the attribute timeout passes. Beside a writer reopened that way, which writes past the old size,
  a reader opened by path reads one page while the write is out, and the writer's three once it
  returns.
- **A late reply** (`TestALateAttributeReplyHidesAnotherNodesClose`): B's `LOOKUP` answered with
  the size before A's close and held lands after a later open's `LOOKUP` was sent, and that open's
  read passes the check because Tier 1's daemon fetches the attributes again for having read the
  later request. Written as fetched, the old size lands first, the kernel drops the fresh reply
  (`attr_version`) and the read fails the check.
- **`inval_inode` at open** (`TestAnInvalInodeAtOpenWouldDropTheSizeAnotherOpenFetches`), the guard
  against that alternative: an open of a changed file on B is answered after A's close, while a
  writer's `LOOKUP` with the fresh size is out; the writer writes past the size it took, and a
  reader opened by path after A's close reads all three pages. Had the daemon sent `inval_inode`
  for the attributes at that open, the kernel would drop the writer's fresh size, and the reader
  would read one page and fail the check.
- **A miss** (`TestAMissIsNotCached`): an open of a missing name answered `ENOENT` is looked up
  again by the next open, which finds the file created since; answered with an entry of node ID 0,
  the next open within its timeout fails with `ENOENT` (`fs/fuse/dir.c` `fuse_lookup`).
- **[property]** `TestFileHistoriesKeepCloseToOpen`: two nodes, two processes each, two files;
  sessions that open by name, read, read through a mapping, `fsync` and write the whole file, one
  writer of a file at a time; the daemons answer requests in any order and hold a quarter of their
  replies to write later in any order, time moves up to 1.5 s at once past the 1 s attribute
  timeout, `max_write` is one to three pages and `big_writes` is off on a quarter of the seeds.
  Tier 1's daemon gives files' entries a timeout of 0, answers an open of a changed file without
  `keep_cache`, and fetches a held reply's attributes again once it has read another request for
  the inode: every history passes over 10,000 seeds, in 2 s. Opens by node ID stay out of it, as
  the known limit lets them read the node's size.
- **[property]** `TestPlantedDaemonsBreakCloseToOpen`, entries cached for 1 s, over 1,000 seeds:
  `keep_cache` after another node's close fails 457 (first seed 1), Tier 1's daemon otherwise 307
  (first 3), and that with `inval_inode` of the attributes at open 5 (first 147).
- **Mutations** of the model, each failing a test above: `keep_cache` ignored, no `auto_inval_data`,
  attributes never fetched again, mapped reads revalidated, direct handles cached, `inval_inode`
  dropping no page, no `FUSE_I_SIZE_UNSTABLE`, no `attr_version` guard, entries never expiring,
  negative entries not kept, readers ignoring page locks, a part page not locked, a whole page not
  uptodate, direct writes dropping no page before their `WRITE`s, or none after them, writes
  leaving attributes fresh, a size change keeping pages, a page copied from its start instead of
  the read's offset, a read's record ignoring offsets or zeros. Of the check: no word check, no
  size check, closes counted late, an open timed from its return, no closes counted, zeros past
  the close's end failing, a word at another offset passing without a close. Of Tier 1's daemon:
  attributes written as fetched, a miss answered with node ID 0, entries cached for 1 s,
  `inval_inode` at open.
- **Cost:** a seed of the property run, about 300 operations, takes under a millisecond.

## Chunk client

From [Data layer: ChunkStore](design.md#data-layer-chunkstore) and
[Sessions and fencing](design.md#sessions-and-fencing).

- A chunk's PG is the top bits of `xxh3_64` of its ID, checked against core's golden vectors for a
  pool of 64 PGs, and its write goes to that PG's primary tagged with the table's epoch and the PG's
  interval; a write crossing a chunk's end is one write per chunk, each completing on its own.
- A connection's first send, and the first after it is lost, is a hello naming the session and
  incarnation, which every write and punch names too.
- A refusal naming a newer table holds the write until the client holds that table, which it asks
  for, and then sends it under its request ID to the primary the table names; a refusal naming
  none, or an answer of unfound, sends it again after a wait that doubles per answer from 100 ms
  to 3.2 s (`TestARefusedWriteBacksOff`), and a late refusal from the primary a new table moved the
  write from sends nothing (`TestALateRefusalFromTheOldPrimaryIsIgnored`). A refusal for space
  completes as `ENOSPC` and is never sent again. A read goes to the primary, again after a refusal,
  and hands the caller its bytes; a read answered unfound completes.
- The client's writes and reads allocate nothing per operation (`BenchmarkClientWrite`,
  `BenchmarkClientRead`).
- **[property]** The request ID rules, checked on every send of seeded runs of writes against
  replicas that answer, refuse for space, refuse with or without a newer table, answer unfound or
  not at all, lose connections and move primaries or leave a PG with none
  (`TestAClientKeepsItsRequestIDRules`), and of one write left unsent behind two windows of others
  (`TestAClientTakesNoIDPastTheWindow`): a send names its own ID at most `RequestWindow` past an
  oldest at or below it, no ID below the oldest lacks a final answer, a write goes again only under
  its ID and never after its final answer, a write completes once, on its first final answer and
  with that answer's status and version, and every byte written completes. Planted, a resend under
  a new ID, a write naming its own ID as the oldest, an oldest past an ID assigned and not sent, a
  refusal taken as final, a write sent again after its final answer, IDs taken past the window and
  a refused write completed OK and sent again each break a rule.
- An epoll event names the whole connection ID: a hang-up of a muted client closed, and its slot
  taken by a new client, after `Wait` reported it closes only the old one
  (`TestAHangUpClosesNoReplacementInItsSlot`).
- **[property]** The [read run](#placement-faults-and-invariants)'s writers as chunk clients, the
  second a new session that starts once every node with a disk up holds the first's fence, each
  client taking the newest table up to 200 ms late
  (`TestChunkClientsWriteAcrossPrimaryChangesAndAFence`): across primary changes, table changes
  and the fence, no acknowledged write is lost, no fenced session's write is applied, every
  chunk's history passes the [consistency check](#consistency-check-of-chunk-histories), and each
  part of a client's request completes once, from a final answer its primary gave to that part,
  with that answer's status and version. Planted in the clients, a resend under a new ID (1 of the
  first 30 seeds) and a write naming its own ID as the oldest (26 of 30) each have a primary answer
  a write stale before its client heard a final answer to it; a refusal taken as final and a
  refused write completed OK and sent again (each 27 of 30) complete a part on an answer that is
  not final, and a write sent again after its final answer completes twice (30 of 30).

## Client sessions

From [Sessions and fencing](design.md#sessions-and-fencing) and the [sessions
model](#sessions-and-fencing-model).

- A client-only node (`rock-solid node -role client`, no devices) starts a session at `rock-solid
  ctl` over TCP and renews it: the one session it started is live past `dead_wait` from its start.
- The holder counts from the send of its last answered renewal, on both clocks, and ends the lease
  on `Resumed`; requests wait while the lease is lapsed and go once a renewal is answered.
- Request IDs rise with every send within a run, a resend included; a restarted daemon starts a new
  session.
- A fence learned from a renewal or a refused write starts a new session.
- A start resent after a lost answer, and one resent to a new leader, give one session; one resent
  once its session is fenced gives a new session. Two daemons started on one node draw their start
  requests independently and get two sessions, even from draws whose first 32 bits match.
- **[property]** The session run's clients are `meta.SessionClient`s, with VMs that stand still,
  leader nodes that start a run at another rate or rise within the headroom, delayed answers and
  lost start answers. Plants `neg-count-from-reply` and `neg-ignore-resumed` fail "no session is
  fenced while its client's own lease still runs", and `neg-fixed-step-check` and
  `neg-window-per-run` fail "the step check never trips for a client that never stood still", on
  the run's seeds. `neg-no-drift` fails the first only in a scenario with exact rate bounds: in the
  run, the leader's bound overshoots by its round trips more than a rise within the headroom, and
  the plant's smaller margin also tightens the step check, so on some seeds (5 of 200) a rise trips
  it, failing the second, safely, since a trip ends the lease.

## Filesystem client

From [Client design](design.md#client-design), [Cache coherence tiers](design.md#cache-coherence-tiers)
and [Key layout](design.md#metadata-layer-metastore). Scripted in `internal/fsclient` against a real
`meta.State`, chunks in memory, each `Txn` checked as a shard checks it; seeded against a real shard
and chunk devices.

- Each namespace operation sends the `Txn` the design's table gives, built by `meta.FS`, with its
  replay key; a failed final check returns `EEXIST`, `ENOENT` or `ENOTEMPTY`; a directory renamed
  over a non-directory is `ENOTDIR` and the reverse `EISDIR`, with nothing sent
  (`TestNamespaceRequestsAnswerTheirChecksErrnos`). A `create` without `O_EXCL` that loses the
  name to another node opens that node's file, `EISDIR` for a directory
  (`TestACreateWithoutExclOpensTheFileAnotherNodeCreatedFirst`).
- A write past `alloc_end` raises it by 1, 2, 4, … up to 16 chunks first, committing the size
  written so far in the same `Txn` (`TestWritesRaiseAllocEndFirstByDoublingSteps`); `close` and
  `fsync` commit size and `mtime = max(last write's time, mtime + 1 ns)`, and a read past the size
  is clamped (`TestCloseCommitsSizeAndMtimeAndReadsAreClamped`).
- `LOOKUP` answers current attributes and a missing name `ENOENT`
  (`TestLookupAnswersCurrentAttributesAndAMissingNameWithENOENT`); an attribute reply fetched
  before a later request for its inode is fetched again
  (`TestAnAttributeReplyFetchedBeforeALaterRequestIsFetchedAgain`); an open after the attributes
  changed is answered without `keep_cache` (`TestAnOpenAfterAChangeDropsTheCache`);
  `READDIRPLUS` lists every name across calls (`TestReaddirplusListsEveryNameAcrossCalls`).
- The first create in a slot waits for one reservation `Txn`; a `mkdir` in a fresh slot creates in
  it with no further reservation (`TestTheFirstCreateInASlotWaitsForOneReservation`).
- The opcodes whose `ENOSYS` the kernel remembers get their per-call answers
  (`TestPerCallAnswersOfOpcodesTheKernelRemembers`); `setattr` changes mode and times and refuses a
  size change (`TestSetattrChangesModeAndTimesAndRefusesASizeChange`).
- A cycle of lookup, getattr, open, write, flush, read and release allocates nothing
  (`TestTheRequestPathAllocatesNothing`).
- The plant `neg-raise-after-write` leaves a chunk past `alloc_end` that the purge of the file,
  unlinked after a crash, misses (`TestAWriteBeforeItsRaiseLeavesAChunkThePurgeMisses`).
- **[property]** `TestAMountsHistoriesKeepTheirInvariantsAcrossCrashes`: one node's `sim.Mount`,
  four processes on two root-directory files as in `TestFileHistoriesKeepCloseToOpen`, against
  three `meta.Shard` replicas over the meta wire and three `node.Device` chunk devices; partitions,
  replicas' nodes rebooted so leaders change, and the daemon crashed, half the time within 3 ms of
  a file's first chunk write, restarting as a new mount that may unlink and create each file
  again. Histories pass close-to-open, every system call succeeds, no inode is handed out twice,
  no `mtime` goes backwards, every file's entry is in its directory's slot, no directory is its
  own ancestor, and at each daemon crash every chunk written lies below `alloc_end` or within its
  purge entry. Until **MetaStore reads over the wire**, the run serves reads from a replica that
  has applied every entry any replica has. The devices do not crash: a restarted primary asks the
  control plane for a new interval, which the run does not model.
- The plant `neg-raise-after-write` fails "a purge never misses a chunk written before a crash" on
  each of the run's first 30 seeds (`TestARaiseAfterItsChunkWriteFailsTheMountsRun`, seed 1).

## Volume records and the first data group

From [Key layout](design.md#metadata-layer-metastore) and [Sharding](design.md#metadata-layer-metastore).

- `volume/{id}/record` and the counter at `volume/{0}/record` encode as the golden keys say.
- With no shard map, the leader commits one: the control-plane group's entry as its
  configuration, which `PlaceVoters` neither fills onto a storage disk nor counts in any disk's
  load, and the first data group, whose voters `PlaceVoters` fills.
- A create writes the record, the counter past its ID and the root; sent again after its answer was
  lost, it is answered from its replay record and makes one volume; a stale ID fails the counter
  check, whose answer gives the next.
- `rock-solid volume create` reads the membership again while it knows no pool, has no shard map
  or routes to a group with no voter, and refuses a pool the grants do not hold; a create sent and
  never answered fails saying the volume may exist, one never sent does not.
- Over TCP and io_uring: `rock-solid volume create` on one storage node whose shard map gains its
  data group, a second create taking the next ID, and both the group and the volumes kept across a
  restart of the node and the control plane.

## FUSE mount on one node

From [Client design](design.md#client-design) and [Daemon restart and
upgrade](design.md#daemon-restart-and-upgrade)'s mount settings.

- `INIT` negotiates `FUSE_PARALLEL_DIROPS` and `auto_inval_data`, and never `writeback_cache`, a
  request timeout or FUSE over io_uring.
- Through the kernel, on `rock-solid ctl` and one `rock-solid node` over a file-backed disk: create,
  write, read back, close, reopen from another process and read the same bytes, unlink, `ls`.
- Another uid reads the mount (`allow_other`).
- `testing.AllocsPerRun` of a request's path through the driver and the machine is 0.

## Inode owner's open registry

From [Inode owner](design.md#metadata-layer-metastore) and the [purge model](#purge-model).

- `open` costs one round trip and no log write; `release` deregisters.
- An unlink of a file open on another node makes it an orphan, purged at its last close.
- A fenced session's opens are dropped only once its fence version is acknowledged.
- **[property]** "An orphaned inode is never freed while a live session has it open" on seeded
  three-node runs; plants `neg-unlink-open` and `neg-release-on-commit` each fail it.

## Owner failover and grace period

From [Inode owner](design.md#metadata-layer-metastore), the [purge model](#purge-model) and the
[cache-mode recall model](#cache-mode-recall-model).

- The grace period ends once every live session has re-registered, an empty re-registration from a
  node with nothing open counting, or has left the table; never by time alone.
- A session that has not re-registered within a lease is evicted, and the period ends once it is
  fenced.
- During it, new opens wait and an unlink makes an orphan.
- **[property]** Plants `purge/neg-grace-by-time`, `purge/neg-orphan-in-grace`,
  `recall/neg-grace-by-time` and `recall/neg-open-in-grace` each fail their mapped invariant on
  seeded owner failovers with a node partitioned from the new owner.

## Multi-node mounts

- Mounts of one volume on three nodes, one client-only, route every `Txn` to the shard leader on
  another node and follow `NotLeader`.
- **[property]** Seeded runs with failovers, partitions and paused clients: histories pass
  close-to-open.
- Over TCP, in Docker: three node processes, mounts on two, a file written and closed on one read on
  the other.

## Rest of the namespace

From [Key layout](design.md#metadata-layer-metastore) and the Samba spike's xattr counts.

- `link`, `symlink` with a 4,095-byte target in pieces, `readlink`, cross-directory `rename` of a
  file and of a directory, special files.
- A directory renamed under itself is refused; the renamed inode's `ctime` moves.
- A 64 KiB xattr written and read back in pieces; small xattrs answered from the attribute cache
  within its timeout.
- A request resent after a restart whose lookups now fail still reaches its shard and gets its
  replay record's result.

## flock and whole-file locks

From [Cache coherence tiers](design.md#cache-coherence-tiers) and the lock `Txn`s of
[Key layout](design.md#metadata-layer-metastore).

- Open: byte-range `fcntl` locks ([Roadmap and open questions](design.md#roadmap-and-open-questions)).
- Shared and exclusive locks from two nodes; a conversion between modes in one `Txn`; a dead
  session's lock freed by the next holder's `Txn`.
- A blocking request is granted once its holder releases or is fenced.
- **[property]** "At most one lock holder" and "every write of a fenced lock holder that completes is
  ordered before every write of the next holder" on seeded runs.

## Purger

From [Freeing space](design.md#freeing-space) and the [purge model](#purge-model).

- A purge entry's punches go out batched per PG, each naming the shard and its term; a primary that
  has seen a newer term refuses an older one.
- Progress is recorded only once every punch before it completed; a run of entries is removed with a
  check per entry and per gap.
- A punch to a chunk that does not exist succeeds, so a rerun after a crash fails nothing.
- **[property]** "Once a purge settles, no chunk of a deleted inode remains" across elections and
  crashes; plants `neg-missing-punch-fails`, `neg-overwrite-entry`, `neg-progress-before-punch`,
  `neg-purger-no-term`, `neg-unchecked-removal` and a `Delete` without its `Check` each fail it.

## Truncate

From [Freeing space](design.md#freeing-space) and the [purge model](#purge-model).

- A truncate commits size, lowered `alloc_end` and a purge range from the new size's byte offset; the
  purger zeroes the rest of the block and chunk holding the new end and deletes later chunks.
- The purger drains the file through the owner first; an extension over a pending purge waits for it;
  an extending write whose check fails writes its chunk again.
- **[property]** "An extension never exposes a byte a truncate cut off" on seeded runs; plants
  `neg-daemon-punch`, `neg-extend-over-purge`, `neg-no-drain`, `neg-no-rewrite`,
  `neg-skip-partial-block`, `neg-tail-in-memory` and `neg-trunc-at-chunk` each fail it.

## Quotas and statfs

From [Volume size and capacity](design.md#volume-size-and-capacity).

- `statfs` reports the PVC size as total, the slots' sum as used, and as available the smaller of
  the rest and the pool's available figure, cached for `statfs_cache`.
- A write that would extend a file past the PVC size is `ENOSPC` before the grant is looked at.
- Two nodes filling a volume overshoot its size by at most one cache period's writes.

## Write-back buffer under space grants
